lessons.intro: In French, a whole word can turn on a single vowel that English does not even have. This is the deep dive into the twelve everyday vowel sounds: why French vowels stay pure instead of sliding like English ones, and how to finally make the hardest two, the U and the two EU sounds.
lessons.title: Les voyelles, en profondeur

sections.title: Why the vowels carry the meaning
sections.body: Order a coffee in Lyon and ask for tout (all) when you mean tu (you), and the person behind the counter tilts their head. They genuinely cannot tell dessus (on top) from dessous (underneath), or poisson (fish) from poison (poison). In French the whole meaning of a word can ride on one vowel that English has no version of. Vowels here are not decoration, they are load-bearing. Get them close and people relax and understand you. This lesson walks all twelve everyday vowel sounds, slowly, one mouth shape at a time.

sections.title: What you'll master
points: Produce all twelve oral (mouth, not nose) French vowel sounds.
Hear the three e sounds apart: é, è and the light mute e.
Finally say the French U, the sound English simply does not have.
Make the two eu sounds instead of substituting an English 'uh'.
Split the look-alikes: tu and tout, dessus and dessous.
Keep every vowel pure and steady, with no English glide.

sections.title: The one big idea: hold the vowel still
sections.body: In English most long vowels are secretly two sounds glued together. Say 'day' slowly and your mouth slides from 'eh' up into 'ee'. Say 'go' and it slides from 'oh' into 'oo'. That slide is called a glide, and English does it automatically. French vowels are the opposite: they are pure. You pick one mouth shape and hold it dead steady, from the start of the sound to the end. The French é is the start of English 'day', frozen in place before the slide happens. Lock the shape first, then make the sound.

sections.title: Two tricks to kill the glide

hacks.why: Take a mental picture of your mouth (lips and tongue set), then turn on the sound without changing the picture. If your jaw or tongue moves during the vowel, you filmed an English glide by accident.
A short, clean French vowel always beats a long one that slides. Cutting the vowel short leaves no room for the English tail to creep onto the end.

examples.note: Jaw dropped a little, tongue low, lips relaxed. Two clean ah sounds.
Both vowels are the same bright, open ah.
Ends on a pure, open ah, never sliding.

sections.title: The three e sounds
rows: Lips in a slight smile, no slide
Jaw more open, as in bed

sections.title: The three e's in real words

examples.note: Two closed é sounds, both said with a small smile.
The è is the open eh of English bed.
le is the light mute e, and the u is the French U.

sections.title: The accent is a little face

hacks.hack: é points up like a smile.
hacks.why: The mark leans up to the right, like the corner of a smile, and you spread your lips into a smile to say 'ay'.
The mark leans down, so drop your jaw and relax your face for the open 'eh'. The accent literally shows you the mouth.

sections.title: The French U, in four moves
steps: Say 'eee', the French i as in lit. Feel the tongue high and pushed forward, lips spread in a smile.
Freeze the tongue exactly where it is. Do not let it move at all.
Now round and push your lips forward into a tight little circle, as if you were about to whistle or blow out a candle.
Keep the sound going the whole time. Tongue saying 'ee', lips saying 'oo': that collision is the French U.

sections.title: The U family: one recipe, three sounds

hacks.hack: Say EE, then round your lips. That is U [y].
hacks.why: The single most useful trick in beginner French. Do not stop the sound and restart, morph it live while it is still going.

hacks.hack: Say AY and round for closed eu. Say EH and round for open eu.
hacks.why: The two eu sounds are just U's cousins: set a front vowel first, then round the lips. Learn all three as one family and they stop being scary.

sections.title: The lips lie, the tongue tells the truth
points: For both U and OU your lips are rounded and pushed forward. That part is identical.
The whole difference is the tongue: forward for tu [y], pulled back for tout [u].
Slide the tongue, not the lips. This one contrast rescues dessus and dessous, rue and roue.

sections.title: U and OU, side by side

examples.note: Tongue forward, then tongue back. The lips stay the same.

examples.fr: la rue  /  la roue  [lah RÜ / lah ROO]
examples.note: One vowel apart, a completely different word.
Near opposites. French people really do mishear these when the vowel is blurred.

sections.title: The two EU sounds
rows: eu at word end, or before z
eu or œu before a consonant

hacks.why: Say moi like 'mwah', the sound of a kiss. Once you accept that oi is 'wah', dozens of words (moi, toi, trois, boire, voiture) fall into place at once.

errors.why: English has no [y], so the brain grabs 'oo' and the tongue slides back. Keep the tongue in the 'ee' spot.
English 'new' and 'cute' add a 'y' glide. French does not. Round the lips from the first instant, with no run-up.
That little tail is an English glide leaking in. Freeze the vowel and take a mental photo of your mouth.
The spelling looks like English 'oil', but oi is fixed as 'wah'. Memorise the pair, not the letters.

errors.wrong: deux and fleur both said as 'duh'
errors.why: English flattens front rounded vowels to 'uh'. Round the lips and keep the tongue forward.
French usually leaves the final consonant silent. The vowel before it is the real ending.

rows.v: One mouth shape, held still. Photo, not video.
Say EE, keep the tongue forward, round the lips.
Closed eu = say AY and round. Open eu = say EH and round.
é = ay (smile), è = eh (open), plain e = uh (light).
eau and au = oh, oi = wah, ai = eh, ou = oo.
Tongue forward for tu, back for tout. Lips the same.
The nose vowels of pain, bon and un get their own lesson.

questions.q: To make the French U you should:

lessons.intro: French greetings split along one line: tu or vous. Get that right, and « bonjour », « merci » and « au revoir » carry you through almost any first exchange.
lessons.title: Les salutations

examples.note: Formal — a stranger, a shopkeeper, anyone you address as vous.
Informal — friends, family, anyone you’d address as tu.

examples.en: Thank you very much. — You’re very welcome.
examples.fr: Merci beaucoup. — Je vous en prie.
examples.note: The formal reply to merci; de rien is the everyday one.

cases.fr: Bonjour, une baguette, s’il vous plaît.

errors.why: Salut is strictly informal — using it with someone you’d address as vous reads as overly familiar.
De rien is casual; the formal reply to merci in a professional context is je vous en prie.
French switches to bonsoir once evening starts — bonjour then sounds like you didn’t notice the time.

questions.q: You’re greeting your boss at 9am. You say…
Which is the informal way to say goodbye?
A colleague says « Merci beaucoup » at work. The formal reply is…
« Comment allez-vous ? » is asked…
opts: To someone you address as vous

segments.text: Hi, I’m Camille. Today we’ll learn the three French phrases you’ll use in almost every conversation: hello, thank you, and goodbye.
Bonjour !
That’s “bonjour”. It works any time from the morning until early evening, with anyone.
Before we go further, one distinction matters more than any single word: how formal you’re being.
French has two ways to say “you”. “Tu” is for friends, family, and people your own age. “Vous” is for everyone else: a stranger, a shopkeeper, someone older than you.
Get that one thing right, and the rest of the conversation takes care of itself.
Listen to a short exchange. First, the formal version, between two people who don’t know each other.
Bonjour madame, comment allez-vous ?
Hello madam, how are you? That’s “comment allez-vous”, the formal way to ask, because it’s spoken to someone you’d address as “vous”.
Now the informal version, between two friends.
Salut ! Ça va bien, merci, et toi ?
Hi! I’m doing well, thank you, and you? Notice it ends in “et toi”, the informal you, because it’s answering a friend.
Let’s build these one at a time. Repeat each line after Camille.
Merci
Au revoir
Enchanté
Your turn, from English to French. Someone you don’t know greets you in the evening. What do you say back?
And if a friend asks how it’s going, casually, how do you answer?

segments.expected: Ça va bien, merci, et toi ?

segments.text: Comment vous appelez-vous ?
Camille just asked, formally, what your name is. If this were the first time you’d met someone, what would you say back, once you’d told them your name?
Quick recap before you go: “bonjour” for hello, “merci” for thank you, “au revoir” for goodbye, “s’il vous plaît” for please, formally. Use “vous” with strangers, “tu” with friends.
That’s enough to greet, thank, and take your leave anywhere in France.
À bientôt !

lessons.title: L'alphabet français
lessons.intro: Every letter's real sound. Learn the French name and the in-word sound of all 26 letters, master the ones that trip up English speakers, and spell your own name and email aloud with total confidence.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.body:
You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start reading it out: P, A, U, L. There is a long pause. She heard pay, ah, oo, ell, and wrote down something completely different, because in French the letter you call AY is actually E, and the letter you call EE is I. Two minutes later you still do not have your confirmation.

That exact moment happens to travellers every day: dictating an email, spelling a last name at a pharmacy, giving a booking reference. The good news: this is a small, closed skill. There are only 26 letters, they never change, and once you own them you can spell anything in French.
sections.say: Here is a moment that catches almost every learner off guard. You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start spelling: P, A, U, L. And there is a long pause. She wrote down something completely different, because the letter you call AY is actually the French E, and the letter you call EE is the French I. The good news? This is a small, closed skill. Twenty six letters, they never change, and after this lesson you will own every one of them.

sections.title: What you'll master
points: Say the French name of all 26 letters, the way a French person spells out loud.
Tell a letter's NAME (for spelling) from its SOUND (inside words), the mix-up beginners make most.
Handle the ambush letters: E, G, H, I, J, R, U, W, Y and the vowels.
Say double vé for W and i grec for Y like a local, instead of guessing.
Spell your own name out loud in French, slowly and clearly.
Dictate an email address in French, including the @, the dot, and the tricky letters.
Recognise the French alphabet song and why its ending sounds different.
sections.say: By the end of this lesson you will be able to name all twenty six letters the French way, keep a letter's name and its sound in separate boxes, survive the ambush letters, and spell your own name and email out loud, slowly and clearly, like a local.

sections.title: The core concept: name versus sound
sections.body:
A letter has two completely separate jobs, and beginners jam them together.

The NAME of a letter is what you say when you spell a word out loud, letter by letter. The SOUND is the noise it makes inside a word: the B in boat does not go bee, it goes a short buh.

French works the same way. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a French word aloud, you use sounds.

KEY RULE: Spelling out loud = letter NAMES. Reading a word = letter SOUNDS. Different tools for different jobs.
sections.say: Here is the one idea that fixes half your mistakes. A letter has two separate jobs. Its name is what you say when you spell out loud. Its sound is the noise it makes inside a word. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a word aloud, you use sounds. Keep those two jobs in separate boxes in your head, and most of the confusion disappears.

sections.title: How sounds are written here

rows.v: The precise symbols in slashes, like /a/. An anchor, not homework.
A plain English hint: ah as in father.
A respelling with the stressed syllable in CAPS: bonjour is [bon-ZHOOR].
The soft buzz in the middle of measure or vision. The key to G and J.

sections.say: A quick note on how sounds are written in this lesson. Every sound appears three ways: the precise phonetic symbol in slashes, a plain sounds-like hint, and a respelling in brackets with the stressed syllable in capitals. One special code to remember: z h means the soft buzzy sound in the middle of measure. Hold onto that, it is the key to the letters G and J.

sections.title: The 26 letters, name and sound

letters.name: [ah]
letters.memo: Open, pure ah. Never the English ay.

letters.name: [bay]
letters.memo: AY family: B C D G P T V all rhyme on the phone.

letters.name: [say]
letters.sound: k before A O U, s before E I Y
letters.memo: The soft and hard C rule is pattern 3 in the Pattern Bank.

letters.name: [uh]
letters.memo: The number one trap: E is uh. The letter that says ee is I.

letters.name: [zhay]
letters.sound: hard g before A O U, soft zh before E I Y
letters.memo: G goes AY, J goes EE. Both buzz like the s in measure.

letters.name: [ahsh]
letters.memo: It has a name but never a sound. No breathy puff, ever.

letters.name: [ee]
letters.memo: Clean, flat ee. Never the English eye.

letters.name: [zhee]
letters.memo: Sounds close to the English name for G. The great swap.

letters.name: [kah]
letters.memo: Rare in French, behaves like English k.

letters.name: [pay]
letters.memo: AY family. Confirm it with a helper word: P comme Pierre.

letters.name: [koo]
letters.sound: k, the U after it goes silent
letters.memo: QU is just k. Quatre is [KATR], never koo-AT-ruh.

letters.name: [air]
letters.memo: Made at the back of the throat, a soft scrape. Feeling strange is normal.

letters.name: [ess]
letters.memo: Between two vowels S turns to z: maison [meh-ZOHN].

letters.name: [ew]
letters.memo: Say EE, freeze your tongue, round your lips. Not oo.

letters.name: [DOO-bluh-vay]
letters.sound: v in old borrowings, w in new ones
letters.memo: Double vé means double V. Never double-you.

letters.name: [eeks]
letters.memo: ks in taxi, gz in examen, silent at the end of most words.

letters.name: [ee-GREK]
letters.memo: The name means Greek I. Nothing to do with why.

letters.name: [zed]
letters.memo: Zède, like British zed, never American zee.

sections.say: This is the master grid, all twenty six letters. Tap any letter to open its card: you will hear its French name, see the sound it makes inside words, and get an example. Take your time here. And watch the AY family: B, C, D, G, P, T and V all rhyme, which is exactly why they cause email disasters on the phone.

sections.title: The letters that ambush you

cards.label: THE TRAP · E
cards.head: E is [uh], never ee
cards.body: Its name is a soft uh: relaxed, half-open mouth. The English instinct is to call E ee, but that is the French letter I. Inside words French E is often so light it nearly vanishes. Burn it in: E is uh, I is ee.

cards.label: THE TRAP · G and J
cards.head: The great swap
cards.body: In English, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it: G is [zhay], J is [zhee]. Both start with the soft zh of measure, with no hidden d at the front. Remember: G goes AY, J goes EE.

cards.label: THE TRAP · H
cards.head: Always silent, every time
cards.body: The letter is named [ahsh], but inside words it makes no sound at all. Hôtel opens on the O. Heure, the hour, is [ur]. Never puff air for a French H.

cards.label: THE TRAP · R
cards.head: The throaty one
cards.body: Its name is [air], but the sound lives at the back of the throat, near where you gargle: a soft scrape, not the American tongue-curl. Try a gentle kh, as if lightly clearing your throat, then soften it. Feeling strange at first is completely normal.

cards.label: THE TRAP · U
cards.head: The tight whistle vowel
cards.body: English does not have it. The trick that works: say ee as in see, freeze your tongue exactly where it is, then push your lips into a tight kiss shape. Tongue says ee, lips say oo. That collision is U. It is never oo: tu is [tew], not too.

cards.label: EASY WIN · I
cards.head: Just ee
cards.body: Worth stating because of the E and I swap: the letter I is named [ee] and usually sounds ee in words. Clean and flat, no glide.

cards.label: THE BORROWED ONE · W
cards.head: Double vé
cards.body: French borrowed W, so they literally call it double V: [DOO-bluh-vay]. Not double-you. In older borrowings it sounds like v, in newer English ones like w: le week-end.

cards.label: THE GREEK ONE · Y
cards.head: I grec
cards.body: The name means Greek I, because the letter arrived from Greek. Say [ee-GREK]. In words it acts like a French I or a y glide.

cards.label: THE LAST ONE · Z
cards.head: Zède
cards.body: The name is [zed], like British English, never American zee.

sections.say: These are the traps, the letters that ambush English speakers. Spend most of your time here. Swipe through each card, listen, and say each French word out loud. The two biggest offenders: E, which is uh and never ee. And the great G J swap: G goes AY, J goes EE.

sections.title: Vowels: French versus English

detail.title: A is [ah]
detail.body: French A is an open, pure ah, as in father. Never the English ay. Ami, the friend, is [ah-MEE].

detail.title: E is [uh]
detail.body: A soft uh with a relaxed mouth, often nearly silent inside words. The English ee belongs to the letter I. Le is [luh].

detail.title: I is [ee]
detail.body: A clean, flat ee with no glide. English I is a diphthong, eye. French I never glides. Ici, here, is [ee-SEE].

detail.title: O is [oh]
detail.body: Similar to English, but tighter, with no glide at the end. Hôtel is [oh-TELL].

detail.title: U is [ew]
detail.body: No English twin. Say ee, freeze your tongue, round your lips as if to whistle. Tu is [tew], never too.

detail.title: Y is i grec
detail.body: Named Greek I after its origin. Nothing to do with why. In words it sounds ee or glides like y: yoga, [yo-GAH].

sections.say: English vowel letters are lazy and change constantly. French vowels are stable and clean. Tap any row to open that vowel's card and hear it. Your English autopilot will read A as ay, I as eye and E as ee. All three are wrong in French. Retrain them: A is ah, E is uh, I is ee.

cards.label: 7 · CAKE

cards.label: 8 · GIRAFFE
cards.body: Here G is the soft zh, because it comes before I. Same letter, two sounds.

cards.label: 9 · DAY
cards.body: Buzzy J, throaty R.

cards.label: 10 · THANK YOU

cards.label: 11 · HI
cards.body: The final T is silent; the word ends on U.

cards.label: 12 · YES
cards.body: O and U glide together into wee.

cards.label: 13 · WINE
cards.body: V is easy; the in is nasal, roughly van through the nose. Nasals get their own lesson.

cards.label: 14 · ZERO
cards.body: Z like English z, then a light R.

cards.label: 15 · YOGURT
cards.body: Y as a y glide.

cards.label: 16 · KILO
cards.body: K is rare in French but behaves like English k.

cards.label: 17 · TAXI
cards.body: X sounds ks here.

cards.label: 18 · EXAM
cards.body: Here X sounds gz, softer. Same letter, second sound.

cards.label: 19 · FOUR
cards.body: QU is just k; the U is silent after Q.

cards.label: 20 · WEEKEND
cards.body: A modern borrowing: W sounds like English w.

cards.label: 21 · CARRIAGE
cards.body: An older borrowing: W sounds like v.

cards.label: 22 · CHEESE
cards.body: Ends on the buzzy zh, the G sound.

sections.say: Twenty two everyday words showing the tricky letters in real context. Each word gets its own card: tap to hear it, then say it out loud yourself. Watch cards seven and eight closely. The same letter G makes two different sounds depending on the letter after it. That rule, and its friends, live in the Pattern Bank coming up.

sections.title: The sound ladder
sections.hint: Climb one rung at a time

cards.label: RUNG 1 · SINGLE SOUND
cards.head: Just the U
cards.body: The tight rounded ee. Hold it for two full seconds.

cards.label: RUNG 2 · SYLLABLE
cards.head: R plus U
cards.body: Throaty R straight into U. Two of the hardest French sounds, back to back.

cards.label: RUNG 3 · SHORT WORD
cards.head: A real word
cards.body: Same syllable, now a word you will read on every street corner.

cards.label: RUNG 4 · LONGER WORD
cards.head: A full mouth workout
cards.body: Silent H, throaty R in the middle, two rounded vowels.

cards.label: RUNG 5 · FULL PHRASE
cards.head: Put it all together
cards.sub: [zha-BEET roo duh la GAR] · I live on Station Street
cards.body: Buzzy J, silent H, and the throaty R twice. If you can say this, the scary letters are yours.

sections.say: Time to climb the sound ladder. Five rungs, each one adding a little difficulty. Start with a single sound, end with a full phrase. Tap each card to hear it, repeat it out loud, and only move up when the rung below feels easy.

sections.title: Pattern bank
sections.hint: Reusable rules, swipe through all ten

cards.label: PATTERN 1
cards.head: H is always silent
cards.body: Hotel, hour, man. Never puff air.

cards.label: PATTERN 2
cards.head: Final E is usually silent or a faint uh
cards.body: Do not say ee at the end.

cards.label: PATTERN 3
cards.head: C: s before E I Y, k before A O U
cards.body: This, cinema, coffee. One of the two highest-value sound rules in French.

cards.label: PATTERN 4
cards.head: G: soft zh before E I Y, hard g before A O U
cards.fr: la girafe, le gel, le gâteau
cards.body: Giraffe, gel, cake. The twin of pattern 3. Almost every menu and street sign uses these two.

cards.label: PATTERN 5
cards.head: QU is k, the U goes silent
cards.body: Four, who, quiche.

cards.label: PATTERN 6
cards.head: CH is sh, not ch
cards.fr: le chat, le chocolat, le chien
cards.body: Cat, chocolate, dog.

cards.label: PATTERN 7
cards.head: The final consonant is usually silent
cards.body: Silent T, silent S, silent D.

cards.label: PATTERN 8
cards.head: But C, R, F, L are often sounded: CaReFuL
cards.fr: le sac, bonjour, le chef, l'hôtel
cards.body: Bag, hello, chef, hotel. Learn the memory word CaReFuL and you will guess final consonants right most of the time.

cards.label: PATTERN 9
cards.head: S between two vowels is z
cards.fr: la rose, la maison, le poison
cards.body: Rose, house, poison.

cards.label: PATTERN 10
cards.head: Double L after I is often a y glide
cards.fr: la fille, la famille, le billet
cards.body: Girl, family, ticket.

sections.say: The Pattern Bank: ten reusable rules for turning letters into sounds, each with three real examples. Patterns three and four, the soft and hard C and G, are the highest-value sound rules in all of French. And pattern eight gives you the memory word careful: C, R, F, L are the final consonants that usually get pronounced.

sections.title: Vocabulary bank
sections.say: The vocabulary bank. Five themes: greetings, food and drink, travel and town, people and home, and handy small words. Tap a theme card to open its own mini deck, then swipe through and say each word aloud. One gem to notice: aujourd'hui, today, looks terrifying but is just your friends stacked together. The O sound, the buzzy J, the throaty R, a silent H, and the U. Every scary piece is a letter you already met.

sections.title: Spell your name like a local
steps: Use the letter NAMES, slowly. Paul becomes: [pay], [ah], [ew], [ell]. Names, not sounds.
Confirm blurry letters with a helper word, because B, C, D, G, P, T, V all rhyme on the phone. The formula is B comme Bernard: B as in Bernard. Any well-known first name works.
For an email, name the symbols too: arobase for @, point for the dot. The full list is two cards away.
sections.say: This is the part that pays for the whole lesson. When French speakers spell something important on the phone, they do three things you should copy. One: they use the letter names, slowly. Two: they confirm blurry letters with a helper word, B comme Bernard, B as in Bernard. Three: for an email they name the symbols too. Let us build each piece.

sections.title: Helper words for blurry letters

detail.title: B comme Bernard
detail.body: B as in Bernard. The AY family blurs on the phone; the helper name rescues it.

detail.title: D comme David
detail.body: D as in David.

detail.title: G comme Georges
detail.body: G as in Georges. Doubly useful, since G and J swap between English and French.

detail.title: P comme Pierre
detail.body: P as in Pierre.

detail.title: T comme Thomas
detail.body: T as in Thomas.

detail.title: V comme Victor
detail.body: V as in Victor.

detail.title: M comme Marie
detail.body: M as in Marie. M and N blur on a bad line.

detail.title: N comme Nicolas
detail.body: N as in Nicolas.

sections.say: The classic French confirmation formula: the letter, then comme, then a well-known first name. B comme Bernard, P comme Pierre. Tap any row to hear it spoken. These helper words are exactly how French people survive the AY family on the phone.

sections.title: Email words you must know

detail.title: arobase, the @
detail.body: The one email word you absolutely cannot skip. Without it you cannot dictate a single address.

detail.title: point, the dot
detail.body: Point carries the structure of every address: point com, point fr.

detail.title: tiret, the hyphen
detail.body: The plain hyphen.

detail.title: tiret bas, the underscore
detail.body: Literally the low hyphen. Many French speakers also just say underscore.

detail.title: en un seul mot
detail.body: All one word, no space. Useful for usernames.

detail.title: minuscule
detail.body: Lower case.

detail.title: majuscule
detail.body: Upper case, a capital letter.

detail.title: point com
detail.body: Dot com, said as one unit.

detail.title: point F R
detail.body: Dot fr, spelled letter by letter: point, eff, air.

sections.say: To dictate an email you also need the symbols. The word you absolutely cannot skip is arobase, the French name for the at sign. If you memorise only one email word, memorise that one. Tap each row to hear the French.

sections.title: The full email, out loud
lines: P comme Pierre, A, U, L
G comme Georges, M, A, I, L
sections.say: A full worked example. Say you want to give the address paul point h, at gmail dot com. Tap each line in order and repeat it. Hear how the helper words rescue the P and the G, and how arobase and point carry the structure. Then rehearse your own email the same way. It takes ninety seconds and it is the single most useful thing you can prepare before you travel.

sections.title: The alphabet song
sections.body:
Yes, there is a French alphabet song, and it uses the same tune as the English ABC song, which is the same tune as Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. French children learn it exactly the way you did.

The difference is the names: a, bé, cé, dé, e, effe, gé, and so on. The ending feels different because W is double vé, Y is i grec and Z is zède, so the final stretch runs: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. It does not rhyme the way the English ending does.

Hum it a few times. The tune is muscle memory you already own; you are just swapping the words.
sections.say: Good news: you already know the tune of the French alphabet song. It is Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, same as the English ABC song. Only the words change. Slow down at the unfamiliar ending: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. Singing it a few times is a genuinely good way to lock the order in.

sections.title: Sing along, line by line
lines: a, bé, cé, dé, e, effe, gé
ash, i, ji, ka, elle, emme, enne
o, pé, ku, erre, esse, té, u
vé, double vé, iks, i grec, zède
sections.say: Here are the four lines of the song, letter names written out the French way. Tap each line, listen, then sing it back on the Twinkle Twinkle tune.

sections.title: Common mistakes

cards.label: MISTAKE 1
cards.head: Calling E ee
cards.body: Why it happens: in English the letter E literally says ee, so your mouth defaults to it. Retrain: E is uh, I is ee.

cards.label: MISTAKE 2
cards.head: Calling I eye
cards.body: Why it happens: English I is a diphthong, eye. French vowels do not glide; I is a clean ee.

cards.label: MISTAKE 3
cards.head: Saying G and J the English way
cards.body: Why it happens: English swaps them, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it back and softens both to the measure sound. Say: G goes AY, J goes EE.

cards.label: MISTAKE 4
cards.head: Puffing an h in hôtel
cards.body: Why it happens: English H is breathy and strong. French H makes no sound at all, so the word opens on the next letter.

cards.label: MISTAKE 5
cards.head: Saying French U like oo
cards.body: Why it happens: oo is the closest English sound, so learners grab it. Say ee, then round your lips without moving your tongue.

cards.label: MISTAKE 6
cards.head: Calling W double-you
cards.body: Why it happens: you are translating the English name. French names it after V, not U, because that is what it looks like.

cards.label: MISTAKE 7
cards.head: Calling Y why
cards.body: Why it happens: the English name leaks through. French names it Greek I after its origin. Nothing to do with why.

cards.label: MISTAKE 8
cards.head: Forgetting the word for @
cards.body: Why it happens: nobody teaches it, yet you need it for every email. Memorise it as its own vocabulary word.

sections.say: Eight mistakes almost every English speaker makes, one per card. For each one you get the fix and the reason your mouth wants to make it. The reason matters: once you know why a mistake happens, you can catch yourself before it does.

sections.title: Reading practice

cards.label: WORDS · 1 OF 5
cards.body: Forces the throaty R and the tight U.

cards.label: WORDS · 2 OF 5
cards.body: Buzzy J into throaty R.

cards.label: WORDS · 3 OF 5
cards.body: The silent H, the thing most worth drilling.

cards.label: WORDS · 4 OF 5
cards.body: Hard G before A.

cards.label: WORDS · 5 OF 5
cards.body: The R colours the first syllable.

cards.label: SENTENCE · 1 OF 3
cards.sub: [zhuh ma-PELL pol] · My name is Paul.
cards.body: Your first full sentence with the buzzy J.

cards.label: SENTENCE · 2 OF 3
cards.sub: [zha-BEET roo duh la GAR] · I live on Station Street.
cards.body: Buzzy J, silent H, throaty R twice.

cards.label: SENTENCE · 3 OF 3
cards.fr: Mon email, c'est paul arobase gmail point com.
cards.sub: [mon ee-MEL, say pol a-ro-BAZ zhee-MEL pwan KOM] · My email is paul at gmail dot com.
cards.body: The real-world payoff. Practise it with your own email until it is automatic.

cards.label: DIALOGUE · THOMAS
cards.head: Booking a table in Lyon
cards.sub: [bon-ZHOOR, say ta kell NOHN] · Hello, under what name?
cards.body: Restaurants ask à quel nom for every reservation. Have your name ready to spell.

cards.label: DIALOGUE · AMIRA
cards.fr: C'est Amira. A, M, I, R, A.
cards.sub: [say ta-mee-RA. ah, emm, ee, air, ah] · It is Amira. A, M, I, R, A.
cards.body: She spells slowly, using letter NAMES, not sounds.

cards.label: DIALOGUE · THOMAS
cards.sub: [treh byan. ay votr ee-MEL] · Very good. And your email?

cards.label: DIALOGUE · AMIRA
cards.fr: amira point k arobase mail point fr.
cards.sub: [a-mee-RA pwan kah a-ro-BAZ mel pwan eff-AIR] · amira.k at mail.fr
cards.body: Point for the dot, arobase for @, and point F R for the ending.

sections.say: Reading practice, three levels. Five isolated words, three simple sentences, then a real mini dialogue: Amira booking a table by phone in Lyon, spelling her name and her email. Tap each card to hear the French, then read it aloud yourself before you swipe on.

sections.title: Speaking drills
sections.say: Speaking drills. Tap each word to hear it, say it out loud, then grade yourself: got it, or missed it. Your answers feed your review deck, so accurate grading means better practice later.

sections.title: Minimal pairs
sections.hint: Feel your mouth change between the two

cards.label: PAIR 1
cards.head: E versus I, as names
cards.body: The number one spelling mix-up. Say both and feel the difference.

cards.label: PAIR 2
cards.head: tu versus tout
cards.body: Rounded U against plain oo.

cards.label: PAIR 3
cards.head: G versus J, as names
cards.body: The great swap, side by side.

cards.label: PAIR 4
cards.head: dessus versus dessous
cards.body: U versus OU changes the meaning: above versus below.

cards.label: PAIR 5
cards.head: rue versus roue
cards.body: Street versus wheel. The vowel is the only difference.

cards.label: PAIR 6
cards.head: ces versus si
cards.body: The C name against the I sound.

sections.say: Minimal pairs: six pairs of sounds that English speakers blur. Say each pair out loud and feel your mouth change between the two. If a pair sounds identical when you say it, slow down and exaggerate the difference until it splits.

sections.title: Shadowing
lines: Mon email, c'est... arobase... point com.
sections.say: Shadowing: tap each line, then say it three times, matching a smooth rhythm. These are the three sentence starters you will actually use: introducing yourself, saying where you live, and giving your email.

sections.title: Memory hacks

cards.label: HACK 1
cards.head: E = uh, I = ee
cards.body: The one swap that fixes the most mistakes. Chant it.

cards.label: HACK 2
cards.head: G goes AY, J goes EE
cards.body: Rescues the great G J flip. Both buzz like measure.

cards.label: HACK 3
cards.head: French U: say EE, freeze, round your lips
cards.body: Tongue says ee, lips say oo, like you are about to whistle.

cards.label: HACK 4
cards.head: H is a silent ghost
cards.body: It has a name, [ahsh], but never a sound. Words starting with H open on the next letter.

cards.label: HACK 5
cards.head: W is double vé, Y is i grec
cards.body: Two descriptive names: double V and Greek I. Nail these and you instantly sound fluent.

cards.label: HACK 6
cards.head: CaReFuL
cards.body: C, R, F, L: the final consonants that usually get pronounced. Everything else at the end is usually silent.

cards.label: HACK 7
cards.head: arobase = @
cards.body: The one email word people forget. Rehearse your own email out loud before you need it.

cards.label: HACK 8
cards.head: Sing it to Twinkle Twinkle
cards.body: You already own the tune; just swap in the French names and slow down at double vé, iks, i grec, zède.

sections.say: Eight memory hacks, one per card. These are the tricks a good teacher slips you at the end of class. If you keep only three: E is uh and I is ee. G goes AY, J goes EE. And arobase is the at sign.

sections.say: Practice flashcards. Answer out loud, tap the card to flip it, then grade yourself. The effort of recalling is what makes it stick.

sections.title: Round-up
sections.body: Bravo! You just took the French alphabet apart and put it back together. You know every letter's name, the sounds behind them, and how to spell your own name and email out loud like a local. One short quiz stands between you and the finish line.
points: A letter has a NAME for spelling aloud and a SOUND inside words. Keep them separate.
The big swap: E is [uh], I is [ee]. Fixing this alone prevents most spelling errors.
G is [zhay], J is [zhee], both buzzing like measure.
H is always silent. U is a rounded ee, not oo. R lives in the back of the throat.
W is double vé, Y is i grec, Z is zède.
To dictate an email: letter names, helper words like B comme Bernard, arobase and point.
Rehearse your own name and email out loud. Ninety seconds now saves a frustrating phone call later.
sections.say: Bravo! You have taken the whole French alphabet apart and put it back together. Before the quiz, here are your key takeaways. Names for spelling, sounds for reading. E is uh, I is ee. G goes AY, J goes EE. H is silent. And when it is time to give your email: arobase. Ready? The quiz is one tap away. Bonne chance!

questions.q: How do you say the letter E when spelling out loud?
questions.why: E is the soft uh. The letter that says ee is I.

questions.q: Which letter is named i grec?
questions.why: Y means Greek I, reflecting its origin.

questions.q: The French name for W is:
questions.why: French names it after V, double V, not after U.

questions.q: In hôtel, the H is:
questions.why: French H is always silent inside words; the word opens on O.

questions.q: Which word contains the tight, rounded French U?
questions.why: tu is [tew] with the rounded U. The others are plain oo.

questions.q: G before the letter I, as in girafe, sounds like:
questions.why: G before E, I, Y softens to zh; before A, O, U it stays hard.

questions.q: Odd one out: which word has NO open ah sound?
questions.why: tu has the U sound and no A; the others all contain ah.

questions.q: The French name for the letter J is:
questions.why: J is [zhee]; G is [zhay]. English swaps them.

questions.q: To dictate an email, the @ sign is said as:
questions.why: arobase is @. point is the dot, tiret is a hyphen.

questions.q: A learner spells I, C, I as eye, say, eye. The fix is:
questions.why: I is [ee], not eye, and C is [say].

questions.q: Which pair shows the correct French letter names?
questions.why: The core swap to memorise: E is uh, I is ee.

questions.q: quatre is pronounced:
questions.why: QU is k with a silent U, and the final E is nearly silent.

segments.text: Bonjour !
Welcome to your very first Sons lesson. Today we take apart the French alphabet: all twenty six letters, their real names, and the sounds they make inside words.

Picture this: you are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, spelling your email. You say the letters the English way, and the receptionist writes down something completely different. By the end of this lesson, that can never happen to you again.
One idea fixes half your mistakes: a letter has a NAME, for spelling out loud, and a SOUND, the noise it makes inside a word. They are different tools for different jobs.
Our focus today: the letter names, the traps, and spelling your own name and email aloud.
The biggest trap first. In French, the letter E is a soft uh, never ee. The letter that says ee is I. Listen: the word for I, the pronoun, is:
je
That soft ending is the French E. Now the great swap: G is zhay, J is zhee, both buzzing like the s in measure. Listen to the hard and soft G, cake then giraffe:
le gâteau, la girafe
And the silent ghost: H has a name, ahsh, but inside a word it makes no sound at all. The hotel:
l'hôtel
No puff of air. The word opens straight on the O.
Your turn. Repeat after me, slowly. First, the pronoun I:
je
Now thank you, with the French R colouring the first syllable:
merci
And the scariest-looking word that is secretly all your friends: today.
aujourd'hui
Now the payoff. Spell your own first name out loud, letter by letter, using the French names. Slowly. Remember: E is uh, I is ee.
Beautiful. Now say the French word for the at sign, the one you need for every email address:
Quick check. Which letter says ee when you spell out loud: E, or I?
And the French name for W?

Your cheat sheet: names for spelling, sounds for reading. E is uh, I is ee. G goes AY, J goes EE. H is silent. U is a rounded ee. W is double vé, Y is i grec, and the at sign is arobase. Spell your name and email out loud once before you travel, and you are ready.
Bravo, à bientôt !

items.prompt: Il y a une table dans ___ salon.

items.fr: Le pour le masculin, la pour le féminin, l' devant une voyelle.
items.en: Use le for masculine nouns, la for feminine nouns, and l' before a vowel.

items.prompt: Quand utiliser « le », « la » ou « l' » ?

« pain » is masculine, so the partitive is « du », not « de la ».

items.fr: Devant une quantité non comptée : du au masculin, de la au féminin, des au pluriel.
items.en: Use partitive articles for unspecified quantities: du (masculine), de la (feminine), des (plural).

items.en: We have two hours of English on Tuesdays.
items.notes: « deux heures de » + matière ; « de » devient « d' » devant une voyelle.
items.prompt: Nous avons deux heures ___ anglais le mardi.

items.notes: « fort en » + matière, sans article : fort en maths, fort en géographie.
items.prompt: Je suis fort en la géographie.

items.en: I have been studying Spanish for two years.
items.notes: Avec « depuis », une action qui continue se met au présent, pas au passé composé.
items.prompt: J'ai étudié l'espagnol depuis deux ans.

items.fr: Pour une matière, on utilise « faire de » : faire des maths, faire de l'anglais.
items.en: Use « faire de » + subject to say you do or study a subject.
items.notes: Ex : Je fais des maths. · Elle fait de l'histoire. · Nous faisons de la chimie.
items.prompt: « faire de » ou « faire le » avec une matière ?

items.notes: Abréviation très courante de « les mathématiques ».
Une bourse d'études : aide financière pour étudier.
Toujours au pluriel : les frais.

items.fr: Il s'est inscrit à la faculté de droit.
items.en: He enrolled at the law faculty.
items.notes: « s'inscrire à » + établissement ou cursus.
items.prompt: Il s'est inscrit ___ la faculté de droit.

items.fr: Si je réussis mes partiels, je passerai en troisième année.
items.en: If I pass my midterm exams, I will move up to third year.
items.notes: Après « si » + présent, la principale se met au futur simple.
items.prompt: Si je réussis mes partiels, je ___ en troisième année.

items.notes: Verbe pronominal : auxiliaire être et accord du participe.

items.en: you will pass, you will succeed

items.fr: Je vais assister au cours de sociologie demain.
items.en: I am going to attend the sociology class tomorrow.
items.notes: « assister à » = être présent à ; ici « à + le » devient « au ».
items.prompt: Je vais assister le cours de sociologie demain.

items.fr: Passer un examen, c'est le faire ; réussir un examen, c'est l'avoir.
items.en: Passer un examen means to take an exam, not to pass it; réussir un examen means to pass it.
items.notes: Ex : Je passe mon examen lundi. · Elle a réussi son examen. · Il a raté son partiel.
items.prompt: « passer un examen » ou « réussir un examen » ?

items.notes: Abréviation de « la faculté », très courante chez les étudiants.
« Nous » et « manquer » remplacent « on » et « rater » à l'écrit soigné.
items.prompt: « On a raté le cours. » · en soutenu

items.notes: Féminin : une chercheuse.

items.fr: Elle rédige un mémoire sur l'intelligence artificielle.
items.en: She is writing a dissertation on artificial intelligence.
items.notes: « un mémoire sur » + sujet traité.
items.prompt: Elle rédige un mémoire ___ l'intelligence artificielle.

items.fr: Les résultats ont été publiés dans une revue scientifique.
items.en: The results were published in a scientific journal.
items.notes: Passif au passé composé : « ont été » + participe passé accordé.
items.prompt: Les résultats ___ été publiés dans une revue scientifique.

items.en: they were conducting, they were leading
items.notes: Utile dans « mener des recherches ».

items.fr: Il a publié son article dans une revue scientifique.
items.en: He published his article in a scientific journal.
items.notes: « Revue » est féminin : une revue scientifique.
items.prompt: Il a publié son article dans un revue scientifique.

items.fr: Un mémoire est un travail de recherche ; la mémoire est la faculté de se souvenir.
items.en: Un mémoire (masculine) is a dissertation; la mémoire (feminine) is memory.
items.notes: Ex : Il rédige un mémoire. · Elle a une bonne mémoire. · Mon mémoire porte sur la chimie.

items.fr: La recherche désigne le domaine en général ; des recherches désignent des travaux précis.
items.en: La recherche (singular) is research as a field; des recherches are specific investigations.
items.notes: Ex : Il travaille dans la recherche. · Elle mène des recherches sur le climat. · La recherche avance vite.
« Bosser » est l'équivalent familier de « travailler ».
items.prompt: « travailler sur sa thèse » · en familier

items.fr: Mon téléphone n'a plus de batterie, je dois le recharger.
items.en: My phone has no battery left, I need to charge it.
items.notes: Après « plus de », le nom s'emploie sans article.
items.prompt: Mon téléphone n'a plus de ___, je dois le recharger.

items.fr: Éteins ton écran avant de dormir.
items.en: Turn off your screen before going to sleep.
items.notes: « Écran » est masculin, donc « ton », pas « ta ».
Participe passé irrégulier : éteint.

items.fr: J'ai un problème avec la batterie de mon ordinateur.
items.en: I have a problem with my computer's battery.
items.notes: « Batterie » est féminin : la batterie.
items.prompt: J'ai un problème avec le batterie de mon ordinateur.

items.notes: « Téléphone » est masculin : mon téléphone.

items.fr: Pour un appareil, on dit allumer et éteindre, pas ouvrir ou fermer.
items.en: For a device, you say allumer (turn on) and éteindre (turn off), not open or close.
items.notes: Ex : J'allume la télé. · Elle éteint son ordinateur. · N'oublie pas d'éteindre la lumière.
« Un truc » est familier ; « un appareil » est le mot neutre.
On dit aussi un mail ou un e-mail.
Aussi : to upload = téléverser ou mettre en ligne.

items.fr: Tu peux m'envoyer le lien par courriel ?
items.en: Can you send me the link by email?
items.notes: « Par courriel », comme « par téléphone » : pas d'article après « par ».
items.prompt: Tu peux m'envoyer le lien par ___ ?

items.fr: Je me connecte à Internet tous les jours.
items.en: I connect to the Internet every day.
items.notes: Se connecter à : le verbe demande la préposition « à ».
items.prompt: Je me connecte ___ Internet tous les jours.

items.notes: Verbe pronominal : le pronom « nous » se répète.

items.fr: Le wifi ne marche pas, c'est le problème.
items.en: The wifi is not working, that is the problem.
items.notes: « Problème » est masculin malgré le -e final : le problème.
items.prompt: Le wifi ne marche pas, c'est la problème.

items.fr: On dit sur Internet, sans article et avec une majuscule.
items.en: You say sur Internet, with no article and a capital I.
items.notes: Ex : Je cherche sur Internet. · Elle vend ses photos sur Internet. · J'ai lu ça sur Internet.

items.fr: Les trois se disent ; courriel est le terme officiel, mail est le plus courant.
items.en: All three are used; courriel is the official term, mail is the most common.
items.notes: Ex : J'ai reçu un mail. · Envoie-moi un e-mail. · Elle écrit un courriel à son professeur.
items.prompt: « un mail », « un e-mail » ou « un courriel » ?

items.notes: « Ça bugue » est familier ; « cela dysfonctionne » convient à l'écrit formel.
Au féminin : une abonnée.
Pluriel : des réseaux sociaux.
« Une publication » ou, plus familier, « un post ».

items.fr: Elle a publié sa photo sur Instagram hier soir.
items.en: She posted her photo on Instagram last night.
items.notes: Passé composé de publier : action terminée hier soir.
items.prompt: Elle a ___ sa photo sur Instagram hier soir.

items.fr: Il s'est abonné au compte de ce journaliste.
items.notes: S'abonner à : verbe pronominal suivi de « à » (à + le = au).
items.prompt: Il s'est ___ au compte de ce journaliste.

items.notes: Verbe pronominal : auxiliaire être, accord avec le sujet.

items.fr: Beaucoup de gens soutiennent ce créateur sur les réseaux sociaux.
items.en: Many people support this creator on social media.
items.notes: Anglicisme : « supporter » signifie tolérer ; pour to support, on dit soutenir.
items.prompt: Beaucoup de gens supportent ce créateur sur les réseaux sociaux.

items.fr: J'ai reçu une notification, mais je l'ai ignorée.
items.en: I got a notification, but I ignored it.
items.notes: Le participe passé s'accorde avec le COD placé avant : l' = la notification, donc ignorée.
items.prompt: J'ai reçu une notification, mais je l'ai ignoré.

items.fr: On dit sur les réseaux sociaux, comme sur Facebook ou sur TikTok.
items.en: You say sur (on) social media, just like sur Facebook or sur TikTok.
items.notes: Ex : Elle est très active sur les réseaux sociaux. · Je l'ai vu sur Instagram. · Il poste tous les jours sur TikTok.
items.prompt: « sur » ou « dans » les réseaux sociaux ?

items.notes: « Balancer » est familier ; « publier » est le verbe neutre.
Faire la une = to make the front page. Pas d'élision : la une.

items.fr: Ce journaliste a mené une enquête sur la corruption.
items.en: This journalist conducted an investigation into corruption.
items.notes: Mener une enquête sur : collocation fixe du journalisme.
items.prompt: Ce journaliste a mené une ___ sur la corruption.

items.fr: Avant de partager un article, il faut vérifier ses sources.
items.en: Before sharing an article, you have to check its sources.
items.notes: Après « il faut », le verbe reste à l'infinitif.
items.prompt: Avant de partager un article, il faut ___ ses sources.

items.notes: Conditionnel : radical du futur (écrir-) + terminaisons de l'imparfait.

items.fr: L'information est peut-être vraie, mais je ne suis pas sûr que ce soit fiable.
items.en: The information may be true, but I am not sure it is reliable.
items.notes: Après « ne pas être sûr que », on emploie le subjonctif : que ce soit.
items.prompt: L'information est peut-être vraie, mais je ne suis pas sûr que c'est fiable.

items.fr: On utilise selon, d'après ou le conditionnel pour une information non confirmée.
items.en: Use selon, d'après, or the conditional to report unconfirmed information.
items.notes: Ex : Selon le journal, il aurait démissionné. · D'après nos sources, la réunion est annulée. · Le ministre serait en déplacement.
items.prompt: Comment rapporter une information non confirmée ?

items.fr: Nous écoutons de la musique tous les soirs.
items.en: We listen to music every evening.
items.notes: Quantité non comptable : article partitif de la.
items.prompt: Nous écoutons ___ musique tous les soirs.

items.fr: Je joue du piano tous les jours.
items.en: I play the piano every day.
items.notes: On dit jouer de + instrument, jamais jouer + article direct.
items.prompt: Je joue le piano tous les jours.

items.fr: Jouer de + instrument de musique, jouer à + sport ou jeu.
items.en: Use jouer de with musical instruments and jouer à with sports and games.

items.prompt: J'ai vu ce film ___ semaine dernière.

items.en: We watched a movie for two hours.

items.prompt: Nous avons regardé un film pour deux heures.

Abréviation courante : une expo.

items.en: This exhibition is really worth a visit.

items.en: We visited the Louvre for two hours.

items.prompt: Nous avons visité le Louvre depuis deux heures.

items.fr: Les visiteurs doivent acheter leurs billets à l'avance.
items.en: Visitors must buy their tickets in advance.
items.notes: Plusieurs possesseurs et plusieurs objets : leurs, pas ses.
items.prompt: Les visiteurs doivent acheter ses billets à l'avance.

items.fr: Visiter + lieu ; rendre visite à + personne.

items.fr: Fêter est courant et convient aux fêtes familiales ; célébrer est plus formel, souvent officiel ou religieux.

items.notes: Ex : fêter son anniversaire · célébrer un mariage · célébrer la messe

items.fr: Les députés ont voté en faveur de la nouvelle loi.
items.en: The members of parliament voted in favor of the new law.

items.prompt: Les ministres se sont réunis hier pour discuter sur le budget.

items.fr: Après « quand », on emploie le futur si l'action est future.
items.en: After 'quand', use the future tense when the action is in the future (unlike English, which uses the present).

Regular -ir verb: investir conjugates like finir.
Conditional: infinitive + imparfait endings. Do not confuse with the future « je dépenserai ».

items.prompt: L'entreprise a embauché beaucoup des salariés cette année.

items.fr: Après une expression de quantité, on emploie « de » sans article.
items.en: After a quantity expression, use 'de' without an article.

items.notes: « Le fric » is very informal slang; « l'argent » is the neutral everyday word.

items.fr: Bien que la situation soit difficile, des progrès ont été réalisés.

items.notes: « Bien que » always triggers the subjunctive: soit, not est.
items.prompt: Bien que la situation ___ difficile, des progrès ont été réalisés.

items.fr: Le gouvernement a lancé un plan afin de réduire la pauvreté.
items.en: The government launched a plan in order to reduce poverty.
items.notes: « Afin de » + infinitive expresses purpose; more formal than « pour ».

items.notes: Subjunctive after « il faut que »: agir → que nous agissions.
Lutter contre la pauvreté = to fight poverty.

items.fr: Il faut que le gouvernement fasse plus pour les sans-abri.
items.en: The government must do more for the homeless.
items.notes: « Il faut que » requires the subjunctive: fasse, not fait.
items.prompt: Il faut que le gouvernement fait plus pour les sans-abri.

items.fr: Bien que la pauvreté recule, les inégalités augmentent.
items.en: Although poverty is declining, inequalities are increasing.
items.notes: « Malgré que » is widely considered incorrect; use « bien que » + subjunctive, or « malgré » + noun.
items.prompt: Malgré que la pauvreté recule, les inégalités augmentent.

items.fr: « Bien que » est toujours suivi du subjonctif.
items.en: 'Bien que' is always followed by the subjunctive.
items.notes: Ex : Bien que le chômage baisse, la précarité demeure. · Bien qu'il soit riche, il se plaint. · Bien que la loi existe, elle est peu appliquée.

items.fr: Il est difficile de trouver un logement.
items.en: It is hard to find housing.

items.notes: Adopter, voter, promulguer une loi. « Le droit » is the law as a field or a right.
Plural: les tribunaux. Aller au tribunal, comparaître devant le tribunal.
Faire un procès à quelqu'un = to sue someone. Do not confuse with « le processus » (process).

items.fr: L'accusé a été condamné à cinq ans de prison.
items.en: The defendant was sentenced to five years in prison.

items.prompt: L'accusé a été ___ à cinq ans de prison.

items.fr: La loi entrera en vigueur le 1er janvier.
items.en: The law will come into force on January 1st.
items.notes: Fixed legal expression: entrer en vigueur = to take effect.
items.prompt: La loi entrera en ___ le 1er janvier.

items.en: you must comply, you must respect
items.notes: Subjunctive after « il faut que »: respecter → que vous respectiez la loi.

items.en: The researchers formulated a hypothesis that they are going to test in the lab.
items.notes: Collocation clé de la méthode : formuler une hypothèse.
items.prompt: Les chercheurs ont formulé une ___ qu'ils vont tester en laboratoire.

items.fr: Les données ont été analysées afin de confirmer l'hypothèse.
items.en: The data were analyzed in order to confirm the hypothesis.
items.notes: Afin de + infinitif exprime le but en style soutenu.
items.prompt: Les données ont été analysées ___ de confirmer l'hypothèse.

items.notes: Tournure impersonnelle passive, très fréquente dans les articles scientifiques.
items.prompt: démontrer · passé composé, voix passive impersonnelle · il

items.notes: Double i au subjonctif : vérifi + ions.

items.fr: Il faut que nous vérifiions les données avant de publier.
items.en: We must verify the data before publishing.
items.notes: Subjonctif après il faut que : vérifiions avec deux i.
items.prompt: Il faut que nous vérifions les données avant de publier.

items.fr: Les résultats ont été analysés par une équipe indépendante.
items.en: The results were analyzed by an independent team.
items.notes: À la voix passive, le participe s'accorde avec le sujet : analysés.
items.prompt: Les résultats ont été analysé par une équipe indépendante.

items.fr: On emploie par pour l'agent d'une action concrète et de après les verbes de sentiment ou de description.
items.en: Use par for the agent of a concrete action and de after verbs of feeling or description.
items.notes: Ex : L'étude a été menée par une équipe française. · La théorie est connue de tous. · Le laboratoire est entouré de champs.
items.prompt: La voix passive avec « par » ou « de » ?

items.fr: Après il est possible que, on emploie toujours le subjonctif.
items.en: After il est possible que, always use the subjunctive.
items.notes: Ex : Il est possible que l'expérience échoue. · Il est possible que les données soient incomplètes. · Il est possible qu'il faille recommencer.
items.prompt: Quel mode après « il est possible que » ?

items.fr: Cette expérience a été répétée à de nombreuses reprises.
items.en: This experiment was repeated many times.
items.notes: À de nombreuses reprises remplace plein de fois à l'écrit.
items.prompt: « On a testé ça plein de fois » · en soutenu

items.notes: Collocations : faire ou réaliser une découverte.
Découverte par Alexander Fleming en 1928.

items.fr: Marie Curie a découvert le radium, ce qui lui a valu deux prix Nobel.
items.en: Marie Curie discovered radium, which earned her two Nobel Prizes.
items.notes: Ce qui reprend toute la proposition précédente, pas un seul nom.
items.prompt: Marie Curie a découvert le radium, ___ lui a valu deux prix Nobel.

items.fr: La pénicilline a été découverte par hasard par Alexander Fleming.
items.en: Penicillin was discovered by chance by Alexander Fleming.
items.notes: Par hasard est une locution figée signifiant accidentellement.
items.prompt: La pénicilline a été découverte ___ hasard par Alexander Fleming.

items.notes: Participe passé irrégulier : découvert.
Mettre au point signifie développer, perfectionner une invention.

items.fr: Marie Curie a reçu deux prix Nobel pour ses travaux.
items.en: Marie Curie received two Nobel Prizes for her work.
items.notes: Avec avoir, pas d'accord sans COD placé avant : a reçu.
items.prompt: Marie Curie a reçue deux prix Nobel pour ses travaux.

items.fr: Le vaccin contre la rage a été développé par Pasteur.
items.en: The rabies vaccine was developed by Pasteur.
items.notes: Vaccin est masculin, donc développé sans e.
items.prompt: Le vaccin contre la rage a été développée par Pasteur.

items.fr: À l'écrit soutenu, on emploie le passé simple pour les faits historiques, à l'oral le passé composé.
items.en: In formal writing, use the passé simple for historical facts; in speech, the passé composé.
items.notes: Ex : Fleming découvrit la pénicilline en 1928. · Curie obtint deux prix Nobel. · Pasteur mit au point le vaccin contre la rage.
items.prompt: Quel temps pour raconter une découverte historique à l'écrit ?

items.fr: C'est suivi de qui met en relief le sujet, c'est suivi de que met en relief un complément.
items.en: C'est followed by qui highlights the subject; c'est followed by que highlights a complement.
items.notes: Ex : C'est Fleming qui a découvert la pénicilline. · C'est en 1928 que la pénicilline a été découverte. · C'est ce vaccin que Pasteur a mis au point.
items.prompt: « C'est ... qui » ou « c'est ... que » pour la mise en relief ?

items.fr: Ils ont réalisé une découverte majeure.
items.notes: Réaliser une découverte majeure remplace trouver un truc énorme.
items.prompt: « Ils ont trouvé un truc énorme » · en soutenu

items.notes: S'avérer + adjectif est typique de l'écrit soutenu.
items.prompt: « Ce médicament marche bien » · en soutenu

items.notes: De dingue marque l'enthousiasme à l'oral familier.
items.prompt: « Cette découverte s'avère considérable » · en familier

items.fr: Il faut que nous respections les règles.
items.en: We have to respect the rules.
items.notes: Il faut que triggers the subjunctive: respections, not respectons.

items.fr: Oui, il faut que est toujours suivi du subjonctif.
items.en: Yes, il faut que is always followed by the subjunctive.

items.fr: Bien que la loi le permette, ce n'est pas moral.

items.notes: Bien que requires the subjunctive: permette, not permet.
items.prompt: Bien que la loi le permet, ce n'est pas moral.

items.notes: Chacun is singular, so the verb is doit, not doivent.

items.fr: Oui, bien que exige toujours le subjonctif.
items.en: Yes, bien que always requires the subjunctive.
items.notes: Ex : Bien qu'il soit riche · Bien que ce soit légal · Bien qu'elle ait raison

items.fr: Je doute que cette théorie soit vraie.
items.en: I doubt that this theory is true.
items.notes: Douter que triggers the subjunctive: soit.
items.prompt: Je doute que cette théorie ___ vraie.

items.notes: Also in the set phrase pas que je sache, not as far as I know.
Affirmative penser que takes the indicative, not the subjunctive.
items.prompt: Je pense que ce soit vrai.

items.fr: Indicatif à la forme affirmative, subjonctif à la forme négative ou interrogative.
items.en: Indicative in the affirmative, subjunctive in the negative or interrogative.
items.notes: Ex : Je pense que c'est vrai · Je ne pense pas que ce soit vrai · Penses-tu que ce soit utile ?
items.prompt: Indicatif ou subjonctif après « penser que » ?

items.fr: Si + imparfait dans la condition, conditionnel présent dans le résultat.
items.en: Si + imperfect in the condition, present conditional in the result.
items.notes: Ex : Si j'étais libre, je voyagerais · Si tout était déterminé, rien ne changerait · Si on savait tout, on douterait moins
items.prompt: Comment exprimer une hypothèse avec « si » ?

The h of hausser is silent but blocks liaison with a preceding word.
Nodding the head, often to say yes.
Literally to squeeze the hand.
Literally to make a sign with the hand.
Also means size, as in clothing size.

Usually plural: les gencives.
Feminine: la députée, same pronunciation.

Often used for both men and women.
Feminine: la cordonnière.
Also means a woman's suit. Feminine: la tailleuse.
Also the shop itself. Feminine: la teinturière.
From blanchir, to whiten. Feminine: la blanchisseuse.
Feminine: l'ambulancière.
From le brancard, the stretcher. Feminine: la brancardière.
Literally wise woman. The same word is used for men in the job.
Feminine: l'aide-soignante.
Same form for men and women: l'orthophoniste.
Same form for women: la pédiatre.
Short for le médecin généraliste. Same form for women: la généraliste.
Feminine: la marchande.
Sells in bulk to shops. Same form for women: la grossiste.
Sells to the public. Feminine: la détaillante.
Feminine: l'apprentie, same pronunciation.
Feminine: la gérante.
From veiller, to stay awake. Feminine: la veilleuse de nuit.
Feminine: l'agente de sécurité.
L'entretien means upkeep. Feminine: l'agente d'entretien.
Le ménage means housework. A man is un homme de ménage.
Informal, from nourrice. The official term is assistante maternelle.
Borrowed from English. Loads and unloads ships.
Also means a person under 18, so context matters.
Works metal in a forge. Feminine: la forgeronne.
Makes pottery from clay. Feminine: la potière.
The p is silent. Feminine: la sculptrice.
Engraves designs into metal, wood, or stone. Feminine: la graveuse.
An espresso pulled short, with less water and more punch.
An espresso stretched with extra hot water, close to an americano.
Short for un café décaféiné. What you order after dinner.
The default coffee in most French cafés if you just say un café.

items.en: an espresso with a dash of milk
items.notes: Literally a hazelnut. The drink is named for its hazelnut color.
Often shortened to un crème. The closest thing to a latte.
Vert means green. Un thé noir is a black tea.
Any hot drink steeped from herbs or fruit, with no tea leaves.
Chamomile, verbena, mint. Grandmother-approved evening drink.
Served with the juice, water and sugar apart so you mix it yourself.
Bright green café classic: mint syrup topped with fizzy lemonade.
Drinks are often cheaper standing at the counter than at a table.
The small plate under your cup. The bill often arrives on it.
Ask for it with a cold drink: une paille, s'il vous plaît.
French drinks come with few ice cubes by default.
Add it to any drink order when you want it cold.
Sans means without. Avec du sucre means with sugar.
In a café, un demi is a 25 cl glass of draft beer, not a half liter.
A small jug, often of house wine or water.
Literally for drinking. Service is included, so tips are small.
Said the English way, with a French accent.
France has one of the biggest rap scenes outside the US.
The h is silent in French, so it sounds like eep-op.
Same word as English, pronounced the French way.
Dance music born in the French Antilles, Guadeloupe and Martinique.
Congolese rumba is huge across francophone Africa.
Masculine noun: l'afrobeat, un afrobeat moderne.
High-energy dance genre from Ivory Coast.
Popular in French churches and choirs.
You hear them at village festivals and July 14 parades.
A traditional African drum played with the hands.
West African wooden xylophone with gourd resonators.
West African harp with 21 strings, played in Senegal and Mali.
Goblet-shaped West African hand drum.
Feminine plural: les percussions africaines.
Where everyone ends up at a French wedding.
Regular -er verb: je danse, tu danses, nous dansons.
Plural: les festivals. France runs hundreds every summer.
Borrowed from English and feminine in French.
Short for le microphone. Au micro means on the mic.
Je suis de bonne humeur means I am in a good mood.
The opposite of de bonne humeur.
Feminine: énervée. Stronger than simply annoyed.
Feminine: agacée. Mildly irritated, like by a buzzing fly.
Feminine: ravie. Je suis ravi de vous voir means I am delighted to see you.
Feminine: épuisée. Much stronger than fatigué.
Feminine: débordée. Literally overflowing, used for too much work.
Feminine: motivée. Common in work and sport contexts.
Feminine: découragée. The opposite of motivé.
Feminine: curieuse. Can also mean odd, as in c'est curieux.
Feminine: indifférente. Ça me laisse indifférent means it leaves me cold.
Literally crazy with joy. Feminine: folle de joie.
Literally dead of fear. Feminine: morte de peur.
Origin of the French texting abbreviation MDR, the equivalent of LOL.
Idiom, literally to have the cockroach. J'ai le cafard means I feel blue.
Nerves before performing or speaking in public.
J'ai honte means I am ashamed. Uses avoir, not être.
Informal register. J'en ai marre means I have had enough.
Gardez votre calme means stay calm, keep your cool.
Je perds patience means I am losing my patience.
Bon séjour ! means enjoy your stay.
Une croisière sur la Seine is a classic Paris outing.
Faire de la plongée means to go diving.
Faire un safari means to go on a safari.
Literally the lying down of the sun.
Literally the rising of the sun.
Also means point of view in a discussion.
A wide sweeping view, often from a high spot.
A relaxed walk. Une balade en ville means a stroll around town.
Masculine noun. Rent one at museum entrances.
A folding leaflet, from plier, to fold.
Thicker than un dépliant, more like a booklet.
A motorhome. Le camping alone means the campsite.
Monter la tente means to pitch the tent.
Literally the bag for sleeping.
Literally the pocket lamp.
Always plural, like glasses in English. Feminine.
Plural: les cartes postales.
Buy stamps at la poste or un tabac.
J'envoie une carte postale means I am sending a postcard.
Relaxed everyday form of 'oui'. Spoken only, informal; fine with friends, not in an exam.
Casual spoken form of 'non'. Informal; use 'non' in writing or formal settings.
Filler that signals hesitation or that the answer is obvious. Spoken only, informal; fine with friends, not in an exam.
Worn-down form of 'bien' used as a spoken filler. Informal; fine with friends, not in an exam.
Tag that asks for agreement, or means 'what?' when you missed something. Can sound blunt; avoid with strangers or in formal talk.
The classic French shrug word for indifference. Informal but harmless; common with everyone you know.
The standard French hesitation sound, like English 'um'. Neutral in speech; never written in formal prose.
Also the standard word for 'what'. As a tag at the end of a sentence it is spoken only and very informal.
Literally means 'kind' or 'type'. As a filler meaning 'like' it is youth speech; keep it out of formal contexts.
Literally means 'squarely'. Informal intensifier and one-word agreement; fine with friends, too casual for an exam.
Literally means 'serious' or 'grave'. As 'totally' it is youth slang; avoid it in formal settings.
Also the standard word for 'too much'. As a plain intensifier meaning 'so' it is casual spoken French; not for formal writing.
Comes from 'vache', the cow. Very common informal intensifier; fine with friends, not for formal writing.
Greek prefix meaning 'over', as in hypermarket. Casual spoken intensifier; fine in relaxed settings, too slangy for an exam.
Prefix from Greek meaning 'great', as in megabyte. Informal intensifier used by younger speakers; keep it casual.
Prefix meaning 'chief', as in architect. Informal intensifier; 'archi-plein' means packed full. Fine with friends, not in an exam.
Latin prefix meaning 'beyond'. Standard as a prefix in writing, but as a free-standing intensifier it is casual speech.
Prefix from metric units, as in gigabyte. Recent youth slang intensifier; very informal, strictly for casual talk.
Literally means 'to the bottom'. Informal for full speed or full commitment; fine with friends, casual only.
Literally means 'the cow'. Mild exclamation of surprise; informal but safe in any casual company.
Literally 'oh there there'. Expresses surprise or dismay, not romance; informal and completely harmless.
Literally means 'thin' or 'slim'. Polite stand-in for a ruder word; safe in any company, even at work.
Old interjection of annoyance. Mild and slightly dated; safe even with children or teachers.
Literally means 'mashed potatoes'. Softened stand-in for a ruder word; safe in polite company.
Literally means 'bedbug' or 'thumbtack'. Softened swear substitute; fine in polite company.
Vulgar; literally means 'excrement'. Extremely common in speech, but avoid it in polite company, at work, or in an exam.
All-purpose exclamation with a vulgar origin. Heard constantly in France for surprise, joy, or anger; avoid in formal settings.
The French way to ask for silence, like 'shh'. Neutral in itself, but it can sound bossy when aimed at adults.
Literally the imperative 'go' from 'aller'. Used to urge someone on or wrap up a goodbye; informal and friendly.
Sound effect for a quick action, often as 'et hop'. Spoken only, informal; adds a playful flourish.
Combines 'bon' with the filler 'ben' to wrap up a topic or move on. Spoken only, very informal.
Literally 'well then'. Expresses surprise or mild disbelief; spoken only, fine with friends, not in an exam.
Literally means 'say then'. Marks surprise or calls someone out; informal but not rude.
Literally means 'my word'. Old-style exclamation of disbelief; informal and a bit theatrical.
Literally means 'you talk'. Ironic 'yeah right' or emphatic 'you bet' depending on tone; spoken and informal.
Literally means 'and how'. Emphatic agreement; informal, friendly, and slightly old-school.
Also the standard word for 'if'. This 'si' answers yes to a negative question or statement; used at every register but essential in casual argument.
Doubling 'ouais' signals doubt, like 'yeah, sure'. Spoken only; can sound dismissive, so watch your tone.
Blend of a hum and 'ouais' showing weak, unconvinced agreement. Spoken only; mildly dismissive tone.
Literally 'ah good', but it means 'oh really?' whatever the news. Neutral spoken French, fine almost anywhere.
Casual 'oh really' or impressed 'oh wow'; the tone carries the meaning. Spoken only, informal.
Literally means 'it is clear'. Youth slang for strong agreement; keep it for casual conversation.
Literally means 'I admit'. Youth slang for agreeing hard with what was just said; spoken only, very informal.
Literally 'see there'. Marks completion or agreement; neutral register, usable almost anywhere.
A puff of air showing boredom, doubt, or exasperation. Spoken only; easily reads as rude, use with care.
Attention-getter like English 'hey'. Informal; too abrupt for strangers or formal situations.
Alarm or caution noise, like 'whoa'; often doubled as 'ouh là là'. Spoken only, informal.
The French 'ouch' for pain, also 'uh oh' when trouble looms. Neutral register, fine anywhere.
Literally the imperative 'hold' from 'tenir'. Marks surprise, or accompanies handing something over; informal.
Short for 'il n'empêche que', meaning all the same. Spoken shortcut; informal but very common.
Literally means 'all the same'. Adds emphasis or mild outrage as an exclamation; fine in most registers.
Literally means 'serious'. As a one-word question it means 'for real?'; youth speech, informal.
Literally means 'that is it'. Straight agreement, or sarcastic 'yeah right' with a flat tone; informal.
Literally means 'but yes'. Emphatic 'of course'; can sound impatient, so watch your tone.
Literally means 'but no'. Emphatic denial or reassurance; informal and very common in speech.
Literally means 'it walks'. Everyday way to say 'okay, that works'; informal, standard in shops and cafés.
Literally means 'it rolls'. Relaxed 'all good' or 'deal'; informal, fine with friends and colleagues.
Also the name of the shiny metal. Means spotless or perfect; informal but safe in any casual setting.
Clipped form of 'impeccable'. Means great or flawless; informal, fine in everyday speech, not in writing.
Literally the 'chiche' of 'pois chiche', the chickpea. Means 'I dare you' or 'you're on'; playful and informal.
Also literally a trick, as in a magic trick. Everyday informal word for any object or matter.
From the word machine. Use it when the name of a thing escapes you. Informal, spoken only.
A small gadget or contraption you cannot name. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally an owl. Friendly informal word for great or lovely.
Ugly for looks, or lousy for a situation. Informal but very common.
From se marrer, to laugh. Informal, spoken only.
From rigoler, to laugh. Informal and light in tone.
Crazy, or amazing when said of things. Possibly from dengue fever. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally weak or feeble minded in old medical use, now just stupid. Informal and a bit harsh.
Also literally null or zero. Informal way to call something rubbish.
Borrowed from English. As an adjective it means first rate: c'est top. Informal, spoken only.
Borrowed from English and fully adopted in French. Informal, spoken only.
Stylish and elegant. Long standing informal word, also common in fashion talk.
Also literally class, as in school or category. C'est la classe means that is classy. Informal, spoken only.
Tacky, corny, out of fashion. Also an old word for a fire poker. Informal, spoken only.
Literally old game. Old fashioned in taste or attitude. Informal but gentle.
Also literally a cannon. Says a person is stunning: elle est canon. Informal, spoken only.
From craquer, to crack or to give in. So cute that you give in. Informal, spoken only.
Clipped from crado and crasseux, grimy. Filthy, dirty. Informal, spoken only.
Short for dégueulasse, which is coarse. Gross, disgusting. Very informal, avoid in polite settings.
Also literally rotten, like spoiled fruit. Lousy, awful. Informal, spoken only.
Broken, worn out, or useless. From old slang for nose. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a jerrycan or a belly. Fake or phony: une excuse bidon. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a ladle. Shady, suspicious. Informal but widely accepted.
Borrowed from English space. Weird, out there. Informal, spoken only.
Nuts, bonkers. Short for barjot. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally carrying a tare, an inherited defect. Crazy, and quite harsh. Use with care, spoken only.
Also literally inflated, pumped up. Cheeky, daring: il est gonflé. Informal, spoken only.
Literally wearing la culotte, the pants. Cheeky, full of nerve. Informal, spoken only.
Vulgar origin, literally a brothel, but everyone uses it for chaos or a mess. Keep it out of formal settings.
A shambles, things thrown everywhere: en pagaille. From an old southern word for disorder. Informal.
Also literally a bazaar, an eastern market. A mess or clutter: quel bazar. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a circus. A fuss or a ridiculous scene: quel cirque. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally cinema. Drama, an act: arrête ton cinéma means stop your act. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a galley ship rowed by convicts. Hardship, a real struggle: quelle galère. Informal.

items.en: to struggle, to have a hard time
items.notes: From la galère, the galley ship. To struggle, to have a rough time. Informal, spoken only.
Money, cash. Origin unclear, maybe from fricot, a stew. Informal, spoken only.
Money. From an old verb pogner, to grab with the fist. Informal, spoken only.
Money. Once the name of an old five franc coin. Informal, spoken only.
Work or job. Maybe from bouleau, birch wood once carved by workers. Informal but universal.
A book. From an old Dutch word for a little book. Informal and affectionate.
A car. From banne, an old word for a cart. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a crate or a cash register. A car in slang. Informal, spoken only.
A guy, a dude. Can also mean boyfriend: mon mec. Informal, spoken only.
A girl or woman. Can also mean girlfriend: ma nana. Informal, spoken only.
A kid. Avoid it in Quebec, where the word means something rude. Informal in France.
A buddy, a mate. From poteau, a post, an old image for a solid friend. Informal, spoken only.
Food, grub. From bouffer, to eat, originally to puff out the cheeks. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a shack or hut. A house in slang. Informal, spoken only.
Work, the job. Origin debated, maybe from travail à faire. Very informal, spoken only.
A cigarette. Once meant a cigarette butt picked off the street. Informal, spoken only.
A cop. Probably from a German word for fly. Cheeky but not insulting. Informal, spoken only.
Clothes, always plural. From an old verb fringuer, to dress up. Informal, spoken only.

items.en: the village in the middle of nowhere
items.notes: A small town far from everything. From an Arabic word for country or land. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a fruit seed or pip. A hitch, a small problem. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally a roof tile, the kind that falls on your head. A sudden piece of bad luck. Informal.
Also literally a box. A company where you work, or a nightclub. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally mowed down, like cut grass. Broke, out of money. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally punctured, like a flat tire. Exhausted, wiped out. Informal, spoken only.
Also literally deadly or mortal. Awesome in youth slang: c'était mortel. Informal, spoken only.
Familier for la nourriture, food.

Clipped from le petit-déjeuner, breakfast.
Clipped from le déjeuner, lunch.
Clipped from l'apéritif, the pre-dinner drink and snacks.
Clipped from le restaurant.
Familier for un repas, a simple home-cooked meal.
Familier for la cantine, the canteen.
Familier for un en-cas, a quick snack. Literally: break-crust.

Familier for l'eau, water. Literally: fleet. Also familier for rain.
Familier for le bar, a neighborhood bar. Not the same as en rade, broken down.
Familier for un café, a small local café or bar.
Familier for un café. So common it is nearly standard now.
Familier for la faim, hunger, in avoir la dalle, to be starving. Literally: slab.
Familier for mourir de faim, to be starving. Crever literally means to burst or to die, so it is blunt; keep it for friends.
Familier for un festin, a big hearty meal. From la gueule, an animal's mouth, so a bit coarse but jovial.
Familier for trop manger, to pig out.
Familier for boire de l'alcool, to drink, often too much.
Familier for le café, a cup of coffee. Also spelled caoua.
Familier for du supplément, extra helpings. Clipped from le rabiot.
Familier for la cuisine, everyday cooking, in faire la popote, to do the cooking.
Familier for la cuisine, simple everyday cooking, often a bit rough.
Familier for la viande, meat, often hinting at poor quality.
