Familier for prendre un verre, to have a drink. Un coup literally means a blow or a hit.
Familier for ivre, drunk. Literally: stuffed, packed. Blunt; avoid in polite company.
Familier for a hangover. Literally: wooden mouth. La gueule is coarse for mouth, but this set phrase is fine among friends.
Familier for l'argent, money.
Familier for l'argent, money. Originally the name of an old five-franc coin.
Familier for l'argent, money. Un sou was an old French coin.
Familier for un euro when counting money: dix balles, ten euros. Literally: bullet or ball.
Familier for l'argent, money. Literally: wheat.
Familier for l'argent, money. Literally: sorrel, the green plant.
Familier for l'argent, money.
Familier for riche, rich. From le fric, money.
Familier for sans argent, broke. Literally: mowed down, from faucher, to mow.
Familier for ne plus avoir d'argent, to be out of money. Literally: to be dry.

items.en: to pay up, to fork out
items.notes: Familier for payer, to pay, usually unwillingly.
Familier for dépenser, to spend money fast. Literally: to slam or to snap.
Familier for coûter très cher, to be very expensive. Literally: to cost an arm.
Familier for très riche, loaded. Literally: armored.
Familier for c'est cher, it is pricey. Literally: it is not given away.
Familier for le travail, work.
Familier for travailler, to work.
Familier for le travail, work or the workplace.
Familier for travailler, to work. From le taf.
Common anglicism for un emploi, a job, often a small or student job.
Familier for l'entreprise, the company you work for. Literally: box. Also familier for a nightclub.
Familier for le chômage, unemployment: être au chômedu, to be out of work.
Familier for ne rien faire, to do nothing, to loaf about.
Familier for travailler dur, to work hard, often for an exam. Le bûcher literally means a woodpile.
Familier for travailler très dur, to toil.
Familier for quitter son travail, to walk out on your job. Plaquer literally means to pin or to tackle.
Clipped from la faculté; familier for l'université.
Familier for gagner sa vie, to earn a living. Literally: to earn your crust.
Familier set phrase for the daily routine. Literally: metro, work, sleep.
Familier for la maison, the house. Literally: shack or fairground stall.
Familier for chez soi, home, in rentrer au bercail, to head back home. Literally: sheepfold.
Familier for habiter, to live somewhere: tu crèches où? From la crèche, a manger.
Clipped from la colocation, a flatshare. Can also mean the flatmate, la colocataire.
Clipped from l'appartement, the flat.
Familier for le réfrigérateur, the fridge. From the brand Frigidaire.
Vulgar familier for les toilettes. Rude; with strangers say les toilettes or le petit coin instead.
Familier euphemism for les toilettes. Literally: the little corner.
Familier for le lit, the bed. Literally: stake or post.
Familier for se coucher, to hit the sack. From le pieu.
Familier for dormir, to sleep.
Familier for dormir, to sleep.
Familier for une sieste, a nap: faire un roupillon. From roupiller.
Child and familier word for le sommeil, sleep, in faire dodo, to sleep.
Familier for le lit, the bed. From la plume, feather.
Familier for dormir tard, to sleep late. Literally: to do the fat morning.
Familier for épuisé, exhausted. From crever, to burst or to die; blunt but very common.
Familier for la paresse, laziness, in j'ai la flemme, I can't be bothered.
Familier for paresser, to lounge around doing nothing. From la flemme.
Standard: l'homme, le garçon. Also means boyfriend: mon mec, my boyfriend.
Standard: la femme, la fille. Also means girlfriend: ma nana, my girlfriend.
Standard: le garçon, l'homme. The final rs is silent, say GAH.
Standard: l'homme. Literal meaning: a type or kind, so un type de fromage is a kind of cheese, but un type alone is a guy.
Standard: l'enfant. Also an adjective meaning childish: il est gamin.
Standard: l'enfant, la fille. Feminine of le gamin.
Standard: l'enfant. Warning: in Quebec French this word is vulgar slang for testicle, so avoid it there and say enfant instead.
Standard: l'enfant. Classic Paris street word for a kid.
Standard: l'enfant. Slightly cheeky word for a small child.
Standard: l'enfant. Related word: la marmotte is the animal, a marmot.
Standard: l'enfant. Marseille slang, very common in the south of France.
Standard: l'enfant. Literal meaning: a small strip of bacon, the kind you put in a quiche.
Standard: l'ami. Very common and friendly. A woman is la pote.
Standard: le frère.
Standard: la soeur.
Standard: le père. Very old word revived by young speakers, now core street slang.
Standard: la mère. Feminine of le daron. Les darons means the parents.
Standard: le beau-frère, clipped. Other meaning: a tacky, narrow-minded man, a bit like redneck, so watch the context.
Standard: l'oncle. Warm family word, what kids call their uncle.
Standard: la tante. Warm family word, the pair of le tonton.
Standard: le grand-père. Also used for any old man in casual speech.
Standard: la grand-mère. Also used for any old lady in casual speech.
Standard: le policier. The most common slang word for a police officer.
Standard: le policier. Literal meaning: chicken. The Paris police HQ was built on an old poultry market, hence the joke.
Standard: le médecin. From the Arabic word tbib, doctor.
Standard: le professeur, clipped. A woman teacher is la prof.
Standard: l'homme fort. Also an adjective meaning strong or sturdy: il est costaud.
Standard: le menteur. Clipped from mythomane, compulsive liar. Also used as an adjective: c'est mytho, that's a lie.
Standard: les vêtements. Always plural and feminine.
Standard: s'habiller. Bien fringué means well dressed.
Standard: les chaussures. One shoe is une godasse.
Standard: les chaussures. Literal meaning: pumps. Faire des pompes also means to do push-ups.
Standard: le pantalon. Other literal meaning: a monk's habit, as in jeter le froc aux orties, to leave the monastery.
Standard: les vêtements. Linked to la SAPE, the Congolese dandy movement, Société des Ambianceurs et des Personnes Élégantes.
Standard: s'habiller avec élégance. Same family as la sape and the Congolese sapeurs, famous for their sharp suits.
Standard: le style. Borrowed from English and fully adopted in casual French.

items.en: the look, the way someone carries themselves
items.notes: Standard: l'allure. Often mocking: quelle dégaine, what a look. From dégainer, to draw a weapon.
Standard: les vieux vêtements. Slightly dismissive word for clothes, often worn-out ones.
Standard: le costume. Un costard-cravate is a suit-and-tie guy.
Standard: la chemise. Casual word for a shirt.
Standard: le pantalon. Casual word for trousers.
Standard: les chaussures. One of several slang words for shoes, like godasses and pompes.
Standard: les chaussures. Yet another slang word for shoes, a bit playful.
Standard: le survêtement, clipped. Everyday word for a tracksuit or joggers.
Standard: la chose. Other literal meaning: a trick, like a magician's trick. The all-purpose word when you forget a name.
Standard: la chose, l'objet. From la machine. Machin with a capital also means what's-his-name.
Standard: l'objet, la chose. Like truc and machin, for an object you cannot name.
Standard: la marchandise de mauvaise qualité. Said of shoddy goods: c'est de la camelote, it's junk.
Standard: les affaires, le désordre. Originally soldier slang for a kit, now any pile of stuff or mess.
Standard: l'équipement, les affaires. From Arabic barda'a, a pack saddle, via soldier slang for a soldier's pack.
Standard: le livre. From old Dutch boeckin, little book. Bouquiner means to read for pleasure.
Standard: le téléphone, clipped. Common in speech and texting: file-moi ton tél, give me your number.
Standard: l'ordinateur, clipped. Everyday word for a computer or laptop.
Standard: le cinéma, clipped. On va au ciné, we're going to the movies.
Standard: le dictionnaire, clipped.
Standard: la cigarette. Very common: t'as une clope, got a cigarette.
Standard: le parapluie. Other literal meanings: a fruit seed, and a snag, as in avoir un pépin, to hit a problem.
Standard: le journal. Literal meaning: duck. The satirical paper Le Canard enchaîné plays on this.
Standard: le comptoir. Literal meaning: zinc the metal, old bar tops were covered in it. Older slang also used it for an airplane.
Standard: le chien. From Arabic kalb, dog. The b is pronounced like a p here.
Standard: le chien. Same Arabic root as le clebs, often a bit dismissive.
Standard: le chat mâle. Affectionate word for a big male cat.
Standard: le petit animal, l'insecte. From la bête, beast. Any small creepy or unidentified creature.
Standard: la voiture. The most common slang word for a car.
Standard: la voiture. Literal meanings: a crate, and a cash register. Une grosse caisse is a big flashy car.
Standard: la voiture. From the verb tirer, to pull. Street slang for a car, like ride in English.

items.en: the old banger, the beat-up car
items.notes: Standard: la vieille voiture. An old car that barely runs.
Standard: la vieille voiture. Other literal meaning: a small mouth harp, the twanging instrument.
Standard: le lycée, le camion. Two slang senses. Literal meaning: a sideboard or big chest of furniture.
Standard: le vélo, la moto. Also means a computer in tech slang: ma bécane, my machine.

items.en: the old bike, the old wreck
items.notes: Standard: le vieux vélo, la vieille voiture, usually as un vieux clou. Literal meaning: a nail.
Standard: le vieux bateau. A rickety boat you would not trust at sea.
Standard: le scooter, clipped. Common among teens for a moped or scooter.
Literally: to sting, to prick (a bee pique). Familier for voler.
Literally: to swing, to sway. Familier: to denounce someone, or to toss something carelessly.
Familier for attraper. Also used for illness: choper un rhume means to catch a cold.
Familier for cacher. Related noun: la planque, a hideout.
Literally: to release, to drop from a plane (larguer des parachutistes). Familier: to break up with someone.
Literally: to pin down, to tackle in rugby. Familier: to leave a partner or a job (tout plaquer).
Literally: to flick through TV channels with the remote. Familier: to forget or skip something (j'ai zappé le rendez-vous).
Literally: to pick up a signal (mon téléphone ne capte pas). Familier for comprendre.
Literally: to scratch. Familier: to get something for free (gratter une cigarette).
Familier for comprendre. Je pige rien means I do not get it at all.
Familier for rire. Also to joke: tu rigoles means you are kidding.

items.en: to laugh, to have a laugh
items.notes: Familier for rire. On s'est bien marrés means we had a good laugh.

items.en: to mess around, to talk nonsense
items.notes: Very common but built on a vulgar root, so keep it for friends. Sans déconner means no kidding.
Familier for paniquer. Also a noun: un flipper is a pinball machine.
Familier in everyday use: ça me stresse means it stresses me out.
Literally: to give a death rattle. Familier: to complain constantly, a French national pastime.
Familier for protester. Un rouspéteur is a chronic complainer.

items.en: to tell off, to yell at
items.notes: From la gueule, an animal's mouth, so it is blunt. Familier for réprimander.
Blunt but very common. Je me suis fait engueuler means I got yelled at.
Literally: to dredge a river. Familier: to chat someone up.
Familier. Un frimeur is a show-off and la frime is the act of showing off.
From le crâne, the skull. Familier: to strut around acting superior.

items.en: to rush, to go for it
items.notes: Literally: to darken a color. Familier: to charge ahead (fonce means go for it).

items.en: to dash off; to hand over
items.notes: Literally: to spin thread. Familier: to leave fast (je file) or to give (file-moi ça).

items.en: to get moving, to go out
items.notes: Standard meaning: to move. Familier: to go out or get going (ça bouge means the place is lively).
Literally: to drag. Familier: to loiter or waste time.
Literally: to bubble. Familier: to do sweet nothing, like floating in a bubble.
Everyday familier. Le bricolage is DIY and un bricoleur is a handyman.
Familier: to arrange shady little deals. Related noun: la magouille.
Familier for escroquer. Je me suis fait arnaquer means I got ripped off.
Literally: to plant oneself. Familier: to fail an exam, crash a car, or simply be wrong.
From a vulgar old root but common today. Ça a foiré means it went wrong.
From le carton, the cardboard shooting target: faire un carton means to score big. Familier: to be a huge success.
Literally: to insure. Familier: to handle it brilliantly (tu assures means you rock).

items.en: to handle it, to have it under control
items.notes: Standard meaning: to manage. Familier: je gère means I have got this.

items.en: to give in, to break down
items.notes: Literally: to crack. Familier: to snap under pressure or give in to temptation (j'ai craqué).

items.en: to crash at, to camp out at
items.notes: Borrowed from English squat. Familier: je squatte chez un pote means I am crashing at a friend's place.
Literally: to disembark from a boat. Familier: to turn up out of nowhere.

items.en: to show up, to come running
items.notes: Familier: to arrive fast, often when called. Ils ont tous rappliqué means they all showed up.
Literally: to point oneself. Familier for arriver: il s'est pointé en retard.
From le poireau, the leek: faire le poireau is standing there planted like a leek. Familier for waiting a long time.
Familier for regarder. Mate ça means check that out.
Built from les yeux, the eyes. Familier for regarder.
From la gueule, an animal's mouth, so it is blunt. Familier for crier.
Familier for pleurer, often a bit mocking. Arrête de chialer means stop bawling.
Familier: to spin a smooth line to convince or seduce. Related noun: le baratin.
Literally: to wind onto a bobbin. Familier: to wrap someone around your finger with words.

items.en: to swindle, to take for a ride
items.notes: Literally: to treat someone like a pigeon. Familier: to fleece a gullible person, le pigeon.
Literally: to pluck a bird's feathers. Familier: to take all of someone's money.
Literally: to roll. Familier: to trick someone (il m'a roulé).
Literally: to get rolled. Familier: je me suis fait rouler means I got cheated.
Literally: to break someone's feet. Familier: tu me casses les pieds means you are getting on my nerves.
Literally: to inflate. Familier: ça me gonfle means it really annoys me.
Literally: to tan leather. Familier: to wear someone down by asking again and again.
Literally: to cart, to haul. Familier: to make fun of someone, or to go too far (tu charries).
Literally: to winnow grain. Familier: to throw jibes. Related noun: la vanne.
Literally: to bring wine to room temperature. Familier: to mock someone in a friendly way.
Familier for se promener. Une balade is a stroll.
Familier: to carry something heavy everywhere. Je trimballe mon sac toute la journée means I lug my bag around all day.

items.en: to dig up, to score (a find)
items.notes: Familier: to find something hard to get. J'ai dégoté une place means I scored a spot.
Literally: to take a bird from its nest (le nid). Familier flavor: to find a rare thing.
Familier: to hunt for secondhand treasures at flea markets and brocantes.
From la fouine, the stone marten. Familier: to poke your nose into other people's business.
Familier for fouiller: to dig around messily in drawers or bags.

items.en: to fiddle with, to hack together
items.notes: Familier: to tinker with something until it sort of works, often tech.
Familier: to repair roughly with whatever is on hand.
Literally: to hit or type again. Familier: to renovate (retaper une maison) or to perk someone up.
Literally: to blaze, to flambé. Familier: to spend big to impress. Un flambeur is a high roller.
Familier for brûler. Also to bust someone: je t'ai cramé means I caught you.
From la paume, the palm of the hand. Familier for perdre: j'ai paumé mes clés means I lost my keys.
Literally: to clear, to free up space. Familier: dégage means get out of here.
Literally: to turn, to veer. Familier: to throw someone out (il s'est fait virer means he got fired).
Literally: to swarm. Familier: grouille-toi means get a move on.
Familier, squeezed from se manier, to handle oneself. Magne-toi means hurry up.
From la cavale, an old word for a mare. Familier: to rush all over the place.

items.en: to struggle, to have a hard time
items.notes: From la galère, the galley ship rowed by prisoners. Familier: je galère means I am struggling.
Literally: to row a boat. Familier: to make painful, slow progress.
Familier: to study a subject hard (potasser un examen).
Literally: to dry. Familier: sécher les cours means to cut class, and je sèche means I am drawing a blank.
Literally: to stall an engine or wedge something in place. Familier: je cale means I am too full to eat more.
From planquer, to hide. A stash spot or hideout, and also a cushy, easy job.
From magouiller. Small-scale shady arrangements and fiddles.
From arnaquer. C'est de l'arnaque means it is a rip-off.
From baratiner. A flood of words meant to convince or seduce.
Literally: a sluice gate. Familier: a teasing one-liner (lancer des vannes means to crack jokes at someone).
Literally: an old word for a mare. Être en cavale means to be on the run from the police.
Literally: a galley ship rowed by convicts. Familier: c'est la galère means it is a nightmare.
Literally: a bazaar, an oriental market. Familier: quel bazar means what a mess.
Literally: a ship's mop. Familier: être en vadrouille means to be out roaming around.
Literally: a pigeon. Familier: a gullible person who gets fleeced, the victim of une arnaque.
Verlan of femme (woman). Extremely common. Also means girlfriend: ma meuf.
Verlan of mec (guy). The male counterpart of meuf. Mon keum can also mean my boyfriend.
Verlan of fête (party). Extremely common among young speakers.
Verb built on teuf, verlan of fête (party). Means to party hard.
Set phrase built on teuf, verlan of fête (party). Means to party, to have a big night.
Verlan of lourd (heavy). Means annoying or tiresome. Extremely common.
Verlan of louche (shady). Means weird or suspicious. Extremely common.
Verlan of fou (crazy). Used as an adjective: c'est ouf. Extremely common.
Phrase built on ouf, verlan of fou (crazy). Means something unbelievable, in a good or bad way.
Verlan of bizarre (strange). Means weird or odd.
Verlan of énervé (annoyed, angry). Extremely common: il est vénère means he is furious.
Verlan of merci (thanks). Jokey and casual, used with friends.
Verlan of à fond (flat out). Means at full speed or full volume: la musique à donf.
Verlan of frère (brother). Also used for a close friend, like bro.
Verlan of sœur (sister).
Verlan of père (father).
Verlan of mère (mother).
Verlan of parents. Usually plural: mes rempas.
Verlan of vieux (old ones). Les ieuvs means the parents. Casual but affectionate.
Verlan of famille (family). Often shortened further to la mif.
Verlan of racaille (riffraff). Pejorative label for street youth. Learn to recognize it, but avoid using it about people.
Verlan of français (French). Un céfran is a French person.
Verlan of arabe. Historical term for French-born North Africans, from the 1980s beur generation. Use with care and respect.
Feminine of beur, from arabe. Today it often carries condescending overtones, so it is better to recognize it than to use it.
Verlan of beur, which is itself verlan of arabe. A rare double verlan. Common and generally neutral among young speakers.
Verlan of toubab (a West African word for a European). Means a white person. Casual banlieue speech, often jokey. Use with care.
Verlan of ricain, itself clipped from américain (American). La kainri means the United States, common in rap lyrics.
Verlan of futur (future). Dans le turfu means in the future, or ahead of its time.
Verlan of argent (money).
Verlan of client (customer).
Verlan of musique (music). Also shortened to la zik.
Verlan of blouson (jacket).
Verlan of disque (record). Means an album, very common in music talk.
Verlan of flic (cop). Lineage: flic became keufli, then shortened to keuf. Extremely common.
Plural of keuf, verlan of flic (cop). Les keufs means the police.
Verlan of photo. The syllables flipped, then the word shortened to tof. Everyday word for a pic.
Verlan of métro (metro). Sometimes shortened to trom.
Verlan of café (coffee). Can mean the drink or the place.
Verlan of chien (dog).
From cité (housing estate): cité became téci, then shortened to tess. Means the hood.
Verlan of cité (housing estate). Often shortened further to tess.
Verlan of quartier (neighborhood). Means the hood, your home turf.
Variant of tiéquar, verlan of quartier (neighborhood).
Verlan of punk. A classic from the 1980s alternative scene.
Verlan of misère (misery). C'est la zermi means things are rough.
Verlan of honte (shame). Avoir la teuhon means to be embarrassed.
Verlan of maison (house). À la zonmai means at home.
Verlan of bouteille (bottle), flipped then shortened to teille.
Verlan of pourri (rotten). Means a corrupt cop, made famous by the film Les Ripoux.
Verlan of pigeon (sucker). Someone easily fooled.
Verlan of sac (bag).
Verlan of truc (thing). Un keutru de ouf means a crazy thing.
Verlan of lascar (street lad). A tough young guy from the neighborhood.
Verlan of cheveux (hair), flipped then shortened. Usually plural: les veuchs.
Verlan of jobard (gullible fool). Now simply means crazy. Also spelled barjot.
Verlan of moche (ugly). Very common with younger speakers.
Verlan of dingue (crazy). Un truc de guedin means something wild.
Verlan of bête (stupid).
Verlan of méchant (mean). The meaning flipped: chanmé means wicked in the good sense, amazing.
Verlan of branché (plugged in, trendy). A classic from the 1980s, now a bit retro.
Verlan of bloqué (blocked). Means stuck, or unable to stop thinking about someone or something.
Verlan of chaud (hot). Means risky, difficult, or dodgy: c'est auche.
Verlan of cher (expensive). C'est reuch means it costs too much.

items.en: to grab, to catch; to hook up with
items.notes: Verlan of choper (to grab). Two senses: to catch or grab something, and to hook up with someone. Casual, watch the context.
Phrase built on pécho, verlan of choper (to grab). Se faire pécho means to get caught red handed.

items.en: to look at, to check out
items.notes: Verlan of mater (to look at). Téma ça means check that out.
Set phrase with téma, verlan of mater (to look at). Means look at that, check it out.
Verlan of rigoler (to laugh). Ça me fait golri means that cracks me up.
Verlan of taper (to hit). In slang it means to swipe or pinch something small: il m'a péta mon stylo.
Verlan of moi (me). Chez oim means at my place.
Phrase built on oim, verlan of moi (me). Means at my place, at home.
Verlan of toi (you). Less common than oim but attested.
Verlan of vas-y (go on). An interjection: come on, go ahead.
Verlan of laisse tomber (drop it). Béton flips tomber. Made famous by the 1977 Renaud song.
Scred is verlan of discret (discreet). En scred means on the sly, without anyone noticing.
Deuspi is verlan of speed, the English loanword for hurry. En deuspi means in a rush.
Playful verlan style scramble of n'importe quoi (nonsense). C'est du portnawak means that is rubbish.
Verlan of comme ça (like that). The ça flips to aç.
Phrase built on ouf, verlan of fou (crazy). Means that is insane, said in awe or disbelief.
Older verlan of frère (brother), common in 1990s rap. The modern short form is reuf.
Verlan of prison (prison). Common in rap lyrics; a rougher street register, use only when quoting or joking with close friends.

items.en: the place, the spot; room to sit
items.notes: Verlan of place (place, seat, spot). Heard as fais-moi une cepla, make room for me.

items.en: the village back home; the middle of nowhere
items.notes: Verlan of bled, itself from Arabic blad (village, home country). Means the family village back home, or by extension any tiny remote town.

items.en: the monster; a beast, a freak
items.notes: Verlan of monstre (monster). Can be admiring, like calling someone a beast at what they do, or literal.
Re-verlan: femme became meuf, then meuf was verlanized again into feumeu. A textbook example of double verlan; casual, can sound objectifying in the wrong context.
Re-verlan: arabe gave beur, re-verlanized into reubeu (variant rebeu). Widely used self descriptively; as an outsider, prefer to let people label themselves.
Verlan of noir (Black). Common and mostly neutral in street French, often self descriptive; still an informal ethnic label, so use with care and never in formal settings.
Verlan of ricain, itself clipped from américain (American). Also used as an adjective: le son cainri, American music.
Verlan of clochard (homeless person, tramp). Pejorative; also used loosely for someone looking scruffy. Avoid saying it about actual homeless people.
Verlan of voiture (car). A staple of 1990s cité speech, still understood everywhere.
Verlan adjacent: from vago, old slang from wagon (car), flipped into gova. Very current in rap, as in dans la gova, in the car.
Verlan of soirée (evening party). A step less common than teuf but well attested among younger speakers.
Verlan of copine (girlfriend, female friend). Casual; context decides whether it means partner or just a friend.
Verlan of copain (buddy, boyfriend). Masculine counterpart of pineco; context tells you if it means friend or boyfriend.
Verlan adjacent argot from musicos, slangy form of musicien (musician). Belongs to the same flipped music family as the verlan word for music itself.
Verlan of cheveux (hair). Usually plural: je vais me couper les veuch, I am getting my hair cut.
Verlan of vieux (old, old man). Les yeuvs can mean the parents; cheeky rather than cruel, but disrespectful in front of elders.
Verlan of jeune (young, young person). Les neujeus, the young ones; often said by slightly older speakers about teens.
Verlan of la honte (shame). Avoir la tehon, to be embarrassed; foutre la tehon, to embarrass someone.

items.en: the crew, the gang of friends
items.notes: Verlan of bande (group, crew). Less common than the core set but attested in cité speech; means your group of friends, not a criminal gang by default.
Verlan of flambeur (show off, from flamber, to flash money around). Attested in dictionaries of cité French; mocking but not vulgar.
Verlan of tronche (face, mug). Blunt and jokey; t'as vu ta chetron, look at the state of your face.
The name of the slang itself is verlan of l'envers (backwards). Syllables of a word are flipped; born in the Paris suburbs and spread through rap.
Verlan of nez (nose), an old classic listed in argot dictionaries. Rare in today's speech; do not confuse with zen meaning calm.
Verlan of bouteille (bottle). Often clipped to la teille; common at parties when talking about drinks.
Verlan of falzar, older argot for trousers. Attested in verlan glossaries; rare today, more a 1990s flavor.
Verlan of rap. Heard in rap lyrics themselves; écouter du peura, to listen to rap.
Verlan of métis (mixed race). Common in rap, often self descriptive; informal, so avoid it in formal contexts.
Verlan of déguisé (disguised): a cop in civilian clothes. Older argot attested since the 1980s; still understood.
Verlan of pieds (feet), attested in dictionaries of cité French. Usually plural; venir en ièps, to come on foot.
Verlan of baskets (sneakers). Attested in verlan glossaries; rarer than the plain word but recognizable.
Verlan of parents. Plural only, also spelled renps; mes remps, my folks. The singular forms for mom and dad are separate verlan words.
Verlan adjacent: playful doubling built on prison, sibling of zonpri. En zonzon, inside, doing time; title of a 1998 French film.
Verlan adjacent doubling of plaisir (pleasure): the flipped final syllable zir repeated. Rap favorite; c'est que du zizir, pure pleasure.
Verlan style scramble of n'importe quoi (nonsense). C'est du nawak, that is complete nonsense.
Verlan of bien (good). C'est ienb, it is all good; current among younger speakers.
Verlan of chaud (hot, meaning risky or hard). C'est auch, that is rough or sketchy; also heard as c'est l'auche.
Verlan of bloqué (blocked, stuck). Etre keblo sur quelqu'un, to be hung up on someone; also stuck on a problem.
Verlan of dur (hard). C'est reud, that is tough or strict; also describes a hard person.
Verlan of raciste (racist). Used as adjective or noun in street speech to call out racism.
Verlan of manger (to eat). On va géman, we are going to eat; stays invariable like most verlan verbs.
Verlan of flipper (to freak out, be scared). Je péfli, I am freaking out.
Verlan of jeter (to throw). Se faire tèj, to get dumped by a partner or thrown out of a place.
Verlan of barber, old argot for to steal. Se faire bébar, to get robbed or ripped off; very current in street French.
Verlan of chier, in the set phrase ça fait ièch, that is such a pain. The source verb is crude, so keep this for relaxed company.
Verlan of speed, the English loan meaning rushed. En deuspi, in a rush: fais-le en deuspi, do it quick.
Verlan of ça (that). Comme aç, like that; a tiny word that instantly marks street speech.
Verlan adjacent: from en douce (on the sly) via louchebem butcher slang, often grouped with verlan. Il est parti en loucedé, he slipped out quietly.
Verlan of à côté (next to, nearby). J'habite à téco, I live right nearby.
Verlan of peau de balle, old argot for nothing at all. Dated but attested in argot dictionaries; balpeau!, no luck, zilch.
From Algerian Arabic wach meaning what or how. Used as a casual hello between friends. Very informal, keep it for people your own age.
From Arabic semm meaning venom. Frustration or bitterness, almost always heard in avoir le seum. Everyday youth speech.

items.en: to be gutted, to be fed up
items.notes: Literally: to have the venom, from Arabic semm. Means to be gutted or bitter about something. Casual speech only.
From Maghrebi Arabic. Hardship, brokeness, a rough patch, common in être dans la hess. Informal only.
Literally: a lease. In slang it means a thing, a deal, a situation. C'est quoi ce bail means what is this thing. Informal.
Plural of le bail, literally leases. Means stuff, plans, business. Quoi les bails is a common greeting meaning what's up. Informal.
Diminutive of frère, brother. Friendly address for a close friend, like bro. Warm and informal.
Literally: the blood. Mon sang means my closest friend, family by loyalty. Street flavored but affectionate, only for people you are truly close to.
Literally: fat or big. As an address between friends it just means mate or bro, no insult intended. Only with friends, never with strangers.
Old French for the master of the house. Now means dad in youth speech. Cheeky but not rude among friends, avoid it in formal settings.
Feminine of daron, from old French for master of the house. Means mum. Familiar, affectionate or cheeky depending on tone.
From Arabic kif meaning pleasure. To love or really enjoy something. Je te kiffe can mean I am into you. Very common youth speech.
From Arabic kif meaning pleasure. A moment of pure enjoyment. C'est le kif means this is the life. Informal.
Borrowed from English. The person you secretly like. J'ai un crush sur lui. Youth speech, fine among friends.
From English to ghost. To cut off all contact without explanation. Il m'a ghostée. Dating talk, informal.
From English to chill. To hang out and relax with no plan. On chill chez moi ce soir. Casual youth speech.
Borrowed from English. Your tight group of friends. Social media flavored, informal.
Borrowed from English. The mood or atmosphere of a place or person. Bonne vibe means good energy. Informal.
From Antillean Creole boug, itself from old French bougre. Just means a guy. Neutral in youth speech, informal.
From Romani gadjo, originally a non-Romani man. In youth slang just a guy. Informal.
From Romani. A girl or a girlfriend. Common in the south of France and in youth speech everywhere. Informal.
From Romani. A fool, someone acting crazy. Mocking but usually playful between friends. Informal.
From Arabic miskin meaning poor. Said of someone pitiful, poor thing. Can be gentle sympathy or light mockery depending on tone.
From Arabic astaghfirullah, I ask God for forgiveness. Exclamation of shock or disapproval. Religious origin, so use it with respect or simply recognize it.
From Arabic, by God. Means I swear, for real. It is a genuine oath for many speakers, so use it sparingly and with respect.
From Arabic in sha Allah, God willing. Means hopefully, we shall see. Widely used in casual speech, but remember its religious weight and use it respectfully.
From Algerian Arabic. Means as if, supposedly, yeah right. Marks irony or disbelief. Informal.
From Arabic blad meaning country or town. The family's home country or village, and by extension the middle of nowhere. Informal.

items.en: someone fresh from the old country
items.notes: From bled, the home country. Someone recently arrived from there. Can be neutral or a jab about style and accent, so use with care.
Clipped from famille. The family, by blood or by loyalty. Warm and informal.
Playful variant of pote, a buddy. Very common among young speakers. Informal and friendly.
Plural of poto. The crew, the buddies. Salut les potos is a classic streamer greeting. Informal.
French street argot of uncertain origin. Means alcohol, booze. Adult topic, keep it for casual adult company and know that it sounds very street.
Literally: a strike or a hit. Means something or someone impressively good, a banger or a beast. C'est une frappe ce joueur. Informal praise.

items.en: it goes down smooth, no problem
items.notes: Literally: it goes cream. Means it goes smoothly, easily, no problem at all. Everyday casual speech.
Banlieue slang that spread nationwide around 2010, origin debated. A loser or pushover. Pejorative, do not aim it at strangers.
Literally: a jester. Means a fool or a clown. T'es un bouffon is a real schoolyard insult, so use with care.
Clipped from cas social, a welfare case. Means a chaotic mess of a person. Strongly pejorative and classist, learn it to understand it but avoid using it.
From rager, to fume. A hater, someone who trashes everything online. Internet and gaming youth speech.
From rage. To fume or be salty, especially after losing a game. Gaming and youth speech, informal.
From English masterclass. Praise for a flawless performance, often ironic. Quelle masterclass. Internet flavored, informal.
Clipped from référence. A cultural reference or callback to a meme, film or song. Informal.
To catch the cultural callback. T'as pas la ref means you missed the reference. Internet and youth speech, informal.
Literally: delirium. Means a fun mood or a shared thing between friends. C'est pas mon délire means not my thing. Informal.
Literally: styled. Means cool, sharp, impressive. Trop stylé is high praise. Informal.
Literally: serious. As an intensifier it means totally or seriously, as in grave stylé. Also works as a one word yes. Informal.
Clipped from charognard, a vulture. A relentless hustler or a shameless flirt who circles everything. Mocking and mildly pejorative.
From Romani. A gold digger. Pejorative and gendered, so understand it when you hear it but use it with real caution.
Clipped from mythomane, a compulsive liar. Means a liar, or the lie itself. T'es un mytho. A fairly soft informal insult.
From mytho, itself from mythomane. To make things up, to spin stories. Il mythonne means he is making it up. Informal.
Old French argot for a name or nickname. C'est quoi ton blase means what is your name. Street flavored, informal.
From American slang moolah, spread through French rap. Means money. Warning: in some contexts it hints at street money, so read the room before using it.
From older French argot, related to biffeton, a banknote. Means money. Street flavored, informal.
Literally: mail as in chain mail, and the name of an old small coin. Means money. Avoir de la maille is to have cash. Informal.
From Maghrebi Arabic. Means serves you right, well deserved. A playground taunt, playful among friends, stinging with anyone else.
From Arabic khouya meaning my brother. A bro, a mate. Big on French internet forums. Informal.
From Arabic sahbi meaning my friend. A buddy. Warm and informal.
From Arabic sahih meaning true. Means seriously, for real. Sah? on its own asks are you serious. Very current youth speech.
From Maghrebi Arabic. Means watch out, careful. Fais belek means be careful. Informal.
From Maghrebi Arabic. Means nothing at all, zilch. J'ai capté walou means I understood nothing. Informal.
From Arabic baraka meaning blessing. Means luck, good fortune. Avoir la baraka is to be on a lucky streak. Informal and gentle.
From Arabic al hamdu lillah, praise be to God. Means thankfully, all is well. Religious origin, so use it with respect.
From Maghrebi Arabic, literally to your health. Means congrats, well done, enjoy it. Warm and informal.
From Arabic zbel meaning garbage. Means chaos, mayhem. C'est le zbeul means it is total chaos. Informal.
From Arabic zbel, garbage. To stir up chaos, to turn a place upside down. Informal.

items.en: to pretend, to act as if
items.notes: Origin debated, most likely Maghrebi Arabic. To pretend, to act as if. Il fait crari il connaît means he pretends he knows. Informal banlieue speech.
From Romani, first spread in Lyon street slang. A guy. Y a pas un pélo means there is nobody around. Informal.
From Romani pukav meaning to denounce. A snitch. A strongly negative label in street culture, so be careful with it.
From Romani pukav. To snitch, to tell on someone. Informal and loaded, a serious accusation among friends.
From Romani love meaning money. Means cash, common in French rap. Street flavored, informal.
Compressed from à ce qu'il paraît, apparently. Means apparently, word is. Born in texting, now spoken. Very informal.
Clipped from ne t'inquiète pas. Means do not worry, relax, I have it handled. Everyday casual speech.
Nonsense trap word from French TikTok in 2023. Someone baits you into saying quoi, then shouts quoicoubeh. Playground humor, know it to get the joke.
Playful twist on choqué, shocked. Means stunned, flabbergasted, often with irony. Internet youth speech.
Initials of beau gosse, good looking guy. A compliment, sometimes teasing. T'es un BG. Informal.
From Maghrebi Arabic. A girl, a young woman. Casual and a bit blunt, can sound disrespectful, so keep it among close friends.
Literally: a rat. In youth slang, a stingy person who never pays for anything. T'es un rat means you are cheap. Teasing insult.
Literally: the sauce. Means style, flair, energy. Avoir la sauce is to have it, mettre la sauce is to go all out. Informal.
Literally: set down. Means chill, relaxed, laid back. Une soirée posée is a quiet night in. Informal.
Literally: square. Means clean, settled, perfectly arranged. C'est carré means it is all set. Informal.
Literally: fresh or cool in temperature. In youth slang it means good looking, classy. Il est frais. Informal praise.
Literally: it is clean. Praise for anything neat and well executed, from a goal to an outfit. Informal.
Literally: it is the fire. Means it is amazing, it slaps. Informal, very common.
Literally: of a sick person. Means insane, incredible. Un but de malade is a crazy goal. Informal intensifier.
Literally: it is abused. Means it is too much, out of line, or simply unbelievable. Works for complaints and amazement. Informal.
Literally: I am dead. Means I am dying of laughter, or completely exhausted. Context decides which. Informal.

items.en: to be in fits of laughter
items.notes: Literally: to have bars. Means to find something hilarious, to be in fits. J'ai des barres means I am cracking up. Informal.
From craquer, to crack. A moment of losing it, from a meltdown to a wild impulse buy. Often self mocking. Informal.
Literally: to pick up a signal. Means to understand. J'ai rien capté means I understood nothing. Informal.
Literally: to burn. Means to catch or bust someone, or to spot something instantly. Je t'ai cramé means I saw you. Informal.
Literally: to calculate. In slang, to pay attention to someone. Il m'a même pas calculé means he completely ignored me. Informal.
From carotte, a carrot, old argot for a swindle. Means to rip someone off. Je me suis fait carotter means I got scammed. Informal.
From charbon, coal, as in mining work. Means to grind, to work hard. Rap flavored, informal, keep it for real effort.

items.en: to show off, to flash money
items.notes: Literally: to blaze. Means to show off, especially by flashing money. Il flambe trop. Informal, mildly mocking.

items.en: to show off, to act big
items.notes: Literally: to tell it to oneself. Means to show off, to act big. Il se la raconte. An informal jab, teasing between friends.
From old French argot graille meaning food. Means to eat. On va grailler means let's grab food. Informal.
From la sape, old French argot for clothes. Means sharply dressed. Sapé comme jamais means dressed like never before. Informal praise.
Literally: perched. Means spacey, on another planet, a bit odd. T'es perché is a playful jab. Informal.
From dingue, crazy. A wild or unbelievable thing. C'est une dinguerie means that is insane. Very current youth speech.
Youth coinage from gênant, awkward. Secondhand embarrassment, cringe. Quelle gênance. Informal, popular with teens.

From Romani bikrav (to sell). Means selling anything on the street but carries a strong illegal-commerce connotation in rap lyrics. Taught for comprehension; saying it about yourself implies shady dealing.
From se débrouiller (to manage, to get by). Vivre de la débrouille means surviving on odd jobs and clever fixes. Positive or neutral tone; celebrates street smarts rather than crime.
From se débrouiller. Borderline standard French but constant in youth speech; a compliment for someone who always finds a way. Feminine: la débrouillarde. Safe in any casual setting.

Acronym of Brigade Anti-Criminalité, plainclothes units patrolling sensitive areas. Heard constantly in French rap. Not slang itself, but its street usage is; do not confuse with le bac (the school exam).
From Portuguese conde (count), via colonial-era slang for a local authority. Widespread in rap for police. Pejorative; never address an officer this way.
Literally: poultry! Extends the old poulet (chicken) nickname for police to the whole flock. Mocking and pejorative; comprehension vocabulary for rap and street talk.
Literally: scales! From balancer (to toss out, to give up names). Used for men and women alike: c'est une balance. Strong insult in street code; accusing someone of being one is serious.
Standard meaning: to swing or to throw. In slang, il a balancé tout le monde means he gave everyone up to the police. Also used for leaking gossip; context decides how serious it is.
Formal legal term (custody for questioning, up to 24 or 48 hours) that street speech absorbed whole; shortened to la GAV in rap. Knowing it unlocks countless lyrics and news stories. Neutral to use.
Clipped form of le procureur (public prosecutor). Typical of French clipping culture, like le proprio or la clim. Heard in crime series and rap; casual but understood by everyone.
Literally: drooly, from baver (to drool); old argot joke that lawyers talk until they dribble. Still alive in street and prison talk. Mildly mocking; say avocat in any real legal setting.
Great double meaning: in standard French a warrant or mandate, but in street and prison context the money order relatives send an inmate. Envoyer un mandat is a loyalty gesture referenced in rap.
Literally: mare (female horse)! Old argot from cavaler (to run fast). Refers to fleeing justice after an escape. Romanticized in films and rap; neutral to use when telling a story.
Set phrase built on la cavale. Être en cavale means being a fugitive. Also used playfully for dodging someone: je suis en cavale, ma mère me cherche. Safe in joking contexts.
From braquer, whose standard meaning is to point or aim something (like a spotlight or steering wheel). The noun means a stickup or heist. Constant in rap and film titles; comprehension vocabulary.

Standard meanings: to aim or point, and to turn a car's wheels fully. Slang meaning: to hold someone up. Braquer une banque is the classic example. Understand it; using it about yourself sounds criminal.
Old argot from le fourgue (a fence, a reseller of stolen goods). Today also used lightly: il m'a fourgué son vieux canapé means he palmed his old couch off on me. Tone ranges from shady to playful.

items.en: to keep watch, to be lookout
items.notes: Le guet is an old word for a night watch. The phrase survives in street context for the lookout posted during anything risky. Also fine in innocent contexts, like watching for a surprise party guest.
From casser (to break). Faire un casse means pulling a burglary or heist, classically le casse du siècle (the heist of the century). Film and rap staple; neutral when telling stories.
Clipped from indicateur (informer). Older and more police-side than poucave: an indic works with the cops regularly. Common in crime fiction. Pejorative in street code.
Clipped from la perquisition (a home search by police). Typical clipping heard in rap and series: ils ont fait une perquise à six heures. Neutral term describing a legal procedure.
Clipped from en flagrant délit (in flagrante). Se faire prendre en flag means getting caught red-handed. Not the English word flag. Also used for harmless busts, like raiding the fridge at night.
Verlan (back-slang) of flic, itself slang for cop. The everyday street word for police: les keufs arrivent. Pejorative edge; never say it to an officer's face.
Serrer normally means to tighten or squeeze. Il s'est fait serrer means he got picked up by the police. Also used for lesser busts, like being caught cheating on a test. Very common youth phrase.

Old argot, originally a room or shack (also spelled tôle, literally: sheet metal). Faire de la taule means doing time. The default informal word for jail; fine in casual talk, harsh in formal settings.
From la taule (prison) plus the -ard suffix that colors many slang nouns. Feminine: la taularde. Pejorative when aimed at a person; descriptive in stories and lyrics.
Prison argot for the punishment block (officially le quartier disciplinaire). Au mitard means in the hole. Heard in prison films and rap; purely comprehension vocabulary for most learners.

items.en: to go down, get locked up
items.notes: Literally: to dive! Slang meaning: to be sent to prison, often taking the fall: il a plongé pour les autres. The diving image mirrors English going down. Story and lyric vocabulary.
Standard meaning: to fall. In street usage, il est tombé pour braquage means he went down for robbery, and tomber pour quelqu'un can mean taking the blame for them. Context carries the meaning.

items.en: to shake off, lose a pursuer
items.notes: Literally: to sow seeds! Figuratively, on les a semés means we lost them (pursuers, police, a chase). Fully acceptable familier French; also used for outpacing someone in a race.
Literally: to trace or draw a line. Youth slang: to move fast or leave quickly: allez, on trace! The image is leaving a line behind you. Casual and harmless; very common among young speakers.
From embrouiller, literally: to tangle! An embrouille is a conflict or messy dispute between people or crews: il y a eu une embrouille. Also means a confusing scam. Core youth vocabulary.
Literally: to get tangled up. Je me suis embrouillé avec lui means we clashed or fell out. Standard French keeps the literal sense (getting confused); youth speech made the conflict sense dominant.
English loan fully adopted by French youth culture, especially rap battles and social media feuds. Un clash entre deux rappeurs is a standard media phrase. Neutral and safe to use.
English loan, but in French rap culture it means a devastating one-liner in a verse or argument, not the end of a joke. Sa punchline a tué means his line was brutal. Everyday word for rap fans.
English loan naming a rapper's rhythm and delivery: il a un flow de malade. Extended as a compliment for anyone's style or ease. Pronounced the French way, one clean syllable. Safe everywhere casual.
Literally just: zone. Historically the shantytown belt around Paris; today traîner dans la zone means hanging around a rough neighborhood or wasting time outside. Root of zoner and zonard.
From la zone plus -ard. Someone who hangs around the streets with nothing to do, often marginal. Pejorative; describes a lifestyle judgment, so avoid labeling real people with it.
From la zone. On a zoné toute la journée means we wandered around all day doing nothing. Mild and self-deprecating when said about yourself; the verb lost most of the noun's rough edge.
Literally: OVEN! In rap slang, a spot where illegal street business runs day and night, so called because it never cools down. Heavy street connotation; comprehension only, never casual usage.
Clipped from English business. Faire du biz ranges from harmless side hustles to clearly illegal trade; rap usage leans shady. Tone depends entirely on context, so listen before assuming.
Literally: to have the hatred. Popularized by 90s banlieue culture and the film La Haine. J'ai trop la haine means I am seething. Expresses rage or deep frustration, not actual hate of a person.
Literally: to blow a cable, like an overloaded machine. Il a pété un câble means he completely lost his temper or his mind. Variants: péter les plombs (blow the fuses). Casual, very common.

items.en: to go off the rails, lose it
items.notes: Literally: to spin or spiral, like a plane in a tailspin. Youth slang: il a vrillé means he lost the plot, went too far, or acted crazy. Recent, viral on social media. Light and jokey in tone.
From Romani marav (to hit). Je vais le maraver is a common playground and street threat, usually more bluster than plan. Aggressive vocabulary; learn it to understand, not to use.
Literally built on frite: to fry! Se friter avec quelqu'un means having a fight or heated argument. Usually verbal rather than physical. Casual and widely understood across generations.
Literally: BREAD! Mettre un pain à quelqu'un means landing a punch on them. One of several food words for blows (also une patate, a potato). Casual; describes fights rather than starting them.

Old French for rabble. Politically loaded since a 2005 ministerial quote about cleaning out la racaille; can stigmatize whole neighborhoods. Understand it in rap and news, but avoid labeling people with it.
Literally: BADGER (the animal, also a shaving brush)! Insult for someone clueless or pathetic: quel blaireau. Mild by street standards but still an insult; keep it for joking among friends.

Literally: QUICHE, the tart! Être une quiche en maths means being terrible at math. Self-deprecating and gentle; one of the safest insult-shaped words in French, usable about yourself anywhere casual.
From crever (to die, to starve): someone so hungry for money or food they scrounge off everyone. T'es un crevard is a frequent friendly jab among youth. Insulting if said with real anger.
From Romani chorav (to steal); also spelled chouraver. On m'a chouré mon vélo means someone nicked my bike. Everyday word for petty theft; casual and safe to use when telling what happened.
Literally: to tax! Youth slang for taking something off someone, from borrowing (il m'a taxé un stylo) to strong-arm theft (se faire taxer son téléphone). Severity depends on context.

items.en: to strip someone of their stuff
items.notes: Standard meaning: to skin or strip (originally an animal's hide, la dépouille). Street meaning: robbing someone of jacket, phone, or sneakers: il s'est fait dépouiller. Describes victimization; use in stories.

Literally: PIGEON, the bird! A gullible person scammers pluck like a bird: se faire prendre pour un pigeon. Long-standing French argot adopted by youth. Mildly insulting, fine in complaints about being cheated.
From le baratin (smooth patter), old sailor and market argot. Il m'a baratiné means he fed me a smooth story, for flirting or for selling something dubious. Playful; implies charm plus exaggeration.
Literally: SORREL, the tangy green herb! Classic argot for money, revived hard by rap: faire de l'oseille means making money. Green leaves, green bills. Casual and safe among friends.

items.en: to be too lazy to bother
items.notes: Literally: to have the laziness. Means: can't be bothered. Very common, informal.
Literally: the laziness. Means: the can't-be-bothered feeling; often used alone as a full answer, La flemme! Very common, informal.
Literally: it's dead. Means: no way, that plan is over. Very common with young speakers, informal.
Literally: it's square. Means: it's sorted, done cleanly and properly. Trendy street slang, informal.
Literally: it's clean. Means: nicely done, impressive work. Trendy slang, informal.
Literally: it's gift. Means: it's free, my treat, no charge. Casual and friendly, informal.
Literally: it fears. Means: it's bad, dodgy or unsafe. Very common, informal.
Literally: it tears. Means: it's awesome, it rocks. Common, informal.
Literally: it sends. Means: it's powerful, it delivers, it's impressive. Informal, popular with young speakers.
Literally: it slaps. Means: it looks amazing, really stylish. Trendy slang, informal.
Literally: it stings. Means: it's harsh, spicy, or painfully expensive, depending on context. Common, informal.
Literally: it passes. Means: it's acceptable, good enough. Very common, informal.
Literally: it does it. Means: that works, that looks good. Common, informal.

items.en: it annoys me, I'm fed up
items.notes: Literally: it makes me drunk. Means: it annoys me, I'm fed up. Very common but mildly rude, informal.
Literally: it force-feeds me, like a goose. Means: it really annoys me, I've had enough. Informal and a bit blunt.
Literally: I am hallucinating. Means: I can't believe it, this is unreal. Common, informal.
Literally: I am dreaming. Means: I can't believe this, said with outrage or disbelief. Common, informal.
Literally: you are laughing. Means: you're kidding, you can't be serious. Very common, informal.
Literally: you surprise me. Means: no kidding, obviously, used ironically to agree. Very common, informal.
Literally: it would surprise me. Means: I doubt it, unlikely. Common, informal but safe anywhere.
Literally: it has left. Means: here we go, let's start. Very common, informal.
Literally: it's folded. Means: it's a wrap, over and decided. Common, informal.
Literally: it's regulated. Means: sorted, problem solved. Common, informal.
Literally: make see. Means: show me, let me see. Very common, informal.
Literally: go there. Means: go on, go ahead; can also sound annoyed or aggressive, as in Vas-y, arrête! Very common, informal.
Literally: stop your chariot, or your tank. Means: stop exaggerating, quit the act. Familiar, a bit old-school but understood everywhere.
Literally: no matter nawak, where nawak is a playful verlan-style twist on n'importe quoi. Means: total nonsense. Youth slang, informal.
Literally: by the nose, pif being slang for nose. Means: at random, by guesswork. Very common, informal.
Literally: by tearing. Means: done last minute or sloppily. Common youth slang, informal.
Literally: full on the balloons. Means: at full speed, going all out. Playful, informal.
Literally: in mode. Means: a filler meaning acting like or in a certain style, as in en mode discret. Youth slang, informal.
Literally: not even fear. Means: I'm not scared, bring it on. Playful, informal.
Literally: it's cake. Means: it's really easy. Common, informal.
Literally: it's heavy. Means: it's top quality, seriously impressive. Popular slang, informal.
Literally: it curdles. Means: it's freezing cold. Very common, informal.
Literally: we are curdling ourselves. Means: we're freezing out here. Very common, informal.
Literally: to have a little hollow. Means: to be peckish, a bit hungry. Friendly, informal.

items.en: I'm stuffed, I can't eat more
items.notes: Literally: I stall, like an engine. Means: I'm full, I can't eat another bite. Common at the table, informal.
Literally: to burst the shape. Means: to be bursting with energy, in fantastic form. Informal, mildly cheeky.

items.en: to be in top form, to be great
items.notes: Literally: to be at the top. Means: to feel great, or to be excellent. Very common, informal.
Literally: it's hot. Means: it's tricky, risky, or intense. Very common youth slang, informal.
Literally: it's the galley ship. Means: it's a real struggle, such a hassle. Very common, informal.

items.en: to struggle, to have a hard time
items.notes: Literally: to row on a galley ship. Means: to struggle, to have a hard time. Very common, informal.

items.en: to hit a sudden energy crash
items.notes: Literally: to have a hit of the bar. Means: to feel a sudden wave of tiredness. Very common, informal.

items.en: to feel great, full of energy
items.notes: Literally: to have the peach. Means: to feel great, full of energy. Common, informal.
Literally: to have the potato. Means: to be full of energy, in great shape. Common, informal.
Literally: to have the banana. Means: to wear a big smile, to be in a great mood. Common, informal.
Literally: it rolls. Means: all good, ok, deal. Very common, informal.
Literally: it gases. Means: things are going fine; also a greeting, Ça gaze? Informal, slightly retro but well known.
Literally: it bathes. Means: everything is going great. Informal, a bit retro but everyone gets it.
Literally: it's nickel, the shiny metal. Means: spotless, perfect, exactly right. Very common, informal.
Literally: it's ouf, where ouf is verlan, backwards slang, for fou, crazy. Means: it's crazy, unbelievable. Very common youth slang, informal.
Literally: to be at the stuffing. Means: to be running late. Very common, informal.
Literally: of the blow. Means: so, as a result; the number one French filler word. Extremely common, informal.
Literally: squarely. Means: totally, absolutely; also works alone as an enthusiastic yes. Very common, informal.
Literally: serious. Means: totally, so much; also works alone as a strong yes. Youth slang, very common, informal.
Literally: an interjection with no literal meaning. Means: meh, not great, unimpressed. Very common, informal.
Literally: you worry, with the don't part dropped. Means: don't worry, no stress. Very common youth slang, informal.
Literally: it's clear. Means: totally agree, so true. Very common, informal.
Literally: I confess. Means: true, fair point, agreed. Very common youth slang, informal.

items.en: to lose it, to flip out
items.notes: Literally: to burst a cable. Real meaning: to suddenly lose your temper or go crazy. Familier slang, very common among friends when someone snaps under stress.

items.en: to blow a fuse, to freak out
items.notes: Literally: to blow the fuses. Real meaning: to lose control of your emotions, to snap. Familier; interchangeable with péter un câble in everyday speech.
Literally: to trip like a circuit breaker. Real meaning: to go crazy or react wildly. Familier; said of someone acting irrationally, il a complètement disjoncté.
Literally: to break oneself. Real meaning: to leave, often abruptly. Familier; on se casse means we're out of here, casse-toi is rude.
Literally: to bar oneself away. Real meaning: to leave quickly, to run off. Familier; je me barre means I'm out of here.
Literally: to pull oneself. Real meaning: to leave, to slip away. Familier; on se tire is a casual way to say let's go.
Literally: to swarm oneself, from an old verb for teeming. Real meaning: to hurry. Familier; grouille-toi means get moving, used with friends and family.
Literally: to handle oneself, from the old verb manier. Real meaning: to hurry up. Familier; magne-toi is a blunt get moving, slightly stronger than se grouiller.
Literally: to have it level with the brim of the bowl. Real meaning: to be completely fed up. Familier; j'en ai ras le bol means I've had it up to here.
Literally: the brim-of-the-bowl. Real meaning: a general feeling of being fed up, often collective. Familier; newspapers use it too, le ras-le-bol des étudiants.
Literally: to break the feet. Real meaning: to annoy or pester someone. Familier; tu me casses les pieds means you're getting on my nerves, safe in any casual setting.
Literally: to take the head. Real meaning: to annoy, stress, or wear someone down mentally. Familier; ça me prend la tête means it's doing my head in.

items.en: to rack your brain, to bicker
items.notes: Literally: to take the cabbage, where chou is slang for head. Real meaning: to overthink or to argue with someone. Familier; on se prend le chou pour rien means we argue over nothing.
Literally: to dig into one's head. Real meaning: to think hard, to rack your brain for an answer. Familier but polite; fine at school or work.
Literally: to have the slab, old slang where la dalle meant the throat. Real meaning: to be very hungry. Familier; j'ai trop la dalle means I'm starving.
Literally: to have the fry. Real meaning: to feel energetic and upbeat. Familier; a slightly older-generation cousin of avoir la pêche, still heard everywhere.
Literally: to be at the wedge, a taquet is a stop block or cleat. Real meaning: to be at maximum effort or fully motivated. Familier; je suis au taquet means I'm giving it everything.
Literally: to hand over a blow of hand. Real meaning: to help someone out. Familier because of filer, slang for to give; tu peux me filer un coup de main means can you help me.
Literally: to place a rabbit. Real meaning: to not show up to a date or meeting without warning. Familier; il m'a posé un lapin means he stood me up.
Literally: to tell salads. Real meaning: to spin stories, to lie or exaggerate. Familier; arrête de raconter des salades means stop making things up.
Literally: to roll someone. Real meaning: to cheat or swindle someone. Familier; le vendeur m'a roulé means the seller ripped me off.
Literally: to get oneself rolled. Real meaning: to be cheated or scammed. Familier; je me suis fait rouler means I got conned, common after a bad deal.
Literally: to lead by boat. Real meaning: to deceive someone over time, to lead them on. Familier; il nous a menés en bateau pendant des mois means he strung us along for months.
Literally: to take a rake, like stepping on one and getting smacked. Real meaning: to be rejected when flirting or asking someone out. Familier; il a pris un râteau means he got turned down.
Literally: to take a jacket. Real meaning: to be rejected or to fail publicly, in love, business, or politics. Familier; il s'est pris une veste aux élections means he got crushed at the elections.
Literally: to fall in the water. Real meaning: a plan gets cancelled or collapses. Familier; nos vacances sont tombées à l'eau means our holiday plans fell through.
Literally: to fall from the clouds, nues is an old word for clouds. Real meaning: to be astonished by unexpected news. Familier; je suis tombé des nues means I could not believe my ears.
Literally: fingers in the nose. Real meaning: to do something with total ease. Familier; il a gagné les doigts dans le nez means he won without even trying.
Literally: quickly done. Real meaning: in a hurry or in a casual, minimal way. Familier; on mange vite fait means we grab a quick bite, je l'ai lu vite fait means I skimmed it.
Literally: on the thumb. Real meaning: quickly and without sitting down, usually about eating. Familier; manger sur le pouce means to grab food on the go.
Literally: to put the package. Real meaning: to put in maximum effort or resources. Familier; ils ont mis le paquet pour la fête means they went all out for the party.
Literally: to put the rubber, as in tires on the road. Real meaning: to accelerate hard or speed up work. Familier; on met la gomme means we push the pace.
Literally: to press on the mushroom, old gas pedals were mushroom-shaped. Real meaning: to accelerate, to speed up. Familier; mostly about driving, sometimes about work pace.

items.en: to swagger, to show off muscles
items.notes: Literally: to roll one's mechanics, meaning the shoulders. Real meaning: to strut around acting tough. Familier and mocking; il roule des mécaniques means he's playing the tough guy.

items.en: to act smart, to show off
items.notes: Literally: to do the clever one. Real meaning: to show off or act cocky. Familier; fais pas le malin means don't get smart with me, often said to kids.
Literally: to do kind-of. Real meaning: to fake it, to act as if. Familier youth speech; il fait genre il comprend means he's pretending to understand, also used alone as genre.
Literally: to do a boat-hook, the original sense of gaffe. Real meaning: to commit an embarrassing mistake. Familier; j'ai fait une gaffe means I put my foot in it.
Literally: it's not won. Real meaning: success is far from certain, often said with a sigh. Familier; avec lui, c'est pas gagné means with him, good luck with that.

items.fr: c'est pas la mer à boire
items.ipa: sɛ pa la mɛʁ a bwaʁ
items.respell: seh pah lah MEHR ah BWAHR
items.notes: Literally: it's not the sea to drink. Real meaning: it's not such a big deal, the task is doable. Familier; used to encourage someone who is complaining.

items.fr: il y a pas le feu
items.notes: Literally: there's no fire. Real meaning: no need to hurry. Familier; often shortened to y a pas le feu, sometimes extended to y a pas le feu au lac as a joke.
Literally: we're not paid by the piece, like factory piecework. Real meaning: take your time, nobody is timing us. Familier; a relaxed answer to someone hurrying you.
Literally: it tells me nothing. Real meaning: it doesn't appeal to me, or it doesn't ring a bell. Familier; le ciné ce soir, ça me dit rien means I'm not in the mood for the movies tonight.

items.fr: avoir un poil dans la main
items.ipa: avwaʁ œ̃ pwal dɑ̃ la mɛ̃
items.respell: ah-VWAHR uhn PWAHL dahn lah MAN
items.notes: Literally: to have a hair in the hand, it grew because the hand never works. Real meaning: to be very lazy. Familier and teasing; il a un poil dans la main means he never lifts a finger.

items.fr: coûter les yeux de la tête
items.ipa: kute lez jø də la tɛt
items.respell: koo-TAY layz YUH duh lah TEHT
items.notes: Literally: to cost the eyes of the head. Real meaning: to be extremely expensive. Familier; ce téléphone coûte les yeux de la tête means that phone costs an arm and a leg.
Literally: to throw the sponge, from boxing corners. Real meaning: to give up. Familier; après trois essais, j'ai jeté l'éponge means after three tries I quit.
Literally: to pass a soap. Real meaning: to tell someone off firmly. Familier; ma mère m'a passé un savon means my mother chewed me out.

items.en: to feel down, to have the blues
items.notes: Literally: to have the cockroach. Real meaning: to feel gloomy or homesick. Familier; j'ai le cafard ce soir means I'm feeling low tonight.

items.en: to have bigger fish to fry
items.notes: Literally: to have other cats to whip. Real meaning: to have more important things to deal with. Familier; j'ai d'autres chats à fouetter means I've got better things to do.
Literally: to give one's tongue to the cat. Real meaning: to admit you can't guess the answer. Familier; je donne ma langue au chat means I give up, tell me.

items.fr: mettre les pieds dans le plat
items.en: to put your foot in it
items.ipa: mɛtʁ le pje dɑ̃ lə pla
items.respell: MEHTR lay PYAY dahn luh PLAH
items.notes: Literally: to put the feet in the dish. Real meaning: to blurt out something tactless, or to raise a touchy subject bluntly. Familier; il a mis les pieds dans le plat means he said the awkward thing out loud.
Literally: to turn around the pot. Real meaning: to avoid getting to the point. Familier; arrête de tourner autour du pot means just say it already.
Literally: to cut hairs in four. Real meaning: to overanalyze tiny details. Familier; tu coupes les cheveux en quatre means you're nitpicking.

items.en: to make a big deal of it
items.notes: Literally: to make a whole cheese out of it. Real meaning: to blow something small out of proportion. Familier; n'en fais pas tout un fromage means don't make such a fuss.
Literally: to be in the moon. Real meaning: to be distracted, lost in thought. Familier; t'es encore dans la lune means your head is in the clouds again.
Literally: to be to the west. Real meaning: to be out of it, confused or half asleep. Familier; ce matin je suis complètement à l'ouest means I'm totally out of it this morning.

items.fr: ne pas être dans son assiette
items.en: to feel off, under the weather
items.ipa: nə pa ɛtʁ dɑ̃ sɔ̃n asjɛt
items.respell: nuh pah ZEHTR dahn sohn nah-SYEHT
items.notes: Literally: to not be in one's plate, assiette once meant seat or balance. Real meaning: to feel unwell or not yourself. Familier; je suis pas dans mon assiette means I'm feeling off today.
Literally: to fall in the apples. Means to faint or pass out. Everyday informal way to describe fainting, fine in any casual conversation.
Literally: to cost the skin of the backside. Means to be outrageously expensive. Mildly crude because of fesses (buttocks), fine with friends but avoid in formal settings.

items.en: to cost an arm and a leg
items.notes: Literally: to cost an arm. Means to be very expensive, the French cousin of cost an arm and a leg. Safe in any informal context.

items.en: to get ripped off, to be had
items.notes: Literally: to get oneself had. Means to be tricked, cheated or taken in. Very common in complaints about scams, prices or broken promises.
Literally: to get oneself swindled. Means to be ripped off, usually about money, prices or dodgy deals. Everyday informal, no shock value.
Literally: it's of the bullet, balle means bullet or ball. Means it's awesome, top quality. Upbeat youth slang, casual settings only.
Literally: it's deadly. Means it's brilliant or amazing. Watch context: un ennui mortel means deadly boring, so tone and situation decide the meaning.
Literally: it's a killing, a slaughter. Means it's incredible, used above all for amazing food. Casual and enthusiastic, very common among foodies.

items.en: to have friends in high places
items.notes: Literally: to have the long arm. Means to have influence and connections that open doors. Neutral informal, often said with a knowing tone.
Literally: to have the melon. Means to be full of oneself, as if the head swelled to melon size. Mocking but playful, common about athletes and stars.
Literally: to take the melon. Means to start acting cocky after some success. Focuses on the change: someone who used to be modest and no longer is.
Literally: to have the big head. Means to be conceited, too impressed with oneself. Interchangeable with avoir le melon, slightly more standard.
Literally: to tell it to oneself. Means to show off, act like a big shot. Dismissive youth slang: il se la raconte means he thinks he's something.

items.en: to act the part, to pose
items.notes: Literally: to play it for oneself. Means to pose or act a role, often with an adjective: se la jouer star means act like a celebrity. Casual and mocking.

items.fr: péter plus haut que son derrière
items.en: to be too big for one's boots
items.ipa: pete ply o kə sɔ̃ dɛʁjɛʁ
items.respell: pay-TAY PLÜ OH KUH SOHN deh-RYEHR
items.notes: Literally: to fart higher than one's backside. Means to be pretentious, to act above one's station. Crude but iconic, keep it for jokes among friends, never polite company.

items.fr: ne pas avoir inventé l'eau chaude
items.en: to be not the sharpest tool in the shed
items.ipa: nə pa avwaʁ ɛ̃vɑ̃te lo ʃod
items.respell: NUH PA a-VWAHR an-vahn-TAY LOH SHOHD
items.notes: Literally: to not have invented hot water. Means someone is not very bright. Mocking, said behind someone's back rather than to their face.
Literally: to have a grain, as in a grain of madness. Means to be slightly crazy, eccentric. Can be affectionate or mocking depending on tone.
Literally: to work from the hat, as if the head under it malfunctions. Means to be nuts. Dated but colorful, teasing rather than clinical.
Literally: to lose the ball, boule is slang for head. Means to go crazy or become very forgetful. Informal, often about stress or old age, use with tact.
Literally: to lose the pedals, like a cyclist whose feet slip off. Means to get flustered, lose track or lose control of a situation. Everyday informal.
Literally: to pedal in semolina. Means to flounder, to put in effort without any progress. Vivid and common at work or with tricky problems.
Literally: to row, like a galley rower. Means to struggle hard with little to show for it: je rame en maths means I'm struggling in maths. Very common.
Literally: to touch the bottom, like a swimmer reaching the floor of the pool. Means to hit rock bottom, morally or financially. Serious tone, still informal.

items.en: to get back on one's feet
items.notes: Literally: to climb back up the slope. Means to recover after a rough patch, health, money or morale. Encouraging and positive, safe everywhere informal.

items.fr: reprendre du poil de la bête
items.ipa: ʁəpʁɑ̃dʁ dy pwal də la bɛt
items.respell: ruh-PRAHNDR DÜ PWAL DUH LA BEHT
items.notes: Literally: to take back some of the beast's hair, from an old belief that the animal that bit you could cure you. Means to regain strength, to bounce back.
Literally: to have some bowl, bol is old slang for luck. Means to be lucky. Pas de bol means tough luck. Extremely common everyday slang.

items.en: to be jammy, to be lucky
items.notes: Literally: to have some pot or jar. Means to be lucky, same family as avoir du bol. Coup de pot means a stroke of luck. Casual and harmless.
Literally: to lack pot, meaning to lack luck. Means to be unlucky. Manque de pot! as an exclamation means bad luck, what rotten timing.
Literally: to carry the pitch, poisse comes from sticky tar. Means to bring bad luck, to jinx. Avoir la poisse means to be dogged by bad luck.
Literally: to have the scoumoune, a Corsican and Italian borrowing for a curse. Means to be chronically jinxed. Colorful Mediterranean slang, jokey in tone.
Literally: to touch wood. Said to ward off bad luck after mentioning good fortune, like knock on wood. People often tap a table as they say it.
Literally: to break the shack. Means to be a smash hit, to wow the crowd. Casser la baraque à quelqu'un flips it: to wreck someone's plans.
Literally: to set the fire. Figuratively means to set the place alight, to get a crowd or party going wild. Common for DJs, concerts and big nights out.
Literally: built on foutre, an old vulgar verb. Means to not care at all: je m'en fous. WARNING vulgar: extremely common but coarse. With polite company say s'en ficher or ça m'est égal.
Literally: to stick or pin oneself of it. Means to not care, the milder everyday cousin of s'en foutre. Je m'en fiche is fine almost anywhere informal.
Literally: to stick the peace on someone. Means to leave someone in peace: fiche-moi la paix means leave me alone. Blunt but not vulgar.
Literally: to pitch the camp, here to break it and go. Means to clear off, to scram: fiche le camp! Sharp but printable, a notch politer than cruder versions.
Literally: to clear the floor. Means to leave, usually as an order: débarrasse le plancher! means out, now. Theatrical and firm, informal only.

items.fr: prendre ses cliques et ses claques
items.ipa: pʁɑ̃dʁ se klik e se klak
items.respell: PRAHNDR SAY KLEEK AY SAY KLAK
items.notes: Literally: to take one's cliques and claques. In old slang cliques were legs and claques were slaps or old shoes. Means to grab all your stuff and leave for good.
Literally: to set the sails. Means to take off, to leave, like a ship catching the wind. Casual and slightly jaunty: on met les voiles? shall we head off?

items.en: to break camp, to head off
items.notes: Literally: to raise the camp, like soldiers striking their tents. Means to pack up and go. Neutral informal, works for groups leaving a place together.
Literally: to take the escape powder, as if a magic powder helped you vanish. Means to run off, to do a runner. Old-fashioned but beloved and jokey.

items.en: to be at the end of one's rope
items.notes: Literally: to be at the end of the roll, like a spool with no thread left. Means to be exhausted, drained or out of resources. Serious, use with empathy.
Literally: to grind black, like a painter mixing only dark pigment. Means to brood, to dwell on dark thoughts. Informal but a bit literary in flavor.
Literally: to take one's own head. Means to overthink, stress or argue endlessly. Une prise de tête is a headache of a situation. Very common youth speech.

items.en: to get on someone's last nerve
items.notes: Literally: to run on someone's bean. Means to seriously get on someone's nerves: tu me cours sur le haricot. Quirky, jokey, safe among friends.
Literally: to look for the little beast, like hunting for a tiny bug. Means to nitpick, to hunt for flaws on purpose. Mildly reproachful, everyday use.

items.en: to be in a real jam
items.notes: Literally: to be in the kneading trough, stuck in dough like a baker's mixer. Means to be in serious trouble. Common, mild, works in most casual settings.
Literally: to be in the bread soup, panade is a mush of old bread. Means to be in trouble, often broke. Slightly more street than être dans le pétrin.

items.en: to pull the wool over someone's eyes
items.notes: Literally: to roll someone in flour, coating them like a fish before frying. Means to con or dupe someone: je me suis fait rouler dans la farine, I got played.

items.fr: être à côté de la plaque
items.en: to be way off the mark
items.ipa: ɛtʁ a kote də la plak
items.respell: EHTR A koh-TAY DUH LA PLAK
items.notes: Literally: to be beside the plate, like a shot missing the target plate. Means to be way off the mark, to misread the situation completely. Everyday informal.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast), now pan-West African. A girl or girlfriend; crossed into France youth slang in the 2010s.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast), from Mande mogo, person. A guy, a buddy; can also mean an influential man.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast). A guy, a young man; often used to address a friend.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast), from English enjoy. To have a great time; the word later spread to youth slang in France.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast), from Mande. Hard work or a job; aller au bara means to go to work.
West and Central Africa. Literally: okra, the vegetable. In street French, a lucrative side job or a good little deal.
Ivory Coast, spread across West Africa. Also standard French for scrubland and the WWII Resistance hideouts. In Abidjan, a casual spot for grilled fish, attiéké and cold drinks.
Ivory Coast. Cheap street meal of fried tuna served on attiéké; a student and worker staple in Abidjan.
Cameroon and Nigeria border French, from Pidgin English sharp sharp. Do it chap-chap: fast, no dawdling.
Benin. From Fon, roughly: take me quickly. The moto-taxi of Cotonou, usually shortened to zém.
Cameroon and Senegal. Clipped from clandestin, clandestine. An informal, unregistered taxi that works set neighborhoods.
Congo-Brazzaville and DRC. Member of the SAPE, the Société des Ambianceurs et des Personnes Élégantes; a devoted sharp dresser.

items.en: to liven up, to get the party going
items.notes: West and Central Africa, from ambiance. To set the mood, heat up a party, or party hard yourself.
West and Central Africa. The one who brings the fun; it is the A in SAPE, Société des Ambianceurs et des Personnes Élégantes.
Mali, also Burkina Faso. Group of friends who meet daily around strong tea to talk football, politics and life.
