Senegal, Gambia, Mauritania. From Wolof, ultimately Arabic. Three slow rounds of sweet green tea shared with friends; a social institution.
Senegal. From Wolof dibi. Small shop where mutton is grilled and sold by weight, eaten with mustard and onions.
Senegal, from Wolof. The grilled meat itself, sold at a dibiterie and wrapped in kraft paper.
Senegal. From Wolof tanga, hot. Street stall serving coffee, bread, omelettes and beans late into the night.
Senegal. The brightly painted blue and yellow Dakar minibus, an icon of the city despite its age.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast). Privately run minibus of Abidjan, famous for its apprenti hanging out the door calling the route.
Ivory Coast. Cheap shared taxi running a fixed neighborhood route in Abidjan, unlike the metered orange taxis.
Across Francophone Africa. Shared intercity car or van that leaves when full; brousse means the bush.
Mali. From the SOTRAMA transport company. The green minibus of Bamako, packed and cheap.
Senegal, Mali, wider West Africa. From Wolof; one debated origin links it to toubib, doctor. Neutral everyday word for a white person or Westernized foreigner, descriptive rather than insulting.
Cameroon. Juicy gossip or rumor-mongering; faire le kongossa means to trade the neighborhood news.
Everyday word across Francophone Africa. Clipped from paludisme. J'ai le palu is said as casually as having the flu.
DRC and Congo-Brazzaville. Fast Congolese dance and music style of the 1990s and 2000s, popular across the whole continent.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast), from Mande muso, woman. A woman or girlfriend.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast). A naive, clueless person, easy to fool; made famous continent-wide by Magic System's hit Premier Gaou.
Ivory Coast, wider West Africa. Literally: old father. Affectionate, respectful term for an elder or mentor; later picked up by rap in France.
Senegal. From Wolof. The celebrated culture of welcome and generosity; the national football team is the Lions de la Téranga.
Across Francophone Africa. Informal savings group where everyone pays in and each member takes the pot in turn. Also standard French for an old life-annuity scheme.
African French. In standard French it means to associate with someone; in much of Africa, il fréquente simply means he goes to school.
West and Central Africa. Literally: tar. The paved road as opposed to dirt tracks; prendre le goudron means to hit the road.
Francophone Africa and Belgium. The everyday word for a taxi driver; the plural is often taximen.
African French. A lengthy community discussion or a drawn-out dispute; the arbre à palabres is the village tree where matters get debated.
West Africa. Amulet prepared by a marabout for protection or luck; also spelled gri-gri.
Francophone Africa and Belgium. From the Bic brand; the everyday word for any pen. Prête-moi ton bic.
Senegal, wider West Africa. From Wolof. Sweet dark-red drink made from hibiscus flowers, sold chilled in little bags.
Ivory Coast. Grated fermented cassava, the Abidjan staple, served with grilled fish or as the base of garba.
Ivory Coast. Fried sweet plantain sold as street food; a whole Abidjan food spot is called the Allocodrome.
Ivory Coast. Dense pounded dough of plantain or yam eaten with sauce; close cousin of the foufou found elsewhere in Africa.
Senegal. Short for thiéboudienne, from Wolof ceebu jën, rice with fish; the national dish.
West and Central Africa. In standard French, a sweet or a sugar factory; in African French, any fizzy drink. Une sucrerie bien glacée.
West Africa. The neighborhood shopkeeper, often selling in tiny quantities and on credit; a fixture of daily life.
Senegal. From Wolof. Percussion-driven dance music built on sabar drums, made world-famous by Youssou N'Dour.
Ivory Coast. Danceable music born in 1990s student housing, with witty social lyrics; Magic System started in zouglou.
Burkina Faso and Mali. Home-brewed millet beer sold in small cabarets; the woman who brews it is the dolotière.
Senegal. Senegalese French for a station-service, formed from essence, fuel; a proud local coinage.
Ivory Coast, wider West Africa. Small-sided street football played on any patch of ground; named after Brazil's Maracana stadium.
Niger. From Hausa. Group of young people who meet at the same street corner for tea and talk, like the Malian grin.
Ivory Coast, Benin, Togo. Literally: what do we say? Friendly greeting between friends; a classic answer is on est là.
West and Central Africa. Literally: it is how? Casual greeting; with the right tone it can also mean, so what is the problem?
Pan-African. Warm formula of solidarity used to close a conversation: we are in this together, count on me.
Pan-African, emblematic of Ivory Coast. The phrase of everyday optimism, offered for any hardship from a breakup to a breakdown.
West and Central Africa. From gâter, to spoil. Said of anything broken or gone wrong, from a phone to a plan to the traffic.
Ivory Coast, wider West Africa. Literally: it is soft, sweet. High praise for food, music or a good moment.
West Africa. Literally: to ask for the road. Polite way to announce you are leaving a host; tradition allows the host to refuse once.
Ivory Coast, from Akan. Word of sympathy said to someone in trouble or in mourning: sorry, courage.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast). Noun of s'enjailler, from English enjoy; the buzz and thrill of a good party.
Congo-Brazzaville and DRC. The doctrine of the Société des Ambianceurs et des Personnes Élégantes: dressing sharp as an art of living.
DRC and West Africa, humorous. Literally: second office. A married man's mistress, as if he were working late at another office.
Ivory Coast, from the coupé-décalé scene. From boucan, noise, din. Someone who makes a show of designer labels and cash.
Senegal. Literally: the thiof, a prized grouper fish of Senegalese cooking. A desirable, well-off man everyone wants to land.
DRC and Congo-Brazzaville, from Lingala. Everyday word for a white person or European; descriptive and often teasing rather than hostile.
Cameroon, from Duala. Getting things free of charge; manger njoh means to eat without paying a franc.
Cameroon (Camfranglais). Europe, and especially France, seen as the dream destination; partir au Mbeng.

items.en: emigrant who made it to Europe
items.notes: Cameroon. From Mbeng, Europe. Someone living in Europe, expected to come home showing off success.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast). Cash; one of the many Nouchi words for money.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast). Literally: there is no sheet. Nothing to hide, no problem; often shortened to y a pas drap.

items.en: to show off, to throw money around
items.notes: Ivory Coast and Cameroon. To flaunt wealth, buy rounds, spray banknotes at a party; the one who does it is a faroteur.
DRC, humorous. A mythical constitutional article said to read débrouillez-vous, sort yourselves out; shorthand for everyday resourcefulness.
DRC and Congo-Brazzaville. From Lingala mikili, the worlds. Someone who has gone to live in Europe, often tied to sapeur culture.
Ivory Coast. Literally: one who grazes. Online romance scammer, so named because the money comes easy, like a sheep grazing.
Nouchi (Ivory Coast). Nosy person who reports everyone's business around the neighborhood; can also mean a snitch.
Cameroon. Smooth-talking scammer running get-rich schemes; the trade itself is called la feymania.
Ivory Coast, humorous. From titre, headline. Someone who reads and loudly debates the newspaper front pages at the kiosk without buying one.
Cameroon, wider West and Central Africa, humorous. Literally: thousand-eater, from the 1000-franc CFA notes collected at road checkpoints.
DRC and Congo-Brazzaville, from Portuguese matar o bicho. A tip or small grease payment that smooths things along.
Warning: smoking vocabulary, given factually. Originally a cigarette butt in 1800s argot, then the cigarette itself. Extremely current at every age.
Warning: smoking vocabulary, factual. Origin debated, attested since the 1800s; gave the verb megoter, to skimp. Still the everyday word.
Literally: tole, sheet metal. Argot for prison since the 1800s; in older usage also a cheap hotel or any room. Still fully current for prison.
Prison inmate, from taule plus the -ard suffix. Heard in every French crime film. Still current, informal.
Room, digs. Old argot attested since the 1800s, from a dialect word for a drinking den. Still very current, especially for a student room.
Warning: alcohol vocabulary. From the pinot grape; spread by soldiers in the 1914-1918 trenches. Slightly dated but everyone knows it.
Money; from an old verb meaning to grab with the fist. Attested since the 1800s. Still totally current.
Literally: sorrel, the tart green plant. Argot for money since the 1800s. Still heard.
Literally: wheat. Money pictured as grain, argot for centuries. Still very current.
Literally: a flat round cake. Money by the round shape of coins. Avoir de la galette is dated but understood; still met in films.
Money; from Arabic fulus, coins, via North Africa. Also spelled flouse. A bit dated but still heard.
Money in 1950s gangster argot; origin unclear, maybe from gris, an old coin word. Immortalized by the film Touchez pas au grisbi, 1954. Dated; used today for retro flavor.
Doctor; from Arabic tabib, brought back by soldiers from North Africa in the 1800s. Completely current and affectionate.
Same thing either way; from Arabic kif, like. Usually c'est kif-kif. Attested since the 1800s; still current.
Literally: the belly, from bidon. A show that fails fait un bide, falls flat on its belly. Both senses still current.
To flop, of a show or joke; literally to do a belly, like an acrobat landing flat. Showbiz argot since the 1800s. Still current.
Literally: an animal's maw. For a human face or mouth it is rude; ta gueule means shut up and is aggressive. Strong warning, but you will hear it constantly.
Brawl; from baston, the old form of baton, the stick. Often heard as la baston or chercher la baston. Still current, laddish.
Clipped from roman policier in 1950s slang. Fully current and almost standard now.
Literally: turnip. A bad film or painting, a dud, since the 1800s. Still totally current.
Woman in classic argot; feminine of the old gonze, fellow, from Italian gonzo. Dated and can now sound sexist or dismissive; know it from films, use with care.
The cheeky Paris street kid, the titi parisien of Gavroche fame; from a childish doubling of petit. Dated as a social type but alive as a cultural reference.
The mocking, quick wit of old street Paris; from an old verb meaning to jeer. Slightly literary now; the classic word for Piaf-style banter.
Glib talk; from the old verb bagouler, to talk away. Also spelled bagout. Still current.

items.en: to have the gift of the gab
items.notes: To talk a good game, to charm with words; from bagouler, to chatter. Still current and appreciative.
Literally: the bottom of a lamp or crucible, the last bit left. Cheek, nerve: quel culot! Still fully current.
Literally: a tuft of hair, as in toupee. Nerve, audacity: il a du toupet. Slightly dated but still heard.
Literally: a round, a circle, hence a coin. Mostly survives in ne pas avoir un rond, to be broke. Still current in that phrase.
Not a cent, flat broke; literally not one round, one coin. Still very current.
Stingy person; from old argot radin, the shop till, the drawer you refuse to open. Still completely current and mildly teasing.

items.en: to show up, to roll in
items.notes: To show up: radine-toi means get over here. Origin disputed, attested since the 1800s alongside radin. Familiar and still current.
Literally: panade, a humble bread soup. Etre dans la panade is to be in dire straits. Still heard, homely and vivid.
Hard-up poverty; probably from decher, an old gambling word for losing money. Attested since the 1800s. Still current.
To be broke, in the hole. Classic since the 1800s; still what people say when the month outlasts the money.
Literally: mowed down, cut like wheat by the scythe. Broke, cleaned out; the image pairs with ble, money as wheat. Still extremely current.
Deep poverty; from a German dialect word for mush or gruel. Etre dans la mouise. A bit dated but still met.
Warning: pejorative clipping of clochard for a homeless person. You will hear it, but prefer sans-abri or SDF when speaking. Still current, sadly.
Literally: from cloche, the bell; vagrants were said to live by the ringing of the bells. Neutral-dated in old films; today prefer sans-abri in conversation.
Literally: the bell. Also the old vagrant world, etre a la cloche; and se taper la cloche means to feast. One word, three lives; the idioms are dated but known.
To eat royally; literally to hit the bell, probably the dinner bell. Classic and still used with a grin.
Warning: weapon vocabulary, kept factual; you meet it in every crime film. From German Flinte, musket. Still current in fiction and news.
Warning: weapon vocabulary. From flingue. Also figurative: critics flinguent a bad film. Both uses current.
Warning: weapon vocabulary. Derisive word for a clapped-out firearm, from peter, to bang. Dated and comic, found in period fiction.
Clipped and twisted from rendez-vous; also spelled rancard. In older argot it also meant a tip, a piece of information. Still current for a date.
To fill someone in; from rencard in its information sense. Crime-film staple. Still understood, slightly dated.
Literally: pipe. A tip, information whispered as through a pipe; racing slang from the 1800s. Still current: un bon tuyau.
To give someone the inside track; from tuyau, the pipe. Still heard, faintly retro.
Angle, workaround; clipped from combinaison. Il a une combine, he knows a trick. Still very current.
Someone who always has an angle; from combine plus -ard. Mildly pejorative. Still heard.
Literally: a magot is a Barbary macaque, and also a grotesque porcelain figurine in which people hid coins. Hence a hidden pile of money. Still current for a nest egg.
Complicated mess; also spelled bins. Origin obscure, army slang of the early 1900s. Quel binz! Still heard, casual.
Utter mess. Warning: the original sense was a brothel, so it stays coarse; fine among friends, not in a meeting. Still current.
Literally: Capernaum, the Galilean town packed with crowds in the Gospels. A room in total chaos. Literary-familiar and still used with relish.
Literally: the Arabic word for a market. A noisy mess: quel souk dans ta chambre! Current, but stay aware of the borrowed origin.
From Ramadan, for the lively nighttime meals during the fast; a colonial-era borrowing worth naming respectfully. Faire du ramdam. Somewhat dated now.
Literally: an old word for a smokehouse grill, the same root that gave boucanier, the buccaneer who smoked meat. Faire du boucan is still current.
Faire du raffut, to kick up a din; from an old verb raffuter. Also modern rugby slang for a hand-off. Still current.
Noise, and by extension bother: tout ce tintouin. From tinter, to ring. Dated-charming but still heard from older speakers.
From chambarder, to knock everything over, 1800s sailor slang. Dated but met in books and older speech.
Literally: the java, the accordion waltz of the old Paris dance halls. Faire la java came to mean to party hard. Retro flavor, still understood.
To party; from the java, the musette dance craze of the 1920s. Dated but affectionately used.
Faire la bringue, to go on a spree; from a Swiss German word for a toast. Still current, a shade less youthful than faire la fete.
From Arabic nawba, the music of the Maghreb regimental bands. Faire la nouba. Dated but everyone understands.
To celebrate hard; from the nawba regimental music, a colonial-era borrowing. Retro but understood everywhere.
To dance, in old popular Paris; origin obscure, linked to a word for swaying. Dated, kept alive by retro dance halls.
The dancing, or the hall itself: aller au guinche. From guincher. Distinctly old Paris, retro usage.
The riverside dance cafe of the Marne and Seine; from guinguet, the sharp little local wine served there. Back in fashion, fully understood.
Warning: alcohol vocabulary. To drink steadily; from piccolo, a light table wine of the 1800s. Still very current.
Warning: alcohol vocabulary. From picric acid, for the chemical bite of bad red. Dated, found in Audiard dialogue.
Literally: a firing, the baking of pottery or bricks. Being thoroughly cooked by drink. Warning: alcohol vocabulary. Still fully current.
Warning: alcohol vocabulary. Literally to take a firing, like clay in the kiln. Still current.
Literally: a wooden mouth, dry as wood the morning after. Warning: alcohol vocabulary. The standard word, utterly current.
Warning: alcohol vocabulary. From soul, drunk, itself literally sated. Il ne dessoule jamais is a stock phrase. Current.
The old cafe of northern France and Belgium, beer and tobacco smoke; a Walloon word. Historic term, revived on heritage signs in Lille and Flanders.
The owner behind the bistro counter; from bistrot. Everyday word in cafe culture, still current.
Literally: the tour, the round. A round of drinks bought for the whole table. Warning: alcohol vocabulary. Completely current.
Literally: it is my tour. Warning: alcohol vocabulary. The classic cafe sentence, fully current.
Playful reshaping of pourboire with the argot -iche ending. Dated but still heard from waiters of a certain age.
The Marseille classic; from Provencal fadat, touched by the fairies, the same root as fee. Affectionate. Current in the south, known everywhere thanks to Pagnol.
Literally: a foot-breaker, someone who breaks your feet with boredom. Polite enough for any table. Still very current.
Literally: a shaver, someone who scrapes at you until you are numb. Dated-elegant; still met in classic novels and older speech.
Literally: to shave. To bore someone: ca me rase; the 1800s image of the razor dragging on and on. Dated, like the reflexive se raser, to be bored.
Literally: to beard someone, from barbe. Ca me barbe, that bores me. Dated but still said by older speakers.
Literally: the beard!, boredom pictured as an old man's endless beard. Interjection. Dated-charming, still understood.
Any fellow: un pekin moyen. Old military slang for a civilian; origin debated, perhaps from pekin cloth, not the city. Dated but met in fiction.
Some unnamed person; straight Latin quidam, a certain one, from courtroom language. Ironic-literary register. Current in journalism.
An odd customer: faire le zigoto, to fool around. From zig, pal, plus a fancy ending. Dated but affectionate.
Literally: zebra. An odd character: un drole de zebre, a strange stripe of fellow. Attested since the 1800s. Still heard.
From German lustig, merry, via the regiments' jester. Ces petits loustics. Dated-affectionate, still used for kids.
An eccentric; also the adjective. Revived by Malraux in the 1930s from an old word for puffed up. Fully current and gentle.
This is louchebem, the butchers' coded slang: fou with its first letter moved and wrapped, l-oufo-que. Fully current; often shortened to louf.
The butcher shops' code itself: move a word's first consonant to the end, add l- in front and -em after; boucher becomes louchebem. Alive as a curiosity among Paris butchers.
Louchebem-style twist of feuille, leaf, from portefeuille. Classic pickpocket argot. Dated but relished by argot lovers.
Louchebem of en douce: discreetly, without being seen. Crime-film flavor, dated but understood.
Literally: in soft. Partir en douce, to slip away quietly. Fully current.
Literally: in go-fast style. Un travail fait a la va-vite. Still fully current.
Classic explanation: a face dashed off with three strokes shaped like a 6, a 4 and a 2. Dated but still in dictionaries and older mouths.
Literally: at the unbooting, the moment a rider pulls off his boots. Catching someone au debotte means catching them the instant they arrive. Elegant-dated; journalists still use it.
Straight Latin illico, on the spot. Often doubled as illico presto. Familiar and fully current.
Faire fissa, to hurry; from Arabic fi s-sa'a, within the hour, via North Africa army slang. Still current.
From bafouiller, to splutter; a letter as spluttered words on paper. Dated but cherished: je t'ecris une bafouille.
From Godillot, the army bootmaker under Napoleon III whose name became the soldier's boot. Still fully current.
Literally: a fruit pip. A snag: avoir un pepin. In older argot also an umbrella. The snag sense is fully current.
Literally: a stake, a post. The bed: aller au pieu. Attested since the 1800s. Still very current.
From pieu, the stake turned bed. Je vais me pieuter. Still current, relaxed.
To sleep; an old popular verb of obscure origin with roots back in early argot. Still very current.
Piquer un roupillon, to grab forty winks; from roupiller. Still current and cosy.
From costume plus the argot -ard ending. En costard cravate, suited and tied. Still completely current.
Trousers in 1800s argot; origin uncertain, possibly Germanic. Dated but alive in films and banter.
Sales spiel, sweet talk; from old argot barat, deceit, the same root as English barratry. Faire du baratin. Still fully current.

items.fr: Le café est chaud, fais attention.
items.en: The coffee is hot, be careful.
items.notes: “est” (from être) and “ai” sound alike here, but only “est” fits after “le café”.

items.fr: Notre maison a un grand jardin.
items.en: Our house has a big garden.
items.ipa: nɔtʁ mɛ.zɔ̃ a œ̃ ɡʁɑ̃ ʒaʁ.dɛ̃
items.notes: “a” (from avoir) has no accent, unlike “à” (to/at).

items.fr: Elle se réveille tôt et elle se lève sans bruit.
items.en: She wakes up early and gets up quietly.
items.ipa: ɛl sə ʁe.vɛj to e ɛl sə lɛv sɑ̃ bʁɥi
items.notes: “tôt” has a circumflex; it is not the same word as “taux”.

items.fr: Ces chaussures sont trop petites pour moi.
items.en: These shoes are too small for me.
items.ipa: se ʃo.syʁ sɔ̃ tʁo pə.tit puʁ mwa
items.notes: “ces” (these) is not “ses” (his/her) here: the shoes belong to no one in particular.

items.fr: Nous avons acheté tout ce dont nous avions besoin.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ aʃ.te tu sə dɔ̃ nu.z‿a.vjɔ̃ bə.zwɛ̃
items.notes: “dont” replaces “de + quoi”; it never doubles as “don” or takes an extra t.

items.fr: Elle coupe les oignons avant de les faire cuire.
items.en: She cuts the onions before cooking them.
items.ipa: ɛl kup le.z‿ɔ.ɲɔ̃ a.vɑ̃ də le fɛʁ kɥiʁ
items.notes: “oignons” keeps a silent i: it sounds like “ognons”, not “oi-gnons”.

items.fr: Mon frère et ma sœur habitent à Lyon.
items.en: My brother and my sister live in Lyon.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ fʁɛʁ e ma sœʁ a.bit a ljɔ̃
items.notes: “habitent” starts with a silent h, so “et” links smoothly right before it.

items.fr: Mes amis sont arrivés en retard, comme toujours.
items.en: My friends arrived late, as always.
items.ipa: me.z‿a.mi sɔ̃.t‿a.ʁi.ve ɑ̃ ʁə.taʁ kɔm tu.ʒuʁ
items.notes: “sont” (from être) is not “son” (his/her): listen for the nasal sound before “arrivés”.

items.fr: Mon collègue m’a envoyé un courriel important ce matin.
items.en: My colleague sent me an important email this morning.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ kɔ.lɛɡ ma ɑ̃.vwa.je œ̃ ku.ʁjɛl ɛ̃.pɔʁ.tɑ̃ sə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “collègue” takes a grave accent on the second e, never an acute one.

items.en: Good morning madam, how are you today?
items.notes: French keeps a space before a question mark: “vous ?”, never “vous?”.

items.fr: J’ai mal aux dents depuis hier soir.
items.en: I have had a toothache since last night.
items.ipa: ʒe mal o dɑ̃ də.pɥi jɛʁ swaʁ
items.notes: “aux” contracts “à” and “les”: never write “à les dents”.

items.fr: Il tousse beaucoup et il a un peu de fièvre.
items.en: He is coughing a lot and has a slight fever.
items.ipa: il tus bo.ku e i.l‿a œ̃ pø də fjɛvʁ
items.notes: “fièvre” takes a grave accent, not an acute one.

items.fr: Le médecin lui a conseillé de se reposer davantage.
items.en: The doctor advised him to rest more.
items.ipa: lə med.sɛ̃ lɥi a kɔ̃.se.je də sə ʁə.po.ze da.vɑ̃.taʒ
items.notes: “conseillé” ends in é because it follows “a” in the passé composé.

items.fr: Prendre soin de soi n’est pas un luxe, c’est une nécessité.
items.en: Taking care of yourself is not a luxury, it is a necessity.
items.ipa: pʁɑ̃dʁ swɛ̃ də swa nɛ pa.z‿œ̃ lyks sɛ.t‿yn ne.se.si.te
items.notes: “c’est” (it is) is not “s’est” (reflexive past): nothing reflexive happens here.

items.fr: Elle est infirmière dans un grand hôpital.
items.en: She is a nurse in a big hospital.
items.notes: “hôpital” keeps its circumflex, a trace of the s that used to follow it.

items.fr: Nous avons une réunion à neuf heures précises.
items.en: We have a meeting at nine o’clock sharp.
items.notes: “heures” is feminine, so “précises” takes the feminine plural ending.

items.fr: L’entreprise a signé un contrat avec ses nouveaux partenaires.
items.en: The company signed a contract with its new partners.
items.ipa: lɑ̃.tʁə.pʁiz a si.ɲe œ̃ kɔ̃.tʁa a.vɛk se nu.vo paʁ.tə.nɛʁ
items.notes: “ses” (its, possessive) is not “ces” (these): the partners belong to the company.

items.fr: Le train part à huit heures et quart.
items.en: The train leaves at a quarter past eight.
items.ipa: lə tʁɛ̃ paʁ a ɥi.t‿œʁ e kaʁ
items.notes: “huit” starts with a mute h, so “à” links straight onto it.

items.fr: Nous avons visité plusieurs musées pendant notre séjour.
items.en: We visited several museums during our stay.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ vi.zi.te ply.zjœʁ my.ze pɑ̃.dɑ̃ nɔtʁ se.ʒuʁ
items.notes: “musées” ends in ées, agreeing in number with “plusieurs”.

items.fr: Nous avons réservé une chambre avec vue sur la mer.
items.en: We booked a room with a sea view.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ʁe.zɛʁ.ve yn ʃɑ̃bʁ a.vɛk vy syʁ la mɛʁ
items.notes: “réservé” stays invariable here: the direct object “une chambre” comes after the verb.

items.fr: Elle est canadienne, mais elle habite en France.
items.en: She is Canadian, but she lives in France.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿ɛ ka.na.djɛn mɛ.z‿ɛl a.bit ɑ̃ fʁɑ̃s
items.notes: Nationality adjectives like “canadienne” take a lowercase letter in French.

items.fr: Il pleut depuis ce matin, et le ciel est gris.
items.en: It has been raining since this morning, and the sky is grey.
items.ipa: il plø də.pɥi sə ma.tɛ̃ e lə sjɛl ɛ ɡʁi
items.notes: “depuis” never takes a circumflex; do not confuse it with “dès”.

items.fr: Le chat dort sur le canapé toute la journée.
items.en: The cat sleeps on the sofa all day.
items.ipa: lə ʃa dɔʁ syʁ lə ka.na.pe tut la ʒuʁ.ne
items.notes: “dort” (from dormir) ends in a silent t.

items.fr: La vallée est entourée de montagnes couvertes de neige.
items.en: The valley is surrounded by mountains covered in snow.
items.ipa: la va.le ɛ.t‿ɑ̃.tu.ʁe də mɔ̃.taɲ ku.vɛʁt də nɛʒ
items.notes: “entourée” agrees with “la vallée” (feminine), so it ends in ée.

items.fr: Il faut réduire nos déchets pour protéger l’environnement.
items.en: We must reduce our waste to protect the environment.
items.ipa: il fo ʁe.dɥiʁ no de.ʃɛ puʁ pʁo.te.ʒe lɑ̃.vi.ʁɔn.mɑ̃
items.notes: “environnement” doubles the n but takes only one m.

items.fr: Les élèves écoutent attentivement la maîtresse.
items.en: The students listen attentively to the teacher.
items.notes: “maîtresse” keeps the circumflex from “maître”, even with the feminine ending.

items.fr: Les mathématiques sont sa matière préférée.
items.ipa: le ma.te.ma.tik sɔ̃ sa ma.tjɛʁ pʁe.fe.ʁe
items.notes: “mathématiques” is always plural in French, even where English uses a singular.

items.fr: Elle s’est inscrite à l’université l’année dernière.
items.en: She enrolled at the university last year.
items.ipa: ɛl sɛ.t‿ɛ̃.skʁit a ly.ni.vɛʁ.si.te la.ne dɛʁ.njɛʁ
items.notes: “s’est” (reflexive past) is not “c’est” (it is): here she enrolled herself.

items.fr: Les chercheurs ont publié leurs résultats dans une revue scientifique.
items.en: The researchers published their results in a scientific journal.
items.ipa: le ʃɛʁ.ʃœʁ ɔ̃ py.bli.e lœʁ ʁe.zyl.ta dɑ̃.z‿yn ʁə.vy sjɑ̃.ti.fik
items.notes: “leurs” takes an s here: the results belong to several researchers.

items.fr: Mon téléphone n’a plus de batterie.
items.en: My phone has no battery left.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ te.le.fɔn na ply də ba.tʁi
items.notes: The negation is “ne … plus”, not “ne … pas plus”.

items.fr: Elle télécharge un fichier depuis son ordinateur.
items.en: She is downloading a file from her computer.
items.ipa: ɛl te.le.ʃaʁʒ œ̃ fi.ʃje də.pɥi sɔ̃.n‿ɔʁ.di.na.tœʁ
items.notes: “son” agrees with “ordinateur” (masculine), not with the owner’s gender.

items.fr: Beaucoup de jeunes passent trop de temps sur les réseaux sociaux.
items.en: Many young people spend too much time on social media.
items.ipa: bo.ku də ʒœn pas tʁo də tɑ̃ syʁ le ʁe.zo sɔ.sjo
items.notes: “réseaux” takes an x in the plural, not an s.

items.fr: J’écoute de la musique classique le soir.
items.en: I listen to classical music in the evening.
items.ipa: ʒe.kut də la my.zik kla.sik lə swaʁ
items.notes: “j’écoute” elides “je” before a vowel: never write “je écoute”.

items.fr: Ce film raconte une histoire vraie et bouleversante.
items.en: This film tells a true and moving story.
items.ipa: sə film ʁa.kɔ̃t yn is.twaʁ vʁɛ e bul.vɛʁ.sɑ̃t
items.notes: “histoire” starts with a mute h, so “une” elides normally in front of it.

items.fr: Nous fêtons son anniversaire samedi prochain.
items.en: We are celebrating his birthday next Saturday.
items.notes: “fêtons” keeps the circumflex from “fête” across the whole conjugation.

items.fr: Le gouvernement a annoncé de nouvelles mesures économiques.
items.en: The government announced new economic measures.
items.ipa: lə ɡu.vɛʁ.nə.mɑ̃ a a.nɔ̃.se də nu.vɛl mə.zyʁ e.ko.no.mik
items.notes: “gouvernement” has an easy-to-drop e right before the final ment.

items.fr: L’économie du pays dépend beaucoup du tourisme.
items.en: The country’s economy depends a lot on tourism.
items.ipa: le.ko.no.mi dy pe.i de.pɑ̃ bo.ku dy tu.ʁism
items.notes: “économie” takes an accent on the first e.

items.fr: De plus en plus de gens s’inquiètent pour l’avenir de la planète.
items.en: More and more people worry about the future of the planet.
items.ipa: də ply.z‿ɑ̃ ply də ʒɑ̃ sɛ̃.kjɛt puʁ lav.niʁ də la pla.nɛt
items.notes: “s’inquiètent” keeps the grave accent from “inquiète” through the conjugation.

items.fr: La biologie et la chimie sont ses matières préférées.
items.en: Biology and chemistry are her favorite subjects.
items.ipa: la bjɔ.lɔ.ʒi e la ʃi.mi sɔ̃ se ma.tjɛʁ pʁe.fe.ʁe
items.notes: “ses” agrees with the plural “matières”, not with “biologie” alone.

items.fr: Je suis vraiment content de te revoir.
items.en: I am really happy to see you again.
items.ipa: ʒə sɥi vʁɛ.mɑ̃ kɔ̃.tɑ̃ də tə ʁə.vwaʁ
items.notes: “content” ends in a silent t, unlike its feminine form “contente”.

items.en: He has felt tired since he quit smoking.

items.en: We have to finish this report by the end of the day.

items.en: The company is considering entering the international market.

items.fr: Il vaut mieux prendre le métro pour éviter les embouteillages.
items.en: It's better to take the subway to avoid traffic jams.

items.en: We are visiting the Eiffel Tower tomorrow morning.

items.fr: Le respect et l'honnêteté sont des valeurs essentielles pour elle.
items.en: Respect and integrity are essential values to her.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Le respect et l'honnêteté","t":"respect and integrity"},{"w":"sont","t":"are"},{"w":"des valeurs essentielles","t":"essential values"},{"w":"pour elle.","t":"to her"}]}

items.fr: Je prends un café noir le matin.
items.en: I have a black coffee in the morning.
items.ipa: ʒə pʁɑ̃ œ̃ ka.fe nwaʁ lə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: The final letters of “prends” are silent, even though they're written.

items.fr: Elle a commandé un café allongé sans sucre.
items.en: She ordered a long black coffee without sugar.
items.ipa: ɛl a kɔ.mɑ̃.de œ̃ ka.fe a.lɔ̃.ʒe sɑ̃ sykʁ
items.notes: “Commandé” ends in é because it follows “a” in the passé composé.

items.fr: Nous buvons notre café sur la terrasse quand il fait beau.
items.en: We drink our coffee on the terrace when the weather's nice.
items.ipa: nu by.vɔ̃ nɔtʁ ka.fe syʁ la tɛ.ʁas kɑ̃.t‿il fɛ bo
items.notes: “Quand il” is linked by a liaison, pronounced “kɑ̃.t‿il”.

items.fr: Ce café reste bondé bien qu'il y ait moins de touristes cet été.
items.en: This café stays packed even though there are fewer tourists this summer.
items.ipa: sə ka.fe ʁɛst bɔ̃.de bjɛ̃ kil j‿ɛ mwɛ̃ də tu.ʁist sɛ.t‿e.te
items.notes: “Ait”, the subjunctive of avoir, sounds like “est” but is spelled differently after “bien que”.

items.fr: C'est le seul café du quartier où l'on peut encore fumer en terrasse.
items.en: It's the only café in the neighborhood where you can still smoke on the terrace.
items.ipa: sɛ lə sœl ka.fe dy kaʁ.tje u lɔ̃ pø ɑ̃.kɔʁ fy.me ɑ̃ tɛ.ʁas
items.notes: “Où l'on” uses the elided “l'” before “on” for a smoother sound.

items.fr: La maison est grande et blanche.
items.en: The house is big and white.
items.ipa: la mɛ.zɔ̃ ɛ ɡʁɑ̃d e blɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: “Grande” and “blanche” take the feminine ending to agree with “maison”.

items.fr: Nous avons repeint les volets en vert cet été.
items.en: We repainted the shutters green this summer.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ʁə.pɛ̃ le vɔ.lɛ ɑ̃ vɛʁ sɛ.t‿e.te
items.notes: “Repeint” stays invariable even though “volets” is plural, since the object follows the verb.

items.fr: Le grenier est plein de vieux cartons poussiéreux.
items.en: The attic is full of old, dusty boxes.
items.ipa: lə ɡʁə.nje ɛ plɛ̃ də vjø kaʁ.tɔ̃ pu.sje.ʁø
items.notes: The final “x” of “vieux” is silent.

items.fr: Ils ont fait construire une véranda derrière la maison.
items.en: They had a veranda built behind the house.
items.ipa: il.z‿ɔ̃ fɛ kɔ̃s.tʁɥiʁ yn ve.ʁɑ̃.da dɛ.ʁjɛʁ la mɛ.zɔ̃
items.notes: “Fait” stays invariable in this causative construction with “construire”.

items.fr: La maison qu'ils ont achetée a besoin de gros travaux.
items.en: The house they bought needs major renovations.
items.ipa: la mɛ.zɔ̃ ki.l‿ɔ̃.t‿a.ʃə.te a bə.zwɛ̃ də ɡʁo tʁa.vo
items.notes: “Achetée” agrees in the feminine with “maison”, the preceding direct object.

items.fr: Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.
items.en: I get up at seven every day.
items.ipa: ʒə mə lɛv a sɛ.t‿œʁ tu le ʒuʁ
items.notes: “Lève” takes an accent grave because the stem vowel is stressed, unlike in “lever”.

items.fr: D'habitude, je me douche avant de prendre mon petit-déjeuner.
items.en: I usually shower before having breakfast.
items.ipa: da.by.tyd ʒə mə duʃ a.vɑ̃ də pʁɑ̃dʁ mɔ̃ pə.ti de.ʒœ.ne
items.notes: “D'habitude” elides “de” before the vowel of “habitude”.

items.fr: Le soir, ils regardent les informations avant de se coucher.
items.en: In the evening, they watch the news before going to bed.
items.ipa: lə swaʁ il ʁə.ɡaʁd le.z‿ɛ̃.fɔʁ.ma.sjɔ̃ a.vɑ̃ də sə ku.ʃe
items.notes: “Informations” is almost always used in the plural in French, unlike its English equivalent.

items.fr: Depuis qu'elle travaille de nuit, ses horaires ont complètement changé.
items.en: Since she started working nights, her schedule has changed completely.
items.ipa: də.pɥi kɛl tʁa.vaj də nɥi se.z‿ɔ.ʁɛʁ ɔ̃ kɔ̃.plɛt.mɑ̃ ʃɑ̃.ʒe
items.notes: “Ses horaires” is plural, so it takes “ses” rather than the singular “son”.

items.fr: Il faut qu'elle organise mieux ses journées si elle veut tout finir.
items.en: She needs to organize her days better if she wants to finish everything.
items.ipa: il fo kɛl ɔʁ.ɡa.niz mjø se ʒuʁ.ne si ɛl vø tu fi.niʁ
items.notes: “Il faut que” requires the subjunctive “organise”.

items.fr: Elle fait cuire les pâtes dans l'eau bouillante.
items.en: She's cooking the pasta in boiling water.
items.ipa: ɛl fɛ kɥiʁ le pat dɑ̃ lo bu.jɑ̃t
items.notes: “Pâtes” is always plural in French, unlike the English word for pasta.

items.fr: Il a ajouté trop de sel dans la sauce.
items.en: He put too much salt in the sauce.
items.ipa: il a a.ʒu.te tʁo də sɛl dɑ̃ la sos
items.notes: “Sel” sounds exactly like “celle”, but only “sel” fits here.

items.fr: Nous coupons les légumes en petits morceaux.
items.en: We're cutting the vegetables into small pieces.
items.ipa: nu ku.pɔ̃ le le.ɡym ɑ̃ pə.ti mɔʁ.so
items.notes: The final “s” of “légumes” and “morceaux” is silent.

items.fr: Une fois que la pâte a levé, on la met au four.
items.en: Once the dough has risen, you put it in the oven.
items.ipa: yn fwa kə la pat a lə.ve ɔ̃ la mɛ o fuʁ
items.notes: “Levé” stays invariable because “la pâte” is the subject, not a preceding direct object.

items.fr: Le chef nous a expliqué comment on obtient un caramel bien doré.
items.en: The chef explained to us how to get a nicely golden caramel.
items.ipa: lə ʃɛf nu.z‿a ɛk.sply.ke kɔ.mɑ̃.t‿ɔ̃.n‿ɔb.tjɛ̃ œ̃ ka.ʁa.mɛl bjɛ̃ dɔ.ʁe
items.notes: “Comment on” and “on obtient” both call for a liaison before the vowel that follows.

items.fr: Il joue au foot avec ses copains le samedi.
items.en: He plays soccer with his friends on Saturdays.
items.ipa: il ʒu o fut a.vɛk se kɔ.pɛ̃ lə sam.di
items.notes: “Au” is the required contraction of “à le”, never written separately.

items.fr: Elle fait de la natation trois fois par semaine.
items.en: She goes swimming three times a week.
items.ipa: ɛl fɛ də la na.ta.sjɔ̃ tʁwa fwa paʁ sə.mɛn
items.notes: “Fois” is invariable and never takes an s, even after “trois”.

items.fr: Nous avons couru un marathon l'année dernière.
items.en: We ran a marathon last year.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ku.ʁy œ̃ ma.ʁa.tɔ̃ la.ne dɛʁ.njɛʁ
items.notes: “Couru” is the irregular past participle of “courir”, not “couri”.

items.fr: Bien qu'elle se soit entraînée tous les jours, elle n'a pas gagné la course.
items.en: Even though she trained every day, she didn't win the race.
items.ipa: bjɛ̃.kɛl sə swa.t‿ɑ̃.tʁɛ.ne tu le ʒuʁ ɛl na pa ɡa.ɲe la kuʁs
items.notes: “Entraînée” agrees with the feminine subject because the reflexive pronoun acts as the object.

items.fr: Les randonneurs se sont perdus dans le brouillard pendant deux heures.
items.en: The hikers got lost in the fog for two hours.
items.ipa: le ʁɑ̃.dɔ.nœʁ sə sɔ̃ pɛʁ.dy dɑ̃ lə bʁu.jaʁ pɑ̃.dɑ̃ dø.z‿œʁ
items.notes: “Perdus” takes the masculine plural ending to agree with “les randonneurs”.

items.fr: Elle porte une robe bleue avec des chaussures blanches.
items.en: She's wearing a blue dress with white shoes.
items.ipa: ɛl pɔʁt yn ʁɔb blø a.vɛk de ʃo.syʁ blɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: “Bleue” takes an extra e to agree with the feminine “robe”.

items.fr: Il a acheté un nouveau manteau pour l'hiver.
items.en: He bought a new coat for winter.
items.ipa: il a a.ʃə.te œ̃ nu.vo mɑ̃.to puʁ li.vɛʁ
items.notes: “Pour l'hiver” elides “le” before the silent h of “hiver”.

items.fr: Ces chaussettes ne vont pas avec ce pantalon gris.
items.en: These socks don't go with these gray pants.
items.ipa: se ʃo.sɛt nə vɔ̃ pa a.vɛk sə pɑ̃.ta.lɔ̃ ɡʁi
items.notes: “Ces” takes the plural demonstrative form to agree with “chaussettes”.

items.fr: La veste qu'elle a essayée ne lui allait pas du tout.
items.en: The jacket she tried on didn't suit her at all.
items.ipa: la vɛst kɛ.l‿a ɛ.se.je nə lɥi a.lɛ pa dy tu
items.notes: “Essayée” agrees with the feminine “veste”, the preceding direct object.

items.fr: Il faudrait qu'il change de style avant l'entretien d'embauche.
items.en: He should change his style before the job interview.
items.ipa: il fo.dʁɛ kil ʃɑ̃ʒ də stil a.vɑ̃ lɑ̃.tʁə.tjɛ̃ dɑ̃.boʃ
items.notes: “Il faudrait que” calls for the subjunctive “change”.

items.fr: Elle fait les courses au marché le samedi matin.
items.en: She does her shopping at the market on Saturday mornings.
items.ipa: ɛl fɛ le kuʁs o maʁ.ʃe lə sam.di ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “Fait” sounds like “fais”, but only “fait” agrees with “elle”.

items.fr: Nous avons oublié d'acheter du pain.
items.notes: “D'acheter” elides “de” before the vowel of “acheter”.

items.fr: Il faut qu'on fasse les courses avant que les magasins ferment.
items.en: We need to do the shopping before the shops close.
items.ipa: il fo kɔ̃ fas le kuʁs a.vɑ̃ kə le ma.ɡa.zɛ̃ fɛʁm
items.notes: “Il faut que” triggers the subjunctive “fasse”, from the irregular verb “faire”.

items.fr: Les prix ont tellement augmenté que la facture nous a surpris.
items.en: Prices have gone up so much that the bill surprised us.
items.ipa: le pʁi ɔ̃ tɛ.lə.mɑ̃ oɡ.mɑ̃.te kə la fak.tyʁ nu.z‿a syʁ.pʁi
items.notes: “Augmenté” stays invariable since “les prix” is the subject, not a preceding object.

items.fr: Mon sac est resté dans le bus.
items.en: My bag stayed on the bus.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ sak ɛ ʁɛs.te dɑ̃ lə bys
items.notes: “Est” sounds like “ait”, but only “est” fits after “sac”.

items.fr: Ce stylo n'écrit plus très bien.
items.en: This pen doesn't write very well anymore.
items.ipa: sə sti.lo ne.kʁi ply tʁɛ bjɛ̃
items.notes: “N'écrit” elides “ne” before the vowel of “écrit”.

items.fr: Elle a rangé ses clés dans le tiroir du bureau.
items.en: She put her keys away in the desk drawer.
items.ipa: ɛl.z‿a ʁɑ̃.ʒe se kle dɑ̃ lə ti.ʁwaʁ dy by.ʁo
items.notes: “Ses clés” is plural, so it takes “ses” rather than the singular “sa”.

items.fr: Le vase en verre s'est cassé en tombant.
items.en: The glass vase broke when it fell.
items.ipa: lə vaz ɑ̃ vɛʁ sɛ ka.se ɑ̃ tɔ̃.bɑ̃
items.notes: “S'est cassé” uses être because it's a reflexive verb, not avoir.

items.fr: Le marchand vend des fraises fraîches ce matin.
items.en: The vendor is selling fresh strawberries this morning.
items.ipa: lə maʁ.ʃɑ̃ vɑ̃ de fʁɛz fʁɛʃ sə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “Ce” and “se” sound alike, but only “ce matin” fits as a demonstrative here.

items.fr: J'achète des légumes au marché tous les jeudis.
items.en: I buy vegetables at the market every Thursday.
items.ipa: ʒa.ʃɛt de le.ɡym o maʁ.ʃe tu le ʒø.di
items.notes: “Jeudis” keeps a silent final s even in the plural form of the day name.

items.fr: Les prix du marché ont un peu baissé cette semaine.
items.en: Market prices have gone down a little this week.
items.ipa: le pʁi dy maʁ.ʃe ɔ̃.t‿œ̃ pø bɛ.se sɛt sə.mɛn
items.notes: “Ont un” requires a liaison, pronounced “ɔ̃.t‿œ̃”.

items.fr: Elle a acheté un panier plein de tomates bien mûres.
items.en: She bought a basket full of nice, ripe tomatoes.
items.ipa: ɛl.z‿a a.ʃə.te œ̃ pa.nje plɛ̃ də tɔ.mat bjɛ̃ myʁ
items.notes: “Mûres” agrees in the feminine plural with “tomates”.

items.fr: La ville est très animée le week-end.
items.en: The city is very lively on weekends.
items.ipa: la vil ɛ tʁɛ a.ni.me lə wik.ɛnd
items.notes: “Animée” takes an e to agree with the feminine “ville”.

items.fr: Il y a un grand parc au centre-ville.
items.en: There's a big park in the city center.
items.ipa: i.l‿j‿a œ̃ ɡʁɑ̃ paʁk o sɑ̃tʁ.vil
items.notes: “Il y a” links smoothly, pronounced “i.l.j.a”.

items.fr: Les rues sont bondées pendant les heures de pointe.
items.en: The streets are packed during rush hour.
items.ipa: le ʁy sɔ̃ bɔ̃.de pɑ̃.dɑ̃ le.z‿œʁ də pwɛ̃t
items.notes: “Bondées” agrees in the feminine plural with “rues”.

items.fr: On construit une nouvelle station de métro près d'ici.
items.en: They're building a new metro station near here.
items.ipa: ɔ̃ kɔ̃s.tʁɥi yn nu.vɛl sta.sjɔ̃ də me.tʁo pʁɛ di.si
items.notes: “Près d'ici” elides “de” before the vowel of “ici”.

items.fr: Le serveur apporte l'addition à la fin du repas.
items.en: The waiter brings the check at the end of the meal.
items.ipa: lə sɛʁ.vœʁ a.pɔʁt la.di.sjɔ̃ a la fɛ̃ dy ʁə.pa
items.notes: “L'addition” elides “la” before the vowel of “addition”.

items.fr: Nous avons réservé une table pour deux personnes.
items.en: We booked a table for two.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ʁe.zɛʁ.ve yn tabl puʁ dø pɛʁ.sɔn
items.notes: “Réservé” ends in é because it follows “avons” in the passé composé.

items.fr: Le plat du jour était délicieux mais un peu cher.
items.en: The dish of the day was delicious but a bit pricey.
items.ipa: lə pla dy ʒuʁ e.tɛ de.li.sjø mɛ.z‿œ̃ pø ʃɛʁ
items.notes: “Délicieux” keeps the masculine ending to agree with “plat”.

items.fr: Est-ce que le service est compris dans l'addition ?
items.en: Is the service charge included in the bill?
items.ipa: ɛs kə lə sɛʁ.vis ɛ kɔ̃.pʁi dɑ̃ la.di.sjɔ̃
items.notes: Questions with “est-ce que” need a hyphen between “est” and “ce” and a space before the question mark.

items.fr: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Je voudrais","t":"I'd like"},{"w":"un café,","t":"a coffee,"},{"w":"s'il vous plaît.","t":"please"}]}

items.fr: Le café du coin ferme trop tôt le soir.
items.en: The corner café closes too early in the evening.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Le café du coin","t":"the corner café"},{"w":"ferme trop tôt","t":"closes too early"},{"w":"le soir.","t":"in the evening"}]}

items.fr: Bien qu'il soit tard, elle a envie d'un dernier café.
items.en: Even though it's late, she feels like having one last coffee.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Bien qu'il soit tard,","t":"even though it's late,"},{"w":"elle","t":"she"},{"w":"a envie","t":"feels like"},{"w":"d'un dernier café.","t":"having one last coffee"}]}

items.fr: Il vaut mieux boire son café avant qu'il ne refroidisse.
items.en: It's better to drink your coffee before it gets cold.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Il vaut mieux","t":"it's better to"},{"w":"boire son café","t":"drink your coffee"},{"w":"avant qu'il ne refroidisse.","t":"before it gets cold"}]}

items.fr: Elle prend toujours son café en lisant le journal.
items.en: She always has her coffee while reading the newspaper.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Elle prend toujours","t":"she always has"},{"w":"son café","t":"her coffee"},{"w":"en lisant","t":"while reading"},{"w":"le journal.","t":"the newspaper"}]}

items.fr: Ma maison a un grand jardin.
items.en: My house has a big garden.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Ma maison","t":"my house"},{"w":"a","t":"has"},{"w":"un grand jardin.","t":"a big garden"}]}

items.fr: Nous rangeons le salon tous les samedis matin.
items.en: We tidy up the living room every Saturday morning.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Nous rangeons","t":"we tidy up"},{"w":"le salon","t":"the living room"},{"w":"tous les samedis matin.","t":"every Saturday morning"}]}

items.fr: Depuis qu'ils ont changé les fenêtres, la maison garde mieux la chaleur.
items.en: Since they replaced the windows, the house keeps the heat much better.

items.en: Hi, are you doing well today?
items.notes: The “h” in “aujourd'hui” is silent, and the word is never split despite the apostrophe.

items.fr: Nous nous sommes vus hier soir, c'était sympa.
items.en: We saw each other last night, it was nice.
items.ipa: nu nu sɔm vy jɛʁ swaʁ, se.tɛ sɛ̃.pa
items.notes: “vus” takes a plural “s” because the reflexive pronoun “nous” acts as the agreeing direct object.

items.fr: Excusez-moi, est-ce que vous avez l'heure ?
items.en: Excuse me, do you have the time?
items.notes: “l'heure” elides “la” before the silent “h” of “heure”.

items.fr: Ma sœur est plus jeune que moi.
items.en: My sister is younger than me.
items.ipa: ma sœʁ ɛ ply ʒœn kə mwa
items.notes: “sœur” is spelled with the œ ligature, never “oe” or “eu”.

items.fr: Mon père travaille tous les jours sauf le dimanche.
items.en: My father works every day except Sunday.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ pɛʁ tʁa.vaj tu le ʒuʁ sof lə di.mɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: The “s” in “tous” is silent here because it precedes “les jours”; it's only pronounced when “tous” stands alone.

items.fr: Mes parents sont nés en Belgique.
items.en: My parents were born in Belgium.
items.ipa: me pa.ʁɑ̃ sɔ̃ ne ɑ̃ bɛl.ʒik
items.notes: “nés” takes an “s” because the passé composé with “être” agrees with the plural subject “mes parents”.

items.fr: Ma tante habite à côté de chez nous.
items.en: My aunt lives right next door to us.
items.ipa: ma tɑ̃t a.bit a ko.te də ʃe nu
items.notes: “à” needs a grave accent here since it's the preposition, not the verb “a” from avoir.

items.fr: Mes grands-parents se sont mariés il y a cinquante ans.
items.en: My grandparents got married fifty years ago.
items.ipa: me ɡʁɑ̃.pa.ʁɑ̃ sə sɔ̃ ma.ʁje il i a sɛ̃.kɑ̃t ɑ̃
items.notes: “il y a” never takes an apostrophe, even though it's sometimes mispronounced as if it did.
“s'appelle” elides “se” before the vowel of “appelle”.

items.fr: Elle joue avec ses amies après l'école.
items.en: She plays with her friends after school.
items.ipa: ɛl ʒu a.vɛk se.z‿a.mi a.pʁɛ le.kɔl
items.notes: “amies” sounds identical to “amis”; only the spelling shows these are female friends.

items.fr: Mon meilleur ami habite juste en face de chez moi.
items.en: My best friend lives right across from my place.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ mɛ.jœʁ a.mi a.bit ʒyst ɑ̃ fas də ʃe mwa
items.notes: “meilleur” has no final “e” because “ami” is masculine here; it would be “meilleure amie” for a female friend.

items.fr: Mes amis m'ont manqué pendant les vacances.
items.en: I missed my friends during the vacation.
items.ipa: me.z‿a.mi mɔ̃ mɑ̃.ke pɑ̃.dɑ̃ le va.kɑ̃s
items.notes: With “manquer”, the person missed is the subject, so “mes amis” takes the verb, not “me”.

items.fr: Ma collègue arrive toujours à l'heure.
items.en: My colleague always arrives on time.
items.ipa: ma kɔ.lɛɡ a.ʁiv tu.ʒuʁ a lœʁ
items.notes: “collègue” is spelled the same for men and women; only the article “ma” shows this colleague is female.

items.fr: Nous avons une réunion à neuf heures.
items.en: We have a meeting at nine o'clock.
items.notes: In “neuf heures”, the final “f” of “neuf” is pronounced like a “v” before the vowel.

items.fr: Il a envoyé le rapport hier soir.
items.en: He sent the report last night.
items.ipa: il a ɑ̃.vwa.je lə ʁa.pɔʁ jɛʁ swaʁ
items.notes: The past participle of “envoyer” is “envoyé”, keeping the “y” even though the verb stem changes.

items.fr: Mon collègue et moi avons terminé le projet à temps.
items.en: My colleague and I finished the project on time.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ kɔ.lɛɡ e mwa a.vɔ̃ tɛʁ.mi.ne lə pʁɔ.ʒɛ a tɑ̃
items.notes: “terminé” stays masculine singular because with “avoir”, the past participle doesn't agree with the subject.

items.fr: Les tâches qu'elle a accomplies étaient très difficiles.
items.en: The tasks she completed were very difficult.
items.ipa: le tɑʃ kɛl a a.kɔ̃.pli e.tɛ tʁɛ di.fi.sil
items.notes: “accomplies” takes “-es” to agree with “les tâches” (feminine plural), the direct object placed before the verb.

items.fr: Les voisins organisent une fête de quartier chaque été.
items.en: The neighbors organize a neighborhood party every summer.
items.ipa: le vwa.zɛ̃ ɔʁ.ɡa.niz yn fɛt də kaʁ.tje ʃak e.te
items.notes: The “-ent” ending of “organisent” is silent, unlike endings that sound the same in nouns.

items.fr: La mairie a ouvert un nouveau parc près de l'école.
items.en: The town hall opened a new park near the school.
items.ipa: la mɛ.ʁi a u.vɛʁ œ̃ nu.vo paʁk pʁɛ də le.kɔl
items.notes: “près” (near) has a grave accent and should not be confused with “prêt” (ready).

items.fr: Les habitants se sont mobilisés pour empêcher la fermeture de la bibliothèque.

items.ipa: le.z‿a.bi.tɑ̃ sə sɔ̃ mɔ.bi.li.ze puʁ ɑ̃.pe.ʃe la fɛʁ.mə.tyʁ də la bi.bljɔ.tɛk
items.notes: “bibliothèque” needs a grave accent on the second “e”, not an acute one.

items.fr: Le maire a promis que la place serait rénovée avant l'été.
items.en: The mayor promised that the square would be renovated before summer.
items.ipa: lə mɛʁ a pʁɔ.mi kə la plas sə.ʁɛ ʁe.nɔ.ve a.vɑ̃ le.te
items.notes: “serait” ends in “-ait” for the third-person conditional; “serai” with “-ai” would be first-person future.
