items.en: This kind of solidarity between neighbors is becoming rarer, but it still exists.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Ce genre de solidarité","t":"this kind of solidarity"},{"w":"entre voisins","t":"between neighbors"},{"w":"se fait de plus en plus rare,","t":"is becoming rarer,"},{"w":"mais elle existe encore.","t":"but it still exists"}]}
“appelle” doubles both the p and the l, unlike the infinitive “appeler”.
The final “s” in “Dubois” is silent.
Leave a space before the question mark, as in “t'appelles ?”.
“vous appelez” links with a liaison z sound.
Unlike most French endings, the final “m” in “Karim” is fully pronounced.
The ending “-in” in “Martin” makes one nasal sound, not two syllables.
“vingt” links to “ans” with a silent t that becomes pronounced.

items.fr: J'ai trente-cinq ans et je travaille comme comptable.
items.en: I am thirty-five years old and I work as an accountant.
items.ipa: ʒe tʁɑ̃t sɛ̃k ɑ̃ e ʒə tʁa.vaj kɔm kɔ̃.tabl
items.notes: “comptable” keeps a silent p between m and t.
“vingt-huit” is written with a hyphen between the two numbers.
“quarante” is spelled with a qu, not a c, at the start.
“âge” needs a circumflex accent on the a.
Leave a space before the question mark in “vous ?”.
The masculine “canadien” ends in -ien, without a final e.

items.fr: Ma collègue est canadienne, mais elle vit en France.
items.en: My colleague is Canadian, but she lives in France.
items.ipa: ma kɔ.lɛg ɛ ka.na.djɛn mɛ ɛl vi ɑ̃ fʁɑ̃s
items.notes: The feminine “canadienne” doubles the n before adding the final e.
“français” keeps a cedilla under the c to keep the soft s sound.
The feminine form adds an e and changes the final sound to “z”.

items.fr: Je suis québécois, mais je vis à Paris depuis un an.
items.en: I am Quebecois, but I have been living in Paris for a year.
items.ipa: ʒə sɥi ke.be.kwa mɛ ʒə vi a pa.ʁi də.pɥi ɛ̃.n‿ɑ̃
items.notes: “québécois” keeps an acute accent on the first e.
The feminine “québécoise” ends in -oise, unlike the masculine “québécois”.
“belge” has the same spelling for masculine and feminine.

items.fr: Ma sœur est suisse, mais elle habite au Canada.
items.en: My sister is Swiss, but she lives in Canada.
items.ipa: ma sœʁ ɛ sɥis mɛ ɛ.l‿a.bit o ka.na.da
items.notes: “sœur” is written with the œ ligature, not oe.
The masculine “étudiant” ends in a silent t.
The feminine form “étudiante” pronounces the final t, unlike the masculine.
“professeur” doubles the s to keep the sound unvoiced.
The feminine “infirmière” needs a grave accent on the second e.
“ingénieur” stays the same for both men and women in careful usage.
The final t in “avocat” is silent.
“médecin” stays masculine in form even when it refers to a woman.
“habite” starts with a silent h, so “je” elides to “j'” before it.

items.fr: J'habite à Paris depuis deux ans.
items.en: I have been living in Paris for two years.
items.notes: “depuis” with a present tense verb describes an action still going on.
The city name “Lyon” has no accent, unlike many similar-sounding words.

items.fr: Elle habite à Québec avec sa famille.
items.en: She lives in Quebec City with her family.
items.notes: “Québec” keeps its accent even as a proper noun.
The verb “habitons” ends in -ons for the “nous” form.

items.en: I live in a small apartment.
items.notes: “appartement” doubles the p, unlike the phrase “à part”.
“Où” carries a grave accent to distinguish it from “ou” meaning “or”.
“exactement” is spelled with an x, not a cs.
A man writes “né” without a final e after “suis”.

items.fr: Elle est née à Québec en 1995.
items.en: She was born in Quebec City in 1995.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿ɛ ne a ke.bɛk ɑ̃ mil nœf sɑ̃ katʁə.vɛ̃ kɛ̃z
items.notes: A woman adds an extra e to “née” to agree with “elle”.

items.ipa: i.l‿ɛ ne ɑ̃ mil nœf sɑ̃ katʁə.vɛ̃ dis
items.notes: “en” before a year is not the same word as “an”, though they sound alike.

items.fr: Elle est née le premier mai.
items.en: She was born on the first of May.
items.notes: Dates use “premier” for the first day of the month, not “un”.
“du” is used before a masculine country like “le Canada”.
“de” alone is used before a feminine country like “la France”, not “du”.
“de” elides to “d'” before the vowel in “Espagne”.
“Italie” takes one t, unlike the English spelling instinct.
“et” meaning “and” is never written with an s, unlike the verb form “es”.
“couramment” doubles the m, formed from the adjective “courant”.
The masculine “grand” ends in a silent d.
The feminine “petite” pronounces the final t, unlike the masculine “petit”.
“cheveux” takes an x in the plural, not an s.

items.fr: Elle a les cheveux longs et bruns.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿a le ʃə.vø lɔ̃ e bʁœ̃
items.notes: “longs” agrees in the plural with “cheveux”, even though the s is silent.

items.fr: J'ai les yeux bleus et les cheveux blonds.
items.en: I have blue eyes and blond hair.
items.ipa: ʒe le zjø blø e le ʃə.vø blɔ̃
items.notes: “yeux” is an irregular plural of “œil”, not “œils”.

items.fr: Mon frère a les yeux verts.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ fʁɛʁ a le zjø vɛʁ
items.notes: “verts” agrees in the plural, with a silent final s and t.
“travaille” ends in -aille, not -aye, for the “je” form.
“cuisinier” is written with an s, not a z, though it sounds voiced.

items.fr: Elle travaille à l'hôpital du centre-ville.
items.en: She works at the hospital downtown.
items.ipa: ɛl tʁa.vaj a lo.pi.tal dy sɑ̃tʁ vil
items.notes: “hôpital” carries a circumflex accent where an old s used to stand.

items.fr: Je fais des études de droit.
items.notes: “études” needs an acute accent on the first e.

items.fr: Il fait des études de médecine à Lyon.
items.en: He is studying medicine in Lyon.
items.ipa: il fɛ de.z‿e.tyd də med.sin a ljɔ̃
items.notes: “médecine” has only one e before the c, unlike “médecin”.

items.fr: Je suis en deuxième année à l'université.
items.en: I am in my second year at university.
items.ipa: ʒə sɥi.z‿ɑ̃ dø.zjɛm a.ne a ly.ni.vɛʁ.si.te
items.notes: “deuxième” takes a grave accent, not an acute one, on the e before m.

items.fr: Mon adresse est facile à retenir.
items.en: My address is easy to remember.
items.notes: “adresse” doubles the s, unlike the English spelling with two d's.
“de” elides to “d'” before the vowel in “identité”.
“Quelle” agrees in the feminine with “nationalité”, unlike “quel”.
Leave a space before the question mark, as French punctuation requires.

items.fr: Je suis retraité depuis un an.
items.en: I have been retired for a year.
items.notes: A man writes “retraité” without a final e.
The feminine “retraitée” adds a silent final e.
“agriculteur” has no accent on its first e, unlike words such as “agréable”.
“Sénégal” needs an acute accent on both e's.
“célibataire” has the same form for men and women.
A man writes “marié” with a single final e.

items.fr: Elle est mariée depuis dix ans.
items.en: She has been married for ten years.
items.notes: The feminine “mariée” adds a second, silent e.
“divorcé” needs an acute accent on the final e.

items.fr: Je suis pacsé avec mon copain.
items.en: I am in a civil partnership with my boyfriend.
items.ipa: ʒə sɥi pak.se a.vɛk mɔ̃ kɔ.pɛ̃
items.notes: “pacsé” comes from the acronym PACS and takes a final é like a past participle.
“enfant” is the same word for a boy or a girl.
“enfants” takes a silent final s in the plural.
“frères” needs a grave accent on the first e.
“cadette” doubles the t to match the feminine noun “sœur”.

items.en: I do not have any children.
items.notes: “de” elides to “d'” before the vowel in this negative sentence.
“mari” (husband) is a homophone trap next to “marié” (married).
“femme” is pronounced “fam”, not as its spelling might suggest.

items.fr: Mes parents habitent à la campagne.
items.en: My parents live in the countryside.
items.notes: “habitent” ends in a silent -ent for the “ils/elles” form.

items.fr: J'ai un chat et un chien.
items.en: I have a cat and a dog.
items.notes: “et” here is never confused with “est”, even though they sound the same.

items.fr: Nous avons un bébé depuis trois mois.
items.en: We have had a baby for three months.
items.notes: “bébé” takes two acute accents, not one.

items.en: My son is five years old.
items.notes: The final s in “fils” is pronounced, unlike most words ending in s.

items.fr: Ma fille va à l'école primaire.
items.en: My daughter goes to primary school.
items.ipa: ma fij va a le.kɔl pʁi.mɛʁ
items.notes: “à” needs a grave accent to distinguish it from “a” from the verb avoir.

items.fr: J'aime lire le soir avant de dormir.
items.en: I like to read in the evening before going to sleep.
items.ipa: ʒɛm liʁ lə swaʁ a.vɑ̃ də dɔʁ.miʁ
items.notes: “avant de” is followed directly by the infinitive “dormir”.
“week-end” keeps its English spelling with a hyphen in French.

items.fr: Je n'aime pas beaucoup le sport.
items.en: I do not like sports very much.
items.ipa: ʒə nɛm pa bo.ku lə spɔʁ
items.notes: “ne” elides to “n'” before the vowel in “aime”.
“voyager” keeps the y even before the -er ending.

items.fr: Il aime jouer au football avec ses amis.
items.en: He likes to play soccer with his friends.
items.ipa: i.l‿ɛm ʒu.e o fut.bɔl a.vɛk se.z‿a.mi
items.notes: “au” contracts “à” and “le” before “football”.
“musique” ends in -que, not -c, even though it sounds like a k.

items.fr: Le week-end, je fais du sport.
items.ipa: lə wik.ɛnd ʒə fɛ dy spɔʁ
items.notes: “fais” (from faire) sounds like “fait”, but only “fais” fits with “je”.

items.fr: Le matin, je bois du café noir.
items.en: In the morning, I drink black coffee.
items.ipa: lə ma.tɛ̃ ʒə bwa dy ka.fe nwaʁ
items.notes: “bois” (from boire) is a homophone of “bois” meaning wood.

items.fr: Le soir, je regarde la télévision et je me détends.
items.en: In the evening, I watch television and relax.
items.ipa: lə swaʁ ʒə ʁə.gaʁd la te.le.vi.zjɔ̃ e ʒə mə de.tɑ̃
items.notes: “télévision” needs two acute accents on the e's.

items.fr: Je me lève tôt tous les jours.
items.en: I get up early every day.
items.ipa: ʒə mə lɛv to tu le ʒuʁ
items.notes: “tôt” keeps a circumflex accent on the o.

items.fr: Je me couche tard le vendredi.
items.en: I go to bed late on Fridays.
items.ipa: ʒə mə kuʃ taʁ lə vɑ̃.dʁə.di
items.notes: “vendredi” is easy to misspell by dropping the silent e before dr.

items.fr: Tous les matins, je fais du vélo.
items.en: Every morning, I ride my bike.
items.ipa: tu le ma.tɛ̃ ʒə fɛ dy ve.lo
items.notes: “vélo” needs an acute accent on the first e.
“animaux” takes an x in the plural, not an s.
“déteste” needs an acute accent on the first e.

items.fr: Mon passe-temps préféré est la lecture.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ pas tɑ̃ pʁe.fe.ʁe ɛ la lɛk.tyʁ
items.notes: “passe-temps” is written with a hyphen and stays the same in the plural.

items.fr: Mon collègue aime jouer aux échecs.
items.en: My colleague likes to play chess.
items.notes: “aux” contracts “à” and “les” before “échecs”.

items.fr: Ma sœur préfère le cinéma au théâtre.
items.en: My sister prefers movies to the theater.
items.ipa: ma sœʁ pʁe.fɛʁ lə si.ne.ma o te.ɑtʁ
items.notes: “théâtre” keeps a circumflex accent on the a.
“aimons” ends in -ons for the “nous” form.

items.fr: Ils aiment se promener dans le parc.
items.en: They like to walk in the park.
items.ipa: il.z‿ɛm sə pʁɔ.mə.ne dɑ̃ lə paʁk
items.notes: “aiment” keeps a silent final -ent for the “ils” form.

items.fr: Elles adorent danser le samedi soir.
items.en: They love dancing on Saturday evenings.
items.notes: “adorent” ends in a silent -ent to agree with “elles”.

items.fr: Je fais du yoga chaque matin.
items.ipa: ʒə fɛ dy jo.ga ʃak ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: There is no elision before “yoga” since the y acts like a consonant.

items.fr: Je pratique la natation depuis dix ans.
items.en: I have been practicing swimming for ten years.
items.ipa: ʒə pʁa.tik la na.ta.sjɔ̃ də.pɥi di.z‿ɑ̃
items.notes: “natation” ends in -tion but is pronounced “sjɔ̃”, not “tjɔ̃”.

items.fr: J'apprends le français depuis six mois.
items.en: I have been learning French for six months.
items.ipa: ʒa.pʁɑ̃ lə fʁɑ̃.sɛ də.pɥi si mwa
items.notes: “apprends” doubles the p, a letter easy to drop when writing quickly.

items.en: I have been learning English for a year.
items.notes: “le” elides to “l'” before the vowel in “anglais”.

items.fr: Mon meilleur ami habite près de chez moi.
items.en: My best friend lives near my place.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ mɛ.jœʁ a.mi a.bit pʁɛ də ʃe mwa
items.notes: “meilleur” is spelled with -eille-, a common trap for this sound.

items.en: My best friend's name is Camille.
items.notes: The feminine “meilleure” adds a final e that is not pronounced.
“vis” (from vivre) ends in a silent s for the “je” form.

items.fr: Je vis seul dans un studio.
items.en: I live alone in a studio apartment.
items.notes: A man writes “seul” without a final e.

items.fr: Elle vit seule dans un studio.
items.en: She lives alone in a studio apartment.
items.notes: The feminine “seule” adds a silent final e.

items.fr: Nous vivons ensemble depuis deux ans.
items.en: We have been living together for two years.
items.notes: “vivons” comes from the irregular verb “vivre”, not a regular -er verb.

items.fr: J'ai grandi dans une petite ville.
items.en: I grew up in a small town.
items.notes: “grandi” is the past participle of “grandir”, ending in -i, not -is.
“fils” pronounces its final s, an exception among many silent-s words.

items.en: My cousin is an only child (female).
items.notes: “fille” and “fils” look related but sound completely different.

items.fr: Mon grand-père a quatre-vingts ans, mais il fait encore du sport.
items.en: My grandfather is eighty years old, but he still plays sports.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ gʁɑ̃ pɛʁ a katʁ vɛ̃.z‿ɑ̃ mɛ il fɛ ɑ̃.kɔʁ dy spɔʁ
items.notes: A comma is required before “mais” when it introduces a contrast.

items.ipa: ma gʁɑ̃ mɛʁ a.bit ʃe nu
items.notes: “grand-mère” keeps “grand” unchanged, without adding a feminine e.

items.fr: Le dimanche, je rends visite à mes grands-parents.
items.en: On Sundays, I visit my grandparents.
items.ipa: lə di.mɑ̃ʃ ʒə ʁɑ̃ vi.zit a me gʁɑ̃ pa.ʁɑ̃
items.notes: “rends” (from rendre) ends in a silent -ds for the “je” form.

items.fr: Je fais souvent la cuisine avec ma mère.
items.en: I often cook with my mother.
items.ipa: ʒə fɛ su.vɑ̃ la kɥi.zin a.vɛk ma mɛʁ
items.notes: “souvent” ends in a silent -ent, not pronounced like a verb ending.

items.fr: J'aime bien sortir avec mes amis.
items.en: I like going out with my friends.
items.notes: “mes amis” links with a liaison s pronounced as z.

items.fr: Je préfère rester à la maison le week-end.
items.en: I prefer to stay home on weekends.
items.ipa: ʒə pʁe.fɛʁ ʁɛs.te a la mɛ.zɔ̃ lə wik.ɛnd
items.notes: “préfère” has an acute accent on the first e and a grave on the second.

items.fr: Le soir, j'écoute de la musique avant de dormir.
items.en: In the evening, I listen to music before going to sleep.
items.ipa: lə swaʁ ʒe.kut də la my.zik a.vɑ̃ də dɔʁ.miʁ
items.notes: “je” elides to “j'” before the vowel in “écoute”.

items.fr: Je passe beaucoup de temps avec ma famille.
items.en: I spend a lot of time with my family.
items.ipa: ʒə pas bo.ku də tɑ̃ a.vɛk ma fa.mij
items.notes: “famille” ends in -ille, pronounced “ij”, unlike “mille” on its own.

items.fr: Je suis quelqu'un de sociable et curieux.

items.ipa: ʒə sɥi kɛl.kœ̃ də sɔ.sjabl e ky.ʁjø
items.notes: “que” elides to “qu'” before the vowel in “un”.

items.fr: Mon collègue est quelqu'un de très sympathique.
items.en: My colleague is a very nice person.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ kɔ.lɛg ɛ kɛl.kœ̃ də tʁɛ sɛ̃.pa.tik
items.notes: “sympathique” keeps the Greek-derived th spelling, though pronounced as a plain t.

“italien” doubles the n before adding e, giving “italienne”.

items.fr: Ces hommes sont bruyants le matin.
items.en: These men are noisy in the morning.
items.notes: “Ces” links to “hommes” with a z sound.

items.fr: Ces femmes sont bruyantes le soir.
items.en: These women are noisy in the evening.
items.ipa: se fam sɔ̃ bʁɥi.jɑ̃t lə swaʁ
items.notes: “bruyant” adds an e for the feminine, making the final t audible.

items.fr: Il est plus grand que son frère.
items.en: He is taller than his brother.
items.ipa: il ɛ ply ɡʁɑ̃ kə sɔ̃ fʁɛʁ
items.notes: The comparative needs “plus … que”, with “que” before the second term.

items.fr: Elle est plus petite que sa sœur.
items.en: She is shorter than her sister.
items.ipa: ɛl ɛ ply pə.tit kə sa sœʁ
items.notes: “petite” still needs the feminine e even inside a comparison.

items.fr: Ces enfants sont turbulents en classe.
items.en: These children are unruly in class.
items.notes: “turbulent” adds only an s for the masculine plural, “turbulents”.

items.fr: Ces filles sont turbulentes en classe.
items.en: These girls are unruly in class.
items.ipa: se fij sɔ̃ tyʁ.by.lɑ̃t ɑ̃ klas
items.notes: “turbulentes” makes the final t audible thanks to the feminine e.

items.fr: Le petit garçon est déjà très indépendant.
items.en: The little boy is already very independent.
items.ipa: lə pə.ti ɡaʁ.sɔ̃ ɛ de.ʒa tʁɛ.z‿ɛ̃.de.pɑ̃.dɑ̃
items.notes: “déjà” needs a grave accent on the second a.

items.fr: La petite fille est déjà très indépendante.
items.en: The little girl is already very independent.
items.ipa: la pə.tit fij ɛ de.ʒa tʁɛ.z‿ɛ̃.de.pɑ̃.dɑ̃t
items.notes: “indépendant” gets a feminine e, making the final t heard.
“discret” takes a simple s in the masculine plural, “discrets”.
“discret” takes a grave accent when it becomes feminine “discrète”.

items.fr: Cet acteur célèbre semble très discret.
items.en: This famous actor seems very discreet.
items.notes: “célèbre” mixes an acute and a grave accent, don't swap them.
“grand” takes a feminine e to agree with “table”.
The final t of masculine “petit” is silent.
“blanc” becomes “blanche” for the feminine, with c turning into ch.
The final c of masculine “blanc” is not pronounced.
“vert” adds an e to agree with feminine “porte”.
“verts” only adds a silent s for the masculine plural.
“fenêtre” needs a circumflex accent on the e.
“fermé” adds an e to agree with feminine “porte”.
The final d of “lourd” is silent in the masculine.
“lourd” adds an e so the final d is heard, “lourde”.
The final r of “léger” is silent, like a verb ending in -er.
“boîte” needs a circumflex accent on the i.
“propre” already ends in e, so it stays the same for feminine nouns.
“sale” doesn't change form between masculine and feminine.
“neuf” changes f to v before the feminine e, giving “neuve”.
Masculine “neuf” keeps the f sound, unlike its feminine form.
“pantalon” is singular in French even though it's plural in English.
“noir” adds a silent e to agree with feminine “chemise”.
“blanches” combines the feminine ch spelling with the plural s.
“rouge” already ends in e, it never changes for gender.
“verre” and “vert” are pronounced exactly the same way.
“jardin” ends in a nasal sound, don't pronounce the n separately.
“joli” takes a silent e to agree with feminine “cour”.
“plein” is a nasal sound, unlike its feminine form “pleine”.
“vide” already ends in e and stays the same for masculine or feminine.
“rond” adds an e so the final d is pronounced, “ronde”.
The final d of masculine “rond” is silent.
The final s in “tapis” is never pronounced.
“carré” adds an e to agree with feminine “nappe”.
“le” shortens to “l'” before the vowel of “appartement”.
“spacieux” becomes “spacieuse” for the feminine, not “spacieuxe”.
“bleu” takes an s for the masculine plural, “bleus”.
“cassé” adds an e to agree with feminine “chaise”.
Masculine “cassé” stays without a final e.
“propres” only adds an s for the plural, the ending sounds the same.

items.fr: Cette vieille maison a un grand jardin.
items.en: This old house has a big garden.
items.ipa: sɛt vjɛj mɛ.zɔ̃ a œ̃ ɡʁɑ̃ ʒaʁ.dɛ̃
items.notes: “vieux” becomes the irregular feminine “vieille” before “maison”.
“vieux” becomes “vieil” before a vowel sound like “immeuble”.

items.fr: La nouvelle bibliothèque est très moderne.
items.en: The new library is very modern.
items.notes: “bibliothèque” takes a grave accent on the e before the final syllable.
“nouveau” becomes “nouvel” before the silent h of “hôtel”.

items.fr: Cette table basse est en bois massif.
items.en: This low table is made of solid wood.
items.ipa: sɛt tabl bas ɛ.t‿ɑ̃ bwa ma.sif
items.notes: “bas” doubles the s to become feminine “basse”.

items.fr: Ce fauteuil ancien est en cuir marron.
items.en: This armchair is old and made of brown leather.
items.ipa: sə fo.tœj ɑ̃.sjɛ̃ ɛ.t‿ɑ̃ kɥiʁ ma.ʁɔ̃
items.notes: “marron” never changes form, even with a feminine or plural noun.

items.fr: Cette armoire est trop étroite pour mes vêtements.
items.en: This wardrobe is too narrow for my clothes.
items.ipa: sɛt aʁ.mwaʁ ɛ tʁo e.tʁwat puʁ me vɛt.mɑ̃
items.notes: “étroit” adds an e to agree with feminine “armoire”.

items.fr: Le couloir est étroit et sombre.
items.en: The hallway is narrow and dark.
items.ipa: lə ku.lwaʁ ɛ e.tʁwa e sɔ̃bʁ
items.notes: The final t of masculine “étroit” is silent.

items.fr: Ce quartier semblait calme avant la construction du pont.
items.en: This neighborhood seemed calm before the bridge was built.
items.ipa: sə kaʁ.tje sɑ̃.blɛ kalm a.vɑ̃ la kɔ̃.stʁyk.sjɔ̃ dy pɔ̃
items.notes: “semblait” is the imperfect of “sembler”, spelled -ait, not -é.

items.fr: Cette rue est bruyante le matin.
items.en: This street is noisy in the morning.
items.ipa: sɛt ʁy ɛ bʁɥi.jɑ̃t lə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “bruyant” adds an e for feminine “rue”, making the t audible.

items.fr: La cave est humide et froide.
items.en: The cellar is damp and cold.
items.ipa: la kav ɛ y.mid e fʁwad
items.notes: “froid” adds an e to agree with feminine “cave”.

items.fr: Le grenier est sec, mais le sous-sol est humide.
items.en: The attic is dry, but the basement is damp.
items.ipa: lə ɡʁə.nje ɛ sɛk mɛ lə su.sɔl ɛ y.mid
items.notes: Put a comma before “mais” when it joins two contrasting clauses.

items.fr: Les fenêtres sont trop hautes pour les nettoyer.
items.en: The windows are too high to clean.
items.ipa: le fə.nɛtʁ sɔ̃ tʁo ot puʁ le ne.twa.je
items.notes: “haut” becomes “hautes” to agree with feminine plural “fenêtres”.

items.fr: Le plafond est trop bas dans cette pièce.
items.en: The ceiling is too low in this room.
items.ipa: lə pla.fɔ̃ ɛ tʁo ba dɑ̃ sɛt pjɛs
items.notes: Both the d in “plafond” and the s in “bas” stay silent.

items.fr: Cette boîte en carton est déjà pleine.
items.en: This cardboard box is already full.
items.ipa: sɛt bwat ɑ̃ kaʁ.tɔ̃ ɛ de.ʒa plɛn
items.notes: “plein” loses its nasal sound and gains an n sound as feminine “pleine”.

items.fr: Cette bouteille en plastique est presque vide.
items.en: This plastic bottle is almost empty.
items.ipa: sɛt bu.tɛj ɑ̃ plas.tik ɛ pʁɛsk vid
items.notes: “vide” stays exactly the same whether the noun is masculine or feminine.

items.fr: Le pont est long et étroit.
items.en: The bridge is long and narrow.
items.ipa: lə pɔ̃ ɛ lɔ̃ e e.tʁwa
items.notes: The g of masculine “long” is never pronounced.

items.fr: La rivière est large et calme.
items.en: The river is wide and calm.
items.ipa: la ʁi.vjɛʁ ɛ laʁʒ e kalm
items.notes: “large”, unlike “long”, doesn't change spelling for feminine nouns.

items.fr: Ces vieux meubles sont encore solides.
items.en: These old pieces of furniture are still solid.
items.notes: “vieux” stays “vieux” in the masculine plural, it doesn't become “vieuxs”.

items.fr: Cette montre ancienne fonctionne encore bien.
items.en: This old watch still works well.
items.ipa: sɛt mɔ̃tʁ ɑ̃.sjɛn fɔ̃k.sjɔn ɑ̃.kɔʁ bjɛ̃
items.notes: “ancien” doubles the n before adding e, giving “ancienne”.

items.fr: Le nouveau quartier est propre et sûr.
items.en: The new neighborhood is clean and safe.
items.ipa: lə nu.vo kaʁ.tje ɛ pʁɔpʁ e syʁ
items.notes: “sûr” needs a circumflex, otherwise it reads as the preposition “sur”.

items.fr: La vieille église est fermée le lundi.
items.en: The old church is closed on Mondays.
items.ipa: la vjɛj e.ɡliz ɛ fɛʁ.me lə lœ̃.di
items.notes: “vieille” stays feminine even though “église” starts with a vowel.

items.fr: Ce village paisible attire les touristes.
items.ipa: sə vi.laʒ pɛ.zibl a.tiʁ le tu.ʁist
items.notes: “paisible” already ends in e, so it never changes for gender.

items.fr: L'hôtel est complet pour tout le week-end.
items.en: The hotel is fully booked for the whole weekend.
items.ipa: lo.tɛl ɛ kɔ̃.plɛ puʁ tu lə wik.ɛnd
items.notes: “le” shortens to “l'” before the silent h of “hôtel”.

items.fr: Ce vieux pont en pierre traverse la rivière.
items.en: This old stone bridge crosses the river.
items.ipa: sə vjø pɔ̃ ɑ̃ pjɛʁ tʁa.vɛʁs la ʁi.vjɛʁ
items.notes: “vieux” keeps its full form before a consonant like “pont”, unlike before a vowel.

items.en: My grandfather is seventy years old.

items.fr: Ma petite sœur a cinq ans.
items.en: My little sister is five years old.

items.fr: Mon frère est grand, mais il est timide.

items.fr: Le nouvel élève est sympathique et très drôle.
items.en: The new student is nice and very funny.

items.fr: Ma tante est petite, mais elle est très forte.
items.en: My aunt is short, but she is very strong.

items.fr: Le vieil homme marche lentement, il a quatre-vingts ans.
items.en: The old man walks slowly, he is eighty years old.

items.fr: Cette fille est sérieuse quand elle travaille.
items.en: This girl is serious when she works.

items.fr: Mon patron est calme, il ne parle pas beaucoup.
items.en: My boss is calm, he doesn't talk much.

items.fr: La vendeuse est toujours polie avec les clients.
items.en: The saleswoman is always polite with customers.

items.fr: Le nouvel employé est timide, mais il est très gentil.
items.en: The new employee is shy, but he is very kind.

items.fr: J'ai un ami qui est très drôle.
items.en: I have a friend who is very funny.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"J'ai"},{"w":"un ami"},{"w":"qui est"},{"w":"très"},{"w":"drôle."}]}

items.fr: Elle a un frère qui est grand et fort.
items.en: She has a brother who is tall and strong.

items.fr: C'est un homme qui porte toujours un chapeau.
items.en: He is a man who always wears a hat.

items.fr: Ma sœur est douce, mais elle est parfois têtue.
items.en: My sister is gentle, but she is sometimes stubborn.

items.fr: Le professeur est patient avec les élèves difficiles.
items.en: The teacher is patient with difficult students.

items.fr: Cette dame âgée a de longs cheveux blancs.
items.en: This elderly lady has long white hair.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Cette dame âgée"},{"w":"a"},{"w":"de longs cheveux"},{"w":"blancs."}]}

items.fr: Mon petit frère est curieux de tout.
items.en: My little brother is curious about everything.

items.fr: Cet homme est un peu nerveux avant l'examen.
items.en: This man is a bit nervous before the exam.

items.fr: Elle est optimiste, même quand la journée est difficile.
items.en: She is optimistic, even when the day is hard.

items.fr: Nous sommes fiers de notre équipe.
items.en: We are proud of our team.

items.fr: Ils sont paresseux le week-end, mais actifs en semaine.
items.en: They are lazy on weekends, but active during the week.

items.fr: Ma grand-mère est petite, elle a quatre-vingt-dix ans.
items.en: My grandmother is short, she is ninety years old.

items.fr: Le directeur est sérieux au travail, mais drôle avec ses amis.
items.en: The manager is serious at work, but funny with his friends.

items.fr: Cette femme porte des lunettes et elle a les cheveux courts.
items.en: This woman wears glasses and has short hair.

items.fr: Mon oncle est grand et il a une voix grave.
items.en: My uncle is tall and has a deep voice.
The twins look a lot alike.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Les jumeaux"},{"w":"se ressemblent"},{"w":"beaucoup."}]}

items.fr: Elle est timide en public, mais bavarde avec ses amis.
items.en: She is shy in public, but talkative with her friends.

items.fr: La cuisine est spacieuse, elle a une grande fenêtre.
items.en: The kitchen is spacious, it has a big window.

items.fr: Le quartier est tranquille le soir.
items.en: The neighborhood is quiet in the evening.

items.fr: Le restaurant est cher, mais la nourriture est délicieuse.
items.en: The restaurant is expensive, but the food is delicious.

items.fr: La rivière est profonde près du pont.
items.en: The river is deep near the bridge.

items.fr: La rue est bruyante pendant la journée.
items.en: The street is noisy during the day.

items.fr: La voiture est rapide, mais elle est vieille.
items.en: The car is fast, but it is old.

items.fr: L'usine est grande et elle est loin du centre-ville.
items.en: The factory is big and it is far from downtown.

items.fr: La ferme est près de la rivière.
items.en: The farm is near the river.

items.fr: Le musée est à côté de la gare.
items.en: The museum is next to the station.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Le musée"},{"w":"est à côté de"},{"w":"la gare."}]}

items.fr: La pharmacie est en face de l'école.
items.en: The pharmacy is across from the school.

items.fr: La banque est entre le café et la boulangerie.
items.en: The bank is between the café and the bakery.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"La banque"},{"w":"est entre"},{"w":"le café"},{"w":"et"},{"w":"la boulangerie."}]}

items.fr: Les clés sont sur la table.
items.en: The keys are on the table.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Les clés"},{"w":"sont"},{"w":"sur la table."}]}

items.fr: Le chat est sous la chaise.
items.en: The cat is under the chair.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Le chat"},{"w":"est"},{"w":"sous la chaise."}]}

items.fr: La valise est dans le placard.
items.en: The suitcase is in the closet.
The park is behind the school.

items.fr: Le cinéma est près de la gare.
items.en: The cinema is near the station.
The apartment is on the third floor.

items.fr: La maison est de taille moyenne.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"La maison"},{"w":"est"},{"w":"de taille moyenne."}]}

items.fr: Le canapé est en bon état, mais il est un peu vieux.
items.en: The couch is in good condition, but it is a bit old.

items.fr: Le miroir est cassé depuis hier.
items.en: The mirror has been broken since yesterday.

items.fr: Le tapis est coloré et très doux.
items.en: The rug is colorful and very soft.

items.fr: L'immeuble est ancien, mais il est bien entretenu.
items.en: The building is old, but it is well maintained.

items.fr: La place du village est calme le matin.
items.en: The village square is quiet in the morning.

items.fr: La bibliothèque est fermée le lundi.
items.en: The library is closed on Mondays.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"La bibliothèque"},{"w":"est fermée"},{"w":"le lundi."}]}

items.fr: Elle va au marché le matin.
items.en: She goes to the market in the morning.
items.ipa: ɛl va o maʁ.ʃe lə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “va” is the “il/elle” form of aller and has no final -s, unlike “tu vas”.

items.fr: Je vais à l'école à pied.
items.ipa: ʒə vɛ a le.kɔl a pje
items.notes: The irregular stem in “vais” doesn't share its spelling with the infinitive “aller”.

items.fr: Ils vont avec nous au parc.
items.en: They are going with us to the park.
items.notes: The final “t” of “vont” is pronounced before the vowel in “avec”.

items.fr: Je suis allée au cinéma hier soir.
items.en: I went to the movies last night.
items.ipa: ʒə sɥi a.le o si.ne.ma jɛʁ swaʁ
items.notes: “allée” takes a silent extra e because the speaker is female and the auxiliary is être.

items.fr: Nous allions à la piscine chaque samedi.
items.en: We used to go to the pool every Saturday.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.ljɔ̃ a la pi.sin ʃak sam.di
items.notes: The imperfect ending on “allions” is -ions, not the present -ons.

items.fr: Elles sont allées voir un film ensemble.
items.en: They went to see a movie together.
items.ipa: ɛl sɔ̃.t‿a.le vwaʁ œ̃ film ɑ̃.sɑ̃bl
items.notes: “allées” agrees in both gender and number with the feminine plural subject “elles”.

items.fr: Quand il pleut, on va rarement au marché en plein air.
items.en: When it rains, we rarely go to the open-air market.
items.ipa: kɑ̃.t‿il plø, ɔ̃ va ʁaʁ.mɑ̃ o maʁ.ʃe ɑ̃ plɛ̃.n‿ɛʁ
items.notes: “on” always takes the same verb form as “il”, so it is “va”, never “vais” or “vont”.

items.fr: Quand j'étais enfant, j'allais souvent chez mon oncle.
items.en: When I was a child, I often went to my uncle's house.
items.ipa: kɑ̃ ʒe.tɛ.z‿ɑ̃.fɑ̃, ʒa.lɛ su.vɑ̃ ʃe mɔ̃.n‿ɔ̃kl
items.notes: “allais” is spelled with -ais for the imperfect, unlike the past participle “allé”.

items.fr: Tu viens avec moi ce soir ?
items.en: Are you coming with me tonight?
items.ipa: ty vjɛ̃ a.vɛk mwa sə swaʁ
items.notes: “viens” and “vient” sound identical, so only the subject shows who is speaking.
The final t of “vient” is never pronounced.

items.fr: Il est venu nous voir dimanche.
items.en: He came to see us on Sunday.
items.notes: “venu” stays in its plain masculine singular form here, with no extra e.

items.fr: Vous veniez souvent nous rendre visite.
items.en: You used to come visit us often.
items.ipa: vu və.nje su.vɑ̃ nu ʁɑ̃dʁ vi.zit
items.notes: The imperfect stem “ven-” in “veniez” takes -iez, not the present -ez.

items.en: I am going to come before noon.
items.notes: After the conjugated “vais”, the second verb “venir” stays in the infinitive.

items.fr: Bien qu'elle soit fatiguée, elle est venue nous aider.
items.en: Even though she was tired, she came to help us.
items.ipa: bjɛ̃.kɛl swa fa.ti.ɡe, ɛ.l‿ɛ və.ny nu.z‿e.de
items.notes: “venue” takes a final e because it agrees with the feminine subject “elle”.

items.fr: Ils venaient nous voir dès qu'ils avaient un moment libre.
items.en: They used to come see us whenever they had a free moment.
items.ipa: il və.nɛ nu vwaʁ dɛ.kil a.vɛ.z‿œ̃ mo.mɑ̃ libʁ
items.notes: The ending -aient in “venaient” is always silent.

items.fr: Je prends le bus tous les jours.
items.en: I take the bus every day.
items.ipa: ʒə pʁɑ̃ lə bys tu le ʒuʁ
items.notes: The ending -ds in “prends” is completely silent.

items.fr: Il prend son café le matin.
items.en: He has his coffee in the morning.
items.ipa: il pʁɑ̃ sɔ̃ ka.fe lə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “prend” sounds exactly like “prends”, though the final letters differ.

items.ipa: nu pʁə.nɔ̃ lə pə.ti de.ʒø.ne ɑ̃.sɑ̃bl
items.notes: The d of “prendre” disappears in “prenons”, unlike in “il prend”.

items.fr: Elle a pris le train ce matin.
items.en: She took the train this morning.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿a pʁi lə tʁɛ̃ sə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: The past participle of “prendre” is the irregular form “pris”, not “prendu”.

items.fr: Tu prenais toujours le même chemin.
items.en: You always used to take the same path.
items.ipa: ty pʁə.nɛ tu.ʒuʁ lə mɛm ʃə.mɛ̃
items.notes: “prenais” is built on the plural stem “pren-”, not on “prend-”.

items.fr: Ils vont prendre une décision importante.
items.en: They are going to make an important decision.
items.notes: “prendre” stays an infinitive after the conjugated “vont” and never takes an ending.

items.fr: Nous avons pris cette décision ensemble, même si cela n'a pas été facile.
items.en: We made this decision together, even though it wasn't easy.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ pʁi sɛt de.si.zjɔ̃ ɑ̃.sɑ̃bl, mɛm si sə.la na pa e.te fa.sil
items.notes: “pris” stays invariable because its direct object “cette décision” comes after the verb, not before it.

items.fr: Elles prenaient des notes pendant que le professeur parlait.
items.en: They were taking notes while the teacher was talking.
items.ipa: ɛl pʁə.nɛ de nɔt pɑ̃.dɑ̃ kə lə pʁɔ.fɛ.sœʁ paʁ.lɛ
items.notes: The ending -aient in “prenaient” is never pronounced.

items.fr: Je fais mes devoirs après le dîner.
items.en: I do my homework after dinner.
items.ipa: ʒə fɛ me də.vwaʁ a.pʁɛ lə di.ne
items.notes: “fais” is written the same for “je” and “tu”, and the pronunciation is identical too.

items.fr: Elle fait la cuisine le dimanche.
items.ipa: ɛl fɛ la kɥi.zin lə di.mɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: “fait” ends in a silent t that is never heard.

items.fr: Vous faites du sport le samedi ?
items.en: Do you play sports on Saturdays?
items.ipa: vu fɛt dy spɔʁ lə sam.di
items.notes: The “vous” form of “faire” is the irregular “faites”, not “faisez”.
Despite the spelling ai, “faisons” is pronounced with an eu sound, not è.

items.fr: Il a fait beau toute la semaine.
items.en: The weather was nice all week.
items.ipa: i.l‿a fɛ bo tut la sə.mɛn
items.notes: The past participle of “faire” is the irregular form “fait”, not “faisé”.

items.fr: Tu faisais souvent la sieste l'après-midi.
items.en: You often used to take a nap in the afternoon.
items.ipa: ty fə.zɛ su.vɑ̃ la sjɛst la.pʁɛ.mi.di
items.notes: “faisais” keeps the eu sound of “faisons” even though it is written with ai.

items.fr: Nous allons faire des efforts pour que la réunion se passe bien.
items.en: We are going to make an effort so that the meeting goes well.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.lɔ̃ fɛʁ de.z‿e.fɔʁ puʁ kə la ʁe.y.njɔ̃ sə pas bjɛ̃
items.notes: “faire” remains an unconjugated infinitive after “allons”.

items.fr: Elles ont fait de leur mieux, même si le résultat n'était pas parfait.
items.en: They did their best, even though the result wasn't perfect.
items.ipa: ɛl.z‿ɔ̃ fɛ də lœʁ mjø, mɛm si lə ʁe.zyl.ta ne.tɛ pa paʁ.fɛ
items.notes: “fait” stays invariable with “avoir” because there is no direct object placed before it.

items.fr: Je mets mon manteau avant de sortir.
items.en: I put on my coat before going out.
items.ipa: ʒə mɛ mɔ̃ mɑ̃.to a.vɑ̃ də sɔʁ.tiʁ
items.notes: Both final letters of “mets” are silent, giving simply the sound [mɛ].

items.fr: Elle met la table pour le dîner.
items.en: She sets the table for dinner.
items.ipa: ɛl mɛ la tabl puʁ lə di.ne
items.notes: “met” and “mets” are pronounced exactly the same way.

items.en: They put on their shoes quickly.
items.notes: “mettent” keeps the double t of the infinitive, but its final -ent is silent.

items.fr: J'ai mis mes clés sur la table.
items.en: I put my keys on the table.
items.ipa: ʒe mi me kle syʁ la tabl
items.notes: The past participle of “mettre” is the short irregular form “mis”, not “mettu”.

items.fr: Nous mettions nos bottes avant de sortir dans la neige.
items.en: We used to put on our boots before going out in the snow.
items.ipa: nu mɛ.tjɔ̃ no bɔt a.vɑ̃ də sɔʁ.tiʁ dɑ̃ la nɛʒ
items.notes: “mettions” keeps the double t from “mettre”, which is easy to forget when writing.

items.fr: Tu vas mettre ta veste, il fait froid.
items.en: You are going to put on your jacket, it's cold.
items.ipa: ty va mɛtʁ ta vɛst, il fɛ fʁwa
items.notes: After the conjugated “vas”, “mettre” stays an infinitive rather than becoming “mets”.

items.fr: La robe qu'elle a mise était très élégante.
items.en: The dress that she wore was very elegant.
items.ipa: la ʁɔb kɛ.l‿a miz e.tɛ tʁɛ.z‿e.le.ɡɑ̃t
items.notes: “mise” agrees in the feminine with “la robe”, its preceding direct object.

items.fr: Je sors avec mes amis ce soir.
items.en: I'm going out with my friends tonight.
items.ipa: ʒə sɔʁ a.vɛk me.z‿a.mi sə swaʁ
items.notes: The final s of “sors” is never pronounced.

items.fr: Il sort du travail à dix-huit heures.
items.en: He leaves work at six p.m.
items.ipa: il sɔʁ dy tʁa.vaj a di.zɥi.t‿œʁ
items.notes: “sort” and “sors” are pronounced the same, only the subject tells them apart.

items.en: We go out together on weekends.
items.notes: The final n sound of “sortons” links onto the vowel of “ensemble”.

items.fr: Elle est sortie tôt ce matin.
items.en: She went out early this morning.
items.notes: “sortie” takes a final e because the subject “elle” is feminine.

items.fr: Vous sortiez souvent le soir à cette époque.
items.en: You used to go out often in the evenings back then.
items.ipa: vu sɔʁ.tje su.vɑ̃ lə swaʁ a sɛ.t‿e.pɔk
items.notes: “sortiez” is the imperfect “vous” form, built on the stem “sort-” plus -iez.

items.en: They are going to go out for some fresh air.
items.notes: “sortir” stays an infinitive here and is never conjugated after “vont”.

items.fr: Elle a sorti la poubelle avant que les voisins arrivent.
items.en: She took out the trash before the neighbors arrived.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿a sɔʁ.ti la pu.bɛl a.vɑ̃ kə le vwa.zɛ̃.z‿a.ʁiv
items.notes: “sortir” takes “avoir” instead of “être” when it has a direct object, as in “sorti la poubelle”.

items.fr: Je reste à la maison aujourd'hui.
items.ipa: ʒə ʁɛst a la mɛ.zɔ̃ o.ʒuʁ.dɥi
items.notes: “reste” keeps a silent s before the t, easy to drop when writing.

items.en: She stays calm during the exam.
items.notes: “le” shortens to “l'” before the vowel of “examen”.

items.fr: Ils restent dans le jardin l'après-midi.
items.en: They stay in the garden in the afternoon.
items.ipa: il ʁɛst dɑ̃ lə ʒaʁ.dɛ̃ la.pʁɛ.mi.di
items.notes: The ending -ent of “restent” is completely silent.

items.fr: Nous sommes restés à l'hôtel trois nuits.
items.en: We stayed at the hotel for three nights.
items.ipa: nu sɔm ʁɛs.te a lo.tɛl tʁwa nɥi
items.notes: “restés” takes a final s to agree with the plural subject “nous”.

items.fr: Tu restais toujours silencieux en classe.
items.en: You always used to stay quiet in class.
items.ipa: ty ʁɛs.tɛ tu.ʒuʁ si.lɑ̃.sjø ɑ̃ klas
items.notes: “restais” (imperfect) is easy to confuse with “resterais” (conditional), which adds an extra syllable.

items.fr: Elle va rester chez elle ce week-end.
items.en: She is going to stay home this weekend.
items.ipa: ɛl va ʁɛs.te ʃe.z‿ɛl sə wi.kɛnd
items.notes: “rester” stays in the infinitive after the conjugated “va”.

items.fr: Elles sont restées à l'écart, bien qu'elles aient été invitées.
items.en: They stayed apart, even though they had been invited.
items.ipa: ɛl sɔ̃ ʁɛs.te a le.kaʁ, bjɛ̃.kɛl.z‿ɛ e.te.z‿ɛ̃.vi.te
items.notes: “restées” takes both a feminine and plural ending to agree with “elles”.

items.fr: Je pars à huit heures demain.
items.en: I'm leaving at eight o'clock tomorrow.
items.notes: The final s of “pars” is pronounced as a liaison z before the vowel of “à”.

items.fr: Il part en vacances la semaine prochaine.
items.en: He is going on vacation next week.
items.ipa: il paʁ ɑ̃ va.kɑ̃s la sə.mɛn pʁɔ.ʃɛn
items.notes: The verb form “part” sounds exactly like the noun “part” meaning a share.

items.en: We leave early in the morning.
items.notes: “tôt” needs its circumflex accent to distinguish it from other similar-sounding words.

items.fr: Elle est partie sans dire au revoir.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿ɛ paʁ.ti sɑ̃ diʁ o ʁə.vwaʁ
items.notes: “partie” takes a final e to agree with the feminine subject “elle”.

items.en: You always used to leave before us.
items.notes: “partiez” (imperfect) is easy to mix up with “partez” (present), which drops the i.

items.fr: Ils vont partir en train ce soir.
items.en: They are going to leave by train tonight.
items.ipa: il vɔ̃ paʁ.tiʁ ɑ̃ tʁɛ̃ sə swaʁ
items.notes: “partir” remains an infinitive and is never conjugated after “vont”.

items.fr: Nous sommes partis dès que la réunion s'est terminée.
items.en: We left as soon as the meeting ended.
items.ipa: nu sɔm paʁ.ti dɛ kə la ʁe.y.njɔ̃ sɛ tɛʁ.mi.ne
items.notes: “partis” takes a final s to agree with the plural subject “nous”.

items.en: I'll be there in five minutes.
items.notes: “je” shortens to “j'” before the vowel of “arrive”.

items.fr: Le train arrive à quinze heures.
items.en: The train arrives at three p.m.
items.notes: The final z sound of “quinze” links onto the vowel of “heures”.

items.fr: Elle est arrivée en retard ce matin.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿ɛ a.ʁi.ve ɑ̃ ʁə.taʁ sə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: “arrivée” ends in a silent e added because the subject “elle” is feminine.

items.en: They always used to arrive first.
items.notes: The ending -aient in “arrivaient” is never pronounced aloud.

items.fr: Vous allez arriver juste à temps.
items.en: You are going to arrive just in time.
items.notes: “arriver” stays an infinitive after the conjugated “allez”.

items.fr: Elles sont arrivées avant que le magasin ferme.
items.en: They arrived before the store closed.
items.ipa: ɛl sɔ̃.t‿a.ʁi.ve a.vɑ̃ kə lə ma.ɡa.zɛ̃ fɛʁm
items.notes: “arrivées” takes both a feminine and plural ending to agree with “elles”.

items.fr: Je dis toujours la vérité à mes parents.
items.en: I always tell my parents the truth.
items.ipa: ʒə di tu.ʒuʁ la ve.ʁi.te a me pa.ʁɑ̃
items.notes: The final s of “dis” is never pronounced.

items.fr: Elle dit bonjour à tout le monde.
items.ipa: ɛl di bɔ̃.ʒuʁ a tu lə mɔ̃d
items.notes: “dit” and “dis” sound exactly the same.

items.fr: Vous dites la même chose que lui.
items.en: You say the same thing as him.
items.ipa: vu dit la mɛm ʃoz kə lɥi
items.notes: The “vous” form of “dire” is the irregular “dites”, not “disez”.

items.fr: Il a dit merci en partant.
items.en: He said thank you as he left.
items.notes: The past participle of “dire” is the irregular form “dit”.

items.fr: Nous disions bonjour chaque matin au gardien.
items.en: We used to say hello to the caretaker every morning.
items.ipa: nu di.zjɔ̃ bɔ̃.ʒuʁ ʃak ma.tɛ̃ o ɡaʁ.djɛ̃
items.notes: “disions” is built on the stem “dis-” plus the imperfect ending -ions.

items.fr: Elles ont dit qu'elles seraient en retard à cause de la circulation.
items.en: They said they would be late because of traffic.
items.ipa: ɛl.z‿ɔ̃ di kɛl sə.ʁɛ.z‿ɑ̃ ʁə.taʁ a koz də la siʁ.ky.la.sjɔ̃
items.notes: “dit” stays invariable with “avoir” even though the subject “elles” is feminine plural.

items.fr: Je parle français avec mes amis.
items.en: I speak French with my friends.
items.notes: The final e of “parle” is silent, so no extra vowel sound is added.

items.fr: Tu parles trop vite pour moi.
items.en: You speak too fast for me.
items.ipa: ty paʁl tʁo vit puʁ mwa
items.notes: “parles” and “parle” are pronounced the same way despite the different spelling.

items.en: They speak English at the office.
items.notes: The ending -ent in “parlent” is completely silent.

items.fr: Elle a parlé à son professeur hier.
items.en: She spoke to her teacher yesterday.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿a paʁ.le a sɔ̃ pʁɔ.fɛ.sœʁ jɛʁ
items.notes: The past participle “parlé” ends in é, unlike the infinitive “parler”.

items.en: You used to speak louder before.
items.notes: “parliez” is spelled with an i before -ez to mark the imperfect.

items.fr: Nous parlions rarement de politique quand nous étions ensemble.
items.en: We rarely talked about politics when we were together.
items.ipa: nu paʁ.ljɔ̃ ʁaʁ.mɑ̃ də pɔ.li.tik kɑ̃ nu.z‿e.tjɔ̃.z‿ɑ̃.sɑ̃bl
items.notes: “parlions” is pronounced with two syllables at the end, even though it looks like it could be three.

items.fr: Je pense que c'est une bonne idée.
items.en: I think that's a good idea.
items.notes: “pense” sounds just like “panse” (belly), but only one fits after “je”.

items.en: He is thinking about his vacation.
items.notes: “penser” needs the preposition à when thinking about something, and it is often dropped by mistake.
The ending -ent of “pensent” adds no extra sound.

items.fr: Tu as pensé à moi, merci.
items.en: You thought of me, thank you.
items.ipa: ty a pɑ̃.se a mwa, mɛʁ.si
items.notes: The past participle “pensé” ends in é, showing it follows “as”.

items.en: We were thinking of leaving earlier.
items.notes: “pensions” (from “penser”) sounds the same as the noun “pensions” (retirement payments).

items.fr: Je pense que tu devrais lui parler avant qu'il parte.
items.en: I think you should talk to him before he leaves.
items.ipa: ʒə pɑ̃s kə ty də.vʁɛ lɥi paʁ.le a.vɑ̃.kil paʁt
items.notes: “avant que” calls for the subjunctive “parte”, not the indicative “part”.

items.fr: Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.
items.ipa: ʒə vø.n‿œ̃ ka.fe, sil vu plɛ
items.notes: “veux” ends in x, not the s one might expect.
The final t of “veut” is always silent.

items.fr: Ils veulent partir en voyage cet été.
items.en: They want to go on a trip this summer.
items.ipa: il vœl paʁ.tiʁ ɑ̃ vwa.jaʒ sɛ.t‿e.te
items.notes: “veulent” changes its stem to “veul-” for the plural, unlike the singular “veut”.

items.en: I wanted to help you yesterday.
items.notes: The past participle of “vouloir” is the irregular form “voulu”.

items.en: You always wanted to be right.
items.notes: “voulais” is built on the stem “voul-”, not on the present singular “veu-”.

items.fr: Nous voulons partir avant que la nuit tombe.
items.en: We want to leave before nightfall.
items.ipa: nu vu.lɔ̃ paʁ.tiʁ a.vɑ̃ kə la nɥi tɔ̃b
items.notes: “avant que” requires the subjunctive “tombe”, not the future “tombera”.
“peux” ends in x, not the s one might expect.
“peut” sounds like “peu” (a little), only with a silent final t added.
The z sound of “pouvez” links onto the vowel that starts “entrer”.

items.fr: Elle n'a pas pu venir à la fête.
items.en: She could not come to the party.
items.ipa: ɛl na pa py və.niʁ a la fɛt
items.notes: “pu” never changes form, even for a feminine subject like “elle”.

items.fr: Nous ne pouvions pas sortir à cause de la pluie.
items.en: We could not go out because of the rain.
items.ipa: nu nə pu.vjɔ̃ pa sɔʁ.tiʁ a koz də la plɥi
items.notes: “ne” and “pas” wrap around the conjugated verb “pouvions”, not around an infinitive.

items.fr: Ils peuvent réussir s'ils travaillent sérieusement.
items.en: They can succeed if they work hard.
items.ipa: il pœv ʁe.y.siʁ sil tʁa.vaj se.ʁjøz.mɑ̃
items.notes: “peuvent” changes its stem to “peuv-” for the plural, unlike the singular “peut”.

items.en: I have to leave early tomorrow.
items.notes: The final s of “dois” is never pronounced.

items.en: She has to finish her work.
items.notes: “doit” sounds exactly like “doigt” (finger), though the spelling is different.

items.en: We have to call the doctor.
items.notes: “devons” uses the stem “dev-”, which is different from the singular stem “doi-”.

items.fr: Il a dû annuler son rendez-vous.
items.en: He had to cancel his appointment.
items.notes: “dû” needs its circumflex accent to be told apart from the article “du”.

items.en: You were supposed to arrive at noon.
items.notes: “deviez” is built on the plural stem “dev-”, plus the imperfect ending -iez.

items.fr: Elles ont dû partir plus tôt parce que le vol avait été avancé.
items.en: They had to leave earlier because the flight had been moved up.
items.ipa: ɛl.z‿ɔ̃ dy paʁ.tiʁ ply to paʁs kə lə vɔl a.vɛ.t‿e.te a.vɑ̃.se
items.notes: “dû” keeps its masculine singular form here and never becomes “dues”, even with a feminine plural subject.

items.en: I have known how to swim since childhood.
items.notes: “sais” sounds exactly like “ses” and “c'est”.

items.en: He knows how to speak three languages.
items.notes: The final t of “sait” is never heard.

items.fr: Nous savons que la réponse est correcte.
items.en: We know the answer is correct.
items.ipa: nu sa.vɔ̃ kə la ʁe.pɔ̃.z‿ɛ kɔ.ʁɛkt
items.notes: “savons” uses the stem “sav-”, different from the singular stem “sai-”.

items.fr: Elle a su garder son calme, même si la situation était tendue.
items.en: She managed to stay calm, even though the situation was tense.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿a sy ɡaʁ.de sɔ̃ kalm, mɛm si la si.tɥa.sjɔ̃ e.tɛ tɑ̃.dy
items.notes: The past participle of “savoir” is the short irregular form “su”.

items.fr: Ils savaient que la réunion allait être annulée.
items.en: They knew the meeting was going to be canceled.
items.ipa: il sa.vɛ kə la ʁe.y.njɔ̃ a.lɛ.t‿ɛtʁ a.ny.le
items.notes: The ending -aient in “savaient” is always silent.

items.fr: Vous savez bien que ce projet demande du temps.
items.en: You know very well that this project takes time.
items.ipa: vu sa.ve bjɛ̃ kə sə pʁɔ.ʒɛ də.mɑ̃d dy tɑ̃
items.notes: “savez” (present) is easy to confuse with “saviez” (imperfect) when listening quickly.
“connais” is written with a double n and a silent final s.

items.fr: Elle connaît toutes les rues du village.
items.en: She knows all the streets in the village.
items.ipa: ɛl kɔ.nɛ tut le ʁy dy vi.laʒ
items.notes: “connaît” needs a circumflex accent on the î before the t, unlike “connais”.

items.fr: Nous connaissons ce restaurant depuis longtemps.
items.en: We have known this restaurant for a long time.
items.ipa: nu kɔ.nɛ.sɔ̃ sə ʁɛs.to.ʁɑ̃ də.pɥi lɔ̃.tɑ̃
items.notes: “connaissons” adds a double ss before the ending, unlike the singular forms.

items.fr: Ils ont connu des difficultés avant que la situation s'améliore.
items.en: They experienced difficulties before the situation improved.
items.ipa: il.z‿ɔ̃ kɔ.ny de di.fi.kyl.te a.vɑ̃ kə la si.tɥa.sjɔ̃ sa.me.ljɔʁ
items.notes: The past participle “connu” has only one n, unlike the infinitive “connaître”.

items.fr: Vous connaissiez cette histoire avant qu'on vous la raconte ?
items.en: Did you know this story before someone told it to you?
items.ipa: vu kɔ.nɛ.sje sɛ.t‿is.twaʁ a.vɑ̃.kɔ̃ vu la ʁa.kɔ̃t
items.notes: “avant que” calls for the subjunctive “raconte”, not the future “racontera”.

items.fr: Elles connaissent bien ce sujet, car elles l'ont étudié en détail.
items.en: They know this subject well, because they studied it in detail.
items.ipa: ɛl kɔ.nɛs bjɛ̃ sə sy.ʒɛ, kaʁ ɛl lɔ̃.n‿e.ty.dje ɑ̃ de.taj
items.notes: “le” shortens to “l'” before the vowel of “ont” in “elles l'ont étudié”.

items.en: I think it's going to rain.
items.notes: “crois” sounds exactly like “croix” (cross).

items.fr: Il croit tout ce qu'on lui dit.
items.ipa: il kʁwa tu sə kɔ̃ lɥi di
items.notes: The final t of “croit” is silent, unlike the y that appears in “croyons”.
A y appears in “croyons” before the plural ending, unlike in the singular “crois”.

items.fr: Elle a cru comprendre la situation avant qu'on lui explique les détails.
items.en: She thought she understood the situation before the details were explained to her.
items.ipa: ɛ.l‿a kʁy kɔ̃.pʁɑ̃dʁ la si.tɥa.sjɔ̃ a.vɑ̃.kɔ̃ lɥi ɛks.plik le de.taj
items.notes: The past participle “cru” sounds just like the adjective “cru” meaning raw.

items.fr: Ils croyaient que le magasin fermait plus tard.
items.en: They thought the store closed later.
items.ipa: il kʁwa.jɛ kə lə ma.ɡa.zɛ̃ fɛʁ.mɛ ply taʁ
items.notes: “croyaient” keeps the y from “croyons” even in the imperfect.

items.fr: Vous croyez vraiment qu'il dira la vérité ?
items.en: Do you really believe he will tell the truth?
items.ipa: vu kʁwa.je vʁɛ.mɑ̃ kil di.ʁa la ve.ʁi.te
items.notes: “croyez” inserts the same y as “croyons”, unlike the singular forms.
The ending -ds in “comprends” is entirely silent.
“comprend” is pronounced the same as “comprends”.
The d of “comprendre” disappears in “comprenons”.

items.fr: Il a compris pourquoi elle était fâchée.
items.en: He understood why she was upset.
items.notes: The past participle of “comprendre” is the irregular form “compris”, not “comprendu”.

items.fr: Elles ne comprenaient pas pourquoi le train avait du retard.
items.en: They didn't understand why the train was late.
items.ipa: ɛl nə kɔ̃.pʁə.nɛ pa puʁ.kwa lə tʁɛ̃ a.vɛ dy ʁə.taʁ
items.notes: “ne” and “pas” frame the conjugated verb “comprenaient” rather than an infinitive.

items.fr: Vous comprenez cette règle, même si elle semble compliquée ?
items.en: Do you understand this rule, even though it seems complicated?
items.ipa: vu kɔ̃.pʁə.ne sɛt ʁɛɡl, mɛm si ɛl sɑ̃bl kɔ̃.pli.ke
items.notes: “comprenez” drops the d found in the infinitive “comprendre”.

items.fr: Je vais à l'école à pied.
items.en: I go to school on foot.

items.fr: Nous allons au marché le samedi.
items.en: We go to the market on Saturdays.
She is going to her grandmother's.

items.fr: Vous allez au parc avec les enfants.
items.en: You are going to the park with the children.

items.fr: Ils sont allés en Espagne l'été dernier.
items.en: They went to Spain last summer.

items.fr: Je vais bientôt changer de travail.
items.en: I am soon going to change jobs.

items.fr: Elle allait souvent au théâtre quand elle était jeune.
items.en: She often used to go to the theater when she was young.

items.fr: Nous connaissons cette histoire depuis longtemps.

items.fr: Il a connu des moments difficiles cette année.
items.en: He went through difficult times this year.

items.fr: Connaissez-vous un bon restaurant près d'ici ?
items.en: Do you know a good restaurant near here?

items.fr: Plus je le connais, plus je l'apprécie.
items.en: The more I know him, the more I like him.

items.en: She already knew the answer even before asking the question.

items.fr: Je crois qu'il fait beau demain.
items.en: I think it will be sunny tomorrow.

items.fr: Nous croyons que ce plan peut fonctionner.

Do you really believe he will come?

items.fr: Même si c'est difficile à croire, l'histoire est vraie.

items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Même si c'est difficile à croire,","t":"even though it's hard to believe,"},{"w":"l'histoire est vraie.","t":"the story is true"}]}

items.en: She firmly believed that everything would eventually work out.

items.fr: Elle pense que c'est une bonne idée.

We are thinking of leaving early tomorrow.

items.fr: Il a pensé à toi pendant tout le voyage.
items.en: He thought of you during the whole trip.

items.fr: Nous pensions que tu étais déjà parti.
items.en: We thought you had already left.

She knows how to speak three languages.

items.en: Do you know where the station is?
